Drift Place What happens to a person-name Pick from
Conservative Threnmaieth, pious Maiethorn The old church sound, kept whole. You hear the th. Maethaem (MAY-thaym), Reimaethe (RYE-may-theh), Thilim (THIL-im), Rithnali (rith-NAH-lee), Valein (vah-LAYN)
Worn Vaethorn, Heskoren folk The th softens. Endings simplify. Nathdo (NATH-doh), Saelid (SAY-lid), Tora, Seine (SAY-neh), Nethiro (neth-EE-ro)
Eroded Lestrand, Strandoren docks Clipped. The th has gone to t or d, or dropped. Valen, Tilim, Mataero (mah-TAY-ro), Ledan, Sorel

Devout places keep the old th, the thorn, which is the th of thin and never the th of the. In worn speech, when that thorn sits between two vowels or right after a vowel, it commonly becomes t, endings simplify, and unstressed vowels flatten. Written Vaethorn is spoken Wetorn. Careful prayer puts the thorn back for as long as the prayer is open. On the docks the thorn becomes t or d, or drops, long vowels clip, and word-ends wear off. A name that still has the th comes from a devout place. A name that has dropped it comes from a dock.

To make a new common-tongue name, start from one of the lists above and keep that drift’s sounds. A named power uses the same roots and the drift that matches how it stands. It does not get a new language unless it refused the Tree. Vaelhesk keeps the older vael and the frontier hesk-, and that is this same speech, worn further. The isle of Kumbaan already has its own speech, and it is the exception.

Stress follows the Old Tongue rule under How to Say It. A compound you can still hear as two roots stresses the first root. The stress marked on first use is the one to trust.

How a place speaks

A traveller can say Turning Tree, the Mother, a hug, a colour, a tree-warden, and a graft, and be understood on every mainland road. The Turning Tree is the shared name for the Tree. The Mother is the one the pious core calls Maieth in the street and the docks call the old rite. A colour is what a Tree speaks when it can already speak one, and a hug is the no-colour, the embrace that leaves a child without a Condition. A tree-warden is the person named with that Tree, under a different word in each column below. A graft is wood that has been brought and set and cannot yet Turn. Use the common words and you will be understood. The table is what a place says when it is being itself, rather than reaching for the word a stranger would already understand.

The pious core keeps the thorn, waiting towns soften that thorn to t, and the docks drop it. Kumbaan speaks a language of its own. Mainlanders call that isle the Sundering Isle, the old liturgical tongue belongs to the mainland, and the hill was never part of it.

Conservative — pious core Worn — waiting lands, the live front Eroded — the docks Kumbaan — the hill
the Tree the Mother’s Hand the Thallow Tallo (TAL-oh) the far tree
the Mother Maieth (MY-eth) Mait (MAYT) the old rite the loud story
a hug a keeping a hug a clear the place
a colour the colour the gift the fall a test
a warden the Reckoned Hands Hands-folk a tree-tender the loud guest
a graft a Hand carried in a carried Thallow a carrying their cutting

A neighbour in Maiethlir or the Tallied Crown says Maieth in the street, the way another town says the Mother, and the polity’s own street-name is still the Tallied Crown. A polity is a land with its own way of standing. The Mother’s Hand is the Tree that can already speak a colour. Wood that has been brought and set, and cannot yet Turn, is a Hand carried in, and at the rite they call the no-colour a keeping. The Tallied Crown’s clerks file that child as unmarked. That word belongs to the desk, and the square does not use it. Maiethvael shares Maieth and the Mother’s Hand, and calls the warden a tree-warden. The Reckoned Hands is the crown’s word for the same person.

Careful prayer in a waiting town puts the thorn back, and Maieth returns for as long as the prayer is open. The kitchen says Mait, which is Maieth with the thorn tired, and the Thallow is their name for the Tree. A colour is the gift, and a no-colour is still a hug, which they do not dress as a prize. Young wood on the road is a carried Thallow. On the live front, a young graft or a neighbour’s canopy such as Harrow’s Green, people say the wood until that wood can Turn.

Tallo is how a quay says the Thallow once the thorn is gone. Say it on the water, and keep it off the charter, because the written name stays the Turning Tree, or the old liturgical name when the paper is a rite. They call her the old rite, and they call a no-colour a clear: the child came up clear, and is free to be hired. A warden there is a tree-tender. A scion in the hold, their word for a graft being carried, is a carrying. Trenledd is this speech with a list behind it. The gate asks the house, and the gate will not put the thorn back to be polite.

Ndenjoo, a hall on the hill, has a table, and it has no Tree and no graft, so it does not grow a word that would put one in the valley. The far tree and their cutting are mainland things, said of someone else’s country. The loud story is what they call the Mother when a guest brings her up, a tale about being chosen, told at noon-volume. The place is what they offer where a mainlander expects a hug. A test is their word for a colour, and they will not use one on a guest. A warden who climbs the hill is the loud guest, and is still fed.

A scene uses one of four ways of talking. Each one is a sentence length, the thing they say again, and the thing they will not say while mixed company is present. Each mainland drift still has one phrase it says whole, and the hill has its own. Nobody stops to translate them.

In a devout square, which is the speech of Threnmaieth, of Maiethlir, and of the Inner Close when the room is a household rather than a file, people use two sentences, and the first one finishes. If that first sentence left the Mother’s Hand or Maieth out, the second puts them back. A fragment sounds like the dock, and they will hear it. What they say again is Maieth, and the Mother’s Hand. While the room is mixed they will not say Tallo, the old rite, or a clear, and they will not say unmarked while the rite is still open, because that word belongs to the desk. They will not lead with a house-name to a neighbour, and they will not joke a colour. While the room is mixed, they greet a neighbour by the given name. A player who needs the sound can say the line below, and then stop. The last words are the phrase, left whole.

“The Mother’s Hand kept her. We say Maieth before the square moves. Lei thulen.” (lay THOO-len)

On a dock, which is Lestrand, Orentel, and the Ledger Coast quays, and Trenledd when the list is what is speaking, people give about six words to a breath, and they take another breath only if the number or the berth needs it. Then the phrase, and the quay lets it go. What they say again is clear, and the number, and the berth. What they repeat is the last hard fact, not a person’s feelings about it. They will not say Maieth or the Mother’s Hand, they will not restore a thorn to sound devout, and they will not call a clear a sadness. They will not ask what house? while the paper is shut. While a filing house has the paper open, they will, house first and then the given name, and they still will not hymn it. They speak the dock form, with the old th gone.

“Clear. Berth five. The fall’s on Tallo. Ka doven.” (kah DOV-en)

One tone covers the waiting towns and the live front, and the two of them repeat different words. Waiting towns, the Waiting Lands and Eolvaeth among them, say again the week that has not come. The live front, Harrow’s Green or a young graft or a neighbour’s canopy, says the wood again. They use one sentence, and that sentence does not close the week. Twelve words is already long for them. They reach for the old word and let the thorn thin. Waiting speech says not this week. The live front says the wood, and then the neighbour if the wood will not speak. They call their Tree the Thallow. They will not promise the week, they will not say the old rite, and they will not offer a house-name. They will not call the Thallow Tallo, because that is the coast, and on this road it sounds like a slight. Prayer puts the thorn back. The kitchen keeps the tired form to itself.

“Not this week, and the Thallow is still the Thallow. Len soret.” (len so-RET)

The live front uses the same length and the same phrase, and the other repeat.

“The wood first, and the neighbour if the wood won’t. Len soret.”

A hill-hall on Kumbaan, Ndenjoo and any attic that is still keeping the table, keeps a night pace. The welcome is the whole of what they are willing to say about it with guests in the room. They spend three short sentences on that welcome, a welcome, then a pause, then one practical thing, and they do not explain a Tree inside it. What they say again is sit, and the place. They will not read a test, they will not point to a graft on the hill, and they will not ask of where? or what house? as the price of a seat. They will not say Maieth, and a mainland house-name, or a mainland of-the-town, is not the name they use at the table. A newcomer is seated on that welcome. The hill’s own phrase stays inside it, untranslated.

“Sit. The place is set. Aman ndo.” (ah-MAHN ndoh)

Names for the Four Custom Kinds

Kitsune, Selkie, Tengu, and Yumboe keep a hearth-register for given names, kin, and in-group talk. On the street they still wear the local second name. You can often hear both homes in one introduction. The own-names, the names the peoples use for themselves, are settled. The common-tongue names outsiders say, Kitsune, Selkie, Tengu, and Yumboe, stay.

Each register is a naming-language: a sound, a short recipe, and a list, rather than a grammar. Nobody writes sentences in Kusawe, Sakoa, or Gonan. If a scene needs an in-group word, coin one word from that Kind’s sounds and say what it means in the same breath.

The tables are how you check a new name. A beat is one syllable. C is a consonant and V is a vowel, so CV is a consonant and then a vowel, the way Ra is, and CVC closes on another consonant, the way Tek does. When the table says F, that is the consonant allowed to end the beat, and it names which ones. A prenasal is the hum on the front of a stop, mb and nd and nj and nk. Ai, ea, and oa are glides, two vowels spoken as one. An onset is whatever consonants begin the word. A sound in the forbidden row already belongs to another home, and the register does not take it.

The lists are what you pick from. To make another is only for when you need a name that is not on the list. Make one that could sit next to the others without anyone blinking.

Kitsune: Kusawe (koo-SAH-way)

A Kitsune hearth-name sounds light, slipping, and a little sibilant, full of s and sh, the sort of name that slips round the corner of a sentence.

At the table

  • Consonants k s sh n r m t w y f h
  • Vowels a i u e o ai
  • Syllables CV · CVF (F = n/m/r) · 2–3 syllables
  • Forbidden th (Maiethren sacred), prenasals mb/nd/nj (Yumboe), kr/gr (Tengu)

Pick from: Raki, Nenyu, Wishi, Kiraye, Suti, Hatu, Ranyu, Sinro, Foryo, Heka, Sofan.

The hearth-name is the one they answer to when someone is trying to pin them down. They consider this funny. A fox raised devout in Threnmaieth, where the clerk says the house first, may still be Raki at home and Maethaem, Raki on the roll.

To make another: two or three short beats, using k, s, sh, n, r, m, t, w, y, f, h, and the vowels a, i, u, e, o, plus ai as in eye, and you can end on n, m, or r. Leave th to the church, kr and gr to the Tengu, and mb, nd, and nj to the Yumboe.

Selkie: Sakoa (sah-KOH-ah)

A Selkie hearth-name sounds liquid, rounded, and coastal. You can say it with cold air in your mouth.

At the table

  • Consonants l r n m s v f d b k w
  • Vowels o u a ea oa i e
  • Syllables CV · CVC · 2–3 syllables
  • Forbidden th, sh, kr/gr, prenasals

Pick from: Lavo, Fesa, Moka, Dovo, Neson, Foaro, Veakea, Didel, Roadoa, Woanun, Laknea.

The day a child is first given the run of their own skin is when the hearth-name is spoken to the water. The civic second name comes later, from the town that watched them Turn, a byname, or a house-name if that town writes people down. Two homes, two names, and they do not consider this a conflict.

To make another: two or three beats, using l, r, n, m, s, v, f, d, b, k, w, and the vowels o, u, a, i, e, plus ea and oa. Leave th, sh, kr, gr, and the prenasals to the homes that already use them.

Tengu: Gonan (GO-nan)

A Tengu hearth-name is clipped, windy, and high-country. The names are shorter, and they start hard, on a single consonant or on an onset such as kr, gr, and hr, said as if the wind might take the end. This is ridge-speech, and it does not sound like Kusawe.

At the table

  • Consonants k t g n r h s b d · onsets kr gr hr
  • Vowels a o u e (few i — that vowel lives in Kusawe)
  • Syllables CVC · CV · 1–3 syllables, prefer 2
  • Forbidden th, sh, prenasals, long ai/ea/oa glides

Pick from: Teku, Kukra, Gobak, Hosen, Kotak, Buka, Rekren, Kuhos, Hrarat, Gonan.

Gonan is also the people-name. Reusing it as a given name is a hearth-honor, like naming a child after the ridge.

To make another: prefer two beats, using k, t, g, n, r, h, s, b, d, with kr, gr, and hr at home at the front, and the vowels a, o, u, and e. Few i, because that vowel lives with the foxes. Leave th, sh, the prenasals, and the long ai, ea, and oa glides to the other homes.

Yumboe

Yumboe is its own tongue. Open vowels, a drum-like rhythm, and mb, nd, nk, nj at the start of a beat. A Yumboe name sounds foreign the instant it is spoken. The Trees never crossed the storm-wall, so the speech stayed the island’s own, and it owes nothing to the Leaf-Mother’s liturgy.

They call themselves Bakhna Rakhna, the good people, and their home is Kumbaan (koom-BAHN), the hidden home, which mainlanders call the Sundering Isle.

Pick from: Ambaa, Njeela, Kumbo, Sambanka, Ndeya, Mbaraan, Njunda, Rakhilo, Sonkaa, Mbindaa, Yumbaka, Ndoolu, Sambiyo, Lunji, Yaaba, Saalo, Mbela, Soonke, Njili, Yendo, Waandi, Koriwaa.

To make another: keep the open vowels and the mb, nd, nk, and nj. No th, and no clipping it down to a Lestrand dock-name. They keep the one register on the mainland.

How to Say It

CAPS is the stressed beat. Mark it the first time, then drop it.

  • ae = “ay” as in day
  • ai and ei = “eye”
  • eo = an “ay-oh” glide
  • a as in father · e as in bed · i as in machine · o as in go · u as in moon
  • th as in thin, never as in the

The Old Tongue feels warm and weighty, a hall-and-hearth tongue. The liquids and the nasals carry the warmth, l and r and m and n. The thorn and the long vowels carry the weight. The consonants in use are m, n, l, r, w, j, p, t, k, b, d, g, f, v, s, h, and th. The vowels are a, e, i, o, u, plus the two-letter sounds ae, ai, ei, and eo.

A word may open on a consonant, and it may open on one of a small inherited set of clusters, consonants that already begin an old word together: br, kr, st, str, and th followed by r. Those are the shapes in bren, crae, stel, strand, and thren. A word may close on a single consonant, and the inherited closings include sk and nd, which is how hesk is licensed. Do not invent a three-consonant opening except str-, and do not invent a four-consonant knot. A new root should prefer the simpler shape. If you cannot say it at the table, it is the wrong name.

A simple root keeps the stress listed for it. A compound you can still hear as two roots takes its main stress on the first root, with a lighter beat on the second: THAEL-oren, VAETH-orn. Old ceremonial forms, and personal names, may keep a stress of their own, the stress that word already had before anyone compounded it. When that happens, the pronunciation given on first use is the one to trust.

How to Name a Place or a Hall

The Old Tongue is Maiethren (MAI-eth-ren), Mother-speech, the church language of the Awakening Tree. It is this world’s Latin. Nobody grows up speaking it at the market, and it is still the language of the Tree, the rite, and the law’s oldest words. Everyone who is not speaking as the devout calls it the Old Tongue. Place-names, crowns, and old offices are built from it. Everyday talk uses plain compounds. People say the Kept, the ranging, and tree-wardens, and you should hear those as worn Old Tongue rather than as a separate language. The common handle is the name spoken at a dock, on a road, in a market, and at the table. It is not a translation sitting after the “real” name. Liturgical forms stay real. They belong to writing, to ritual, and to the moment someone deliberately uses the older form. No new liturgical names are being made.

To name something old or official:

  1. Pick one or two old words from the list below.
  2. Glue them together. Thaeloren is thael + oren. That is Tree and witness.
  3. Wear it the way the land wears it. A devout land keeps the th and the long vowels. A frontier town softens them. A dock town wears the th and the long vowels away. The most worn name belongs to the least-devout place.
  4. Mark the stress on first use.

Same building, three names, and the name shows the stance. A devout land calls the Far-Voiced hall a gift-hall. A merchant coast calls it a release-house. Threnmaieth calls it a counted hall. The lookup tables below are that fact, row by row. Kumbaan’s names are Yumboe, and Kumbaan is not in this box of old words.

The old words

These are the blocks names are built from. The meaning is what the word meant in the rite, even when a dock town has kept the sound and let the meaning slide. A suffix is an ending, and ren used as a suffix means “the speech of” whatever stands in front of it. A month-root is a root the calendar already took. Strand is a loan, a word that arrived from another shore and was made ordinary before the daughter speeches divided. Where the notes contrast thren with ledd, thren is sacred counting, a stewardship reckoned before the Mother, and ledd is the commercial twin, the ledger and the sum. The list is small and settled. No new roots are being added.

Root Says Meaning Where it already sits
oren OR-en to witness; to speak true Citizenship is witnessed, and to witness is to speak truly.
ren ren speech, tongue As a suffix, “the speech of.” Maiethren is Mother-speech.
thael thayl the Tree; sacred motherwood The Turning Tree itself.
maieth MY-eth the Mother The Leaf-Mother, as the faith names her.
vael vayl a gift Given. Older: what the land yields A Condition handed down. The Old Ways say that is a narrowing. The frontier still uses vael for a harvest, a child returned from water, a person the hill kept.
vaeth vayth the waiting; the longing The Kept, and the pilgrim’s wait.
hael hayl whole, hale, sound Untithed wholeness, being kept whole.
thren thren to count, to tally, to number Sacred counting, stewardship before the Mother.
ledd led to reckon, to account The ledger and the sum. The secular twin of thren.
orn orn land, ground, a holding A held or settled land.
neth neth night; the long dark A month-root.
eol AY-ohl a hinge; the year’s turning A month-root, and the liturgical name of the First Cut: Eoloren.
bren bren hearth; the kept fire A month-root.
lir leer thaw; water that runs again A month-root.
sael sayl sowing; the first green A month-root. Not vael (a gift) and not hael (wholeness). Also the greens-keepers’ root.
ael ayl to air; to let feeling out The Far-Voiced outlet, the ael-hall. Not sael, and not hael.
stel stel to still; to hold from moving The Stilled’s craft.
crae kray craft; the working of an element The Answered shops as a sector.
hesk hesk far, outer edge Frontier coinage, not in the old liturgy. The liturgy is older than this grafting. Heskoren, Vaelhesk.
strand strand shore, strand, landing-coast Kept in Strandoren, Lestrand, and Netstrand.

One name carries the setting. The Awakening Tree’s liturgical name is Thaeloren (THAEL-or-en), thael for the Tree set beside oren for witnessing, so the name means the Tree that witnesses. To witness, in this tongue, is to speak truly, and citizenship-by-witness is that witnessing folded into the name of the Tree. Everyday, people say the Thallow.

Each daughter speech is the Old Tongue worn by distance from the Trees and from the faith, a later speech descended from this root, and the changes are regular enough that any old word can be pushed through them. Conservative speech, in Threnmaieth and the pious core, barely moved, so it still sounds like the rite: archaic, formal, and holy. Worn speech, in Vaethorn and on the devout frontier, is rough-warm folk-speech that still reaches for the old holy words. Eroded speech, on Lestrand and the secular coast, is smooth, clipped, and mercantile. The most-drifted sound belongs to the least-devout place.

Closer to the Tree the old sound stays, and farther out the th wears away.

Vaethorn (VAETH-orn; spoken worn Wetorn) joins vaeth, the waiting, to orn, land, and means the Waiting Land. Careful writing and prayer keep the sacred th, ordinary speech wears it down to t, and people say the Waiting Lands, or simply the Waiting.

Lestrand (LES-trand) joins ledd, to reckon, to strand, the shore, and then wears the compound smooth, so the name means the Reckoning Coast. It is the most worn of the original three. People say the Ledger Coast, and formal records keep Lestrand.

Threnmaieth (THREN-mai-eth) joins thren, sacred counting, to maieth, the Mother, and means the Mother’s Reckoning. The pious core keeps the full sacred sound, and it names its census as reverent stewardship of Her gifts. People say the Tallied Crown, and the crown writes Threnmaieth.

The other twelve are built on the same lever, so the written name is the stance you can hear.

On pious Maiethorn the old sound stays. Maiethvael (MAI-eth-vael) keeps maieth and joins it to vael, so the name is the Mother’s Gift, gift rather than count. Orenbren (OREN-bren) is oren and bren, the witnessing-hearth, and it stays clear of brenhael, which is an inn. Saelthael (SAEL-thael) is sael and thael, the sown Tree, and it stays clear of Saelorn, which is a month, and of Saelhael, the greens-keepers. The Hinge Shore is the common name that replaced the retired Eolstrand, a compound that had crowded Eoloren, Eolthael, and Eolvaeth. Current speech and current writing use the common name. Lirorn (LIR-orn) is lir and orn, thaw-land, and it stays clear of Liren and of Ornthael.

On the eroded shore the sacred count will not be said whole. Brenledd (BREN-ledd) sets bren beside ledd, hearths of the ledger, and that name is the compact. Leddvael (LEDD-vael) is ledd and vael, the gift reckoned, and it stays clear of Leddoren and of Leddhael. Trenledd (TREN-ledd) is thren worn down beside ledd, and the reconstruction Threnledd goes unused, because they will not say the holy word. Netstrand (NET-strand) is neth worn down beside strand, the reconstruction Nethstrand goes unused, and people there will not say why the name means night.

On worn Heskoren the sacred th survives in careful writing and thins in the mouth. Ornled (ORN-led) is orn and ledd clipped. On this continent, dropping th is a neglect, so the reconstruction Ornledd goes unused. Vaelhesk (VAEL-hesk) sets vael, in the older sense of what the land yields, beside the frontier hesk-, and it stays clear of Vaeloren and of Vaethorn. The fight is in the first syllable, vael against vaeth. Saelvaeth (SAEL-vaeth) joins sael to vaeth and means sowing into the waiting, and it shares sael with Saelthael on purpose. Kumbaan is not a sixteenth name on this list.

Faiths are named from the same blocks, so a faith sounds like the land that keeps it. Haelthael (HAEL-thael) sets hael, whole and hale, beside thael, the Tree, and means the Tree kept whole, which is what the Watching calls the Tree from before anyone gave it a mother’s name, and its people are the Watchers. Leddoren (LEDD-or-en) is ledd joined to oren, the witnessed account, because the Fair Hand takes the Tree as a signing-table, and its people are the Book-hands. Vaeloren (VAEL-or-en) is vael in the older sense plus oren, the land’s witnessing, which the Old Ways keep, and its people are the door-keepers and the Kin-speakers. Ndeyaan (ndey-AHN) owes this liturgy nothing. It is the Yumboe night-keeping, not Maiethren, and it is the Open Table’s own name, whose people are the table-keepers and the hill-hosts.

The houses that work the faith are named from the same box, and no new ones are being made. Tree-wardens write themselves Orenhael (OREN-hael), witness beside whole, because they speak the fall truly and keep the Tree hale. Road-hands are Thaelvaeth (THAEL-vaeth) when the rite names them, the Tree gone to the waiting. Watchers are Nethoren (NETH-or-en), the night-witnesses. They are not written Haeloren, which would sit too close to Orenhael. Book-hands are Leddhael (LEDD-hael), the accounted-whole. Orenledd was not used, because it collides with Orledd, the Counterparty, the other party named in a Bound’s bargain. Door-keepers are Vaelbren (VAEL-bren). Here vael keeps the older sense, the land’s yield, and beside bren, the hearth, the name means the yield-hearth. It is not Vaelorn, which belongs to the Taking. Njaalo (NJAH-lo) is a Yumboe coinage, not Maiethren, and it means the hall that is kept, the own-name of the table-keepers. The isle’s name for the shore-sitters, also outside Maiethren, is Njawaal (njah-WAHL). The Slide’s cant is Vaethledd (VAETH-ledd), the waiting reckoned. A cant is the house’s other name, neither the everyday word nor the compound a charter writes. Vaethledd is not Orledd, and it is not Nethledd, which was retired with the Back Table, a Slide name that stayed unused.

Greens-keepers are Saelhael (SAEL-hael) in the liturgy, the sown-whole, and that name is not Saelorn, which is a month. Aeloren is retired, because it collided with Vaeloren, Leddoren, and Eoloren, and it never carried information that hall-keepers or ael-hands did not carry better. Old rosters may preserve it as a crossed-out form, and no living house claims it. Stillers are Stelhael (STEL-hael), the held-whole. The Crae (kray) is simply crae, craft, and it is the umbrella over the element-guilds, one name set over the houses rather than a separate liturgy for each. There are four doors under it, and those four do not each receive a liturgy. The Intake has no liturgical name, and its cant is the catching-year. Hall-keepers have no current liturgical form.

Era-names come from the same old words. Brenvaeth (BREN-vaeth) is the Walking Years, the hearth gone to the waiting, and the compound is a deliberate inversion of Thaelvaeth. People walked in, and later the wood walked out. Eoloren (EOL-or-en) is the First Cut, the witnessed hinge, and the same name serves the clerical year-count, the Eoloren-count or the Cut-years. It is not Eolthael, which is a month. Ornthael (ORN-thael) is the Years of Hands, Tree-land. That name is not Maiethorn, the Motherland, and it is not Haelthael, the Watching. Before the Walk stays mostly unnamed on the mainland roads. The Watching keep the Before. Kumbaan keeps moons rather than this count.

A Walking-era road-house has the cant brenhael (BREN-hael), the hearth kept whole, the inn that kept you hale through the waiting, and the everyday word is road-house. The cant is not Brenvaeth, which is the era, and it is not Brenorn, which is a month. The three walks stay in the common tongue on purpose, the Near Mile, the Salt Walk, and the Long Mile, because they were logistics before they were liturgy.

The nameless knife and the nameless green are folk objects of the First Cut, and they have no liturgical form on purpose. Naming the green would pick a hearth, and a hearth would pick a hand, so the everyday name comes first and stays. The generation of argument is the run of summers from the first taking to the first local Leaf-Fall, the stretch when the First Seat could not undo the graft and had not yet written permission for grafting. It stays in the common tongue because it was a quarrel, not a rite. It is not Eoloren, and it is not Brenvaeth.

The extra mile, the First-Hand year, and the neighbour’s week are the walk’s three jobs in the Years of Hands. They stay in the common tongue because they are jobs, not a fourth age. They are not Brenvaeth, which is the requirement, and they are not Ornthael, which is the era. The old mile still means the Long Mile when the neighbour is a continent. The stone in the square, the upper room, and the Held bed are what that walk left sitting in a Hands town. The everyday name comes first. Brenhael remains the inn’s cant, and it does not become the loft’s name.

Ornsael (ORN-sael) sets orn beside sael and means the sown-ground. It is the Rain-Shadow walk-hold on Saelthael, and it is not Saelthael itself, not Saelorn, not Saelhael, and not Ornthael. Brenthael (BREN-thael) sets bren beside thael and means the hearth-Tree. It is the neighbour Hands-town of the Third Hearth, and it is not brenhael, not Brenvaeth, not Brenorn, and not Orenbren. Brenod (BREN-od), Vaelun (VAY-lun), and Ornath (OR-nath) are the worn folk hearth-names of the Three Hamlets Past the Ford. They have no liturgy on purpose, because the Seat’s leave did not write them, and they stay clear of Vaeloren, Brenvaeth, and Ornled. The Mill-hold and the First Bowl are two more squares. The First Bowl’s folk hearth-name is Lonasir, the common tongue comes first, and there is no liturgy. They stay clear of Brenthael and of Vaelun.

Eolvaeth (EOL-vaeth) is eol and vaeth, the hinge-waiting, and it is Vaethorn’s pilgrim-edge seat. Everyday worn speech says Elvaeth (EL-vaeth). The name is not Vaethorn, not Thaelvaeth, and not Eoloren or Eolthael. Orentel (OREN-tel) is eroded oren and thael, the witnessing-Tree, with the th worn off. It is Lestrand’s salt-quay seat, and everyday speech also calls it the Salt Quay. It is not Thaeloren, not Orenbren, and not Lestrand or Netstrand. Maiethlir (MAI-eth-lir) is maieth and lir, the Mother’s thaw, and it is Threnmaieth’s counted river-seat. It stays clear of Threnmaieth, Threnhael, Thaeloren, Maiethvael, Maiethorn, Lirorn, Liren, and Brenthael.

No new roots are spent on ground. The everyday name comes first, and these stay in the common tongue: the Old Crossing, the West Water, the Rain-Wall, which Lirorn calls the Thaw-Wall, the Noon Pass, the Shelf-gate, the Core-thaw, the Well-wash, the Rise-water, and the Chart-run.

What Each Land Calls the Same Thing

Every land has the same institutions. They flow from the Trees and the Conditions, and both are universal. What each land calls them comes from how it stands on the faith, on whether it sits among healthy Trees or at a thin edge, and on how far the state reaches onto a person. A devout land calls the release-hall a gift-hall, a merchant coast calls that same building a release-house, and a surveillance-crown calls it a counted hall. It is the same building under three worldviews.

Use the common tongue column unless you need the local word. Use the local word when a Vaethorn pilgrim, a Lestrand factor, or a Threnmaieth clerk is speaking, or when you want the table to hear the difference. When a cell pauses in parentheses, that parenthesis is the stance in miniature.

Threnmaieth’s census calls itself the Threnhael. That is thren set beside hael, so the name means the keeping-whole. It sounds like care, the keeping of every subject hale, and it is total surveillance. Its own clerks say they keep the realm hale. Its subjects are kept whole. Outsiders hear the Counting. On that roll the second name is the house, said where other lands would say a surname. Witness-lands, which still name you by who saw you, do not do this.

These are the civic buildings the tithe-provision furnishes. Ael in the ael-hall is pronounced AYL, and the word means the airing.

The people

The three standing-terms keep their plain names everywhere: the Given, the Struck, the Kept. The Given are people a Condition was Given to. The Struck were turned later and alone. The Kept are untithed and whole. Each land’s second word is how it feels about them.

Common tongue Vaethorn (devout) Lestrand (secular) Threnmaieth (surveillance)
the Given (a Condition Given) the gifted (blessed) the Given (plain) the marked (on the roll)

the Kept (untithed, whole) the Waited / Mother-kept (pitied — passed over) the free (approving — unencumbered labor) the unmarked / the passed-over (noted as such)

The Kept are pitied in devout Vaethorn, where people say they missed the gift. They are envied as free on mercantile Lestrand, where no Tithe and no guild means a person can go anywhere, and the word is said with approval, as unencumbered labor. They are filed as unmarked in Threnmaieth, a gap in the roll that the crown wants explained.

Everyday words for these people already live beside the faiths. A liturgical name is the name a rite or a charter writes. An own-name is the name the house uses for itself. The three polity columns are the second word, the one that shows the stance.

The common-tongue name is what a traveller says. The own-name is what the house says. The land’s second word is how the state files them, when it files them at all.

Eras and dating

There is no universal year-zero. Travellers call the pilgrimage-required past the Walking Years, the first successful town-graft the First Cut, the still-moving spread of grafts the Grafting, and the town-Tree present the Years of Hands. A year’s number stays local.

Before the Walk goes unnamed on the mainland roads. The Watching keep the Before. Kumbaan keeps moons.

A walk you take because the Tree is missing, young, or sick is the neighbour’s week, and people still say the old mile when that neighbour is a continent. The prestige origin-winter is the First-Hand year. The Years of Hands are the present.

Book IIIThe Tree and the Faiths

The Turning Tree

A Turning Tree is a broad, slow, long-lived hardwood, with a canopy like a great oak or a great beech, though the tree is its own kind. It stands at the ceremonial heart of a town, usually in a square, on a green, or in a walled yard the town keeps for it. Out of season it looks like an unusually grand old tree, and the town treats it as one: children climb the low boughs, courts and markets meet in the shade, and lovers carve nothing into the bark, because cutting a mark there is taboo. In the tenth-year solstice week, the midsummer people call Turning-Week, the tree turns. The canopy shifts through colours no ordinary tree wears, and a leaf falls for a child, or the leaves close around them.

People call it a Turning Tree for what it does at that solstice. It turns, and it turns a child into what that child will become. A coloured leaf settles, and the colour names a Condition, the change that child will grow up carrying. When the leaves close and no colour comes, the child is one of the Kept, wanted as they are. The devout call each Tree a Hand of the Mother, and the liturgical word for that wood is motherwood. In the old tongue the Awakening Tree’s own name is Thaeloren (THAEL-or-en): thael is Tree and oren is to witness. Everyday speech wears that down to the Thallow.

The Awakening Tree

There is one origin Tree, the Awakening Tree, the great first Tree and the place the world’s pilgrimage is aimed at. It is old past any dating the faith can rely on, and it is vast, and it is the one Tree that nobody grafted out of another tree, which is why every other Turning Tree descends from it. The liturgy calls it the First Hand, and people really do make the journey: devout families travel so that a child can be Turned under the origin, and some of those families settle in the country around it. The faith’s central clergy sit in the Tree’s shadow as the First Seat, a college of tree-wardens, the people whose work is the Trees, with no throne in that shadow. The Tree stands on Maiethorn, in the Sacred Core, the old country of hills, river valleys, and Tree-crowned towns around that grove.

Grafts

Every town Turning Tree is a living graft of that one tree. When a town takes root, and especially when the town is so far off that a family could never reach the Awakening Tree, someone carries out a scion and plants it in the new town’s square. A scion is not a seedling that grew from a seed the Tree dropped. It is cut tissue of the one Tree, kept alive on the road, and planted into the new ground so the same wood grows on. That planting is a graft.

A town gets two things from the arrangement. Ordinary families walk to their own Tree for the Leaf-Fall, the ceremony at which a colour falls or the leaves hug, so the rite stays local and the distance of the road does not exile anyone from it. This is the ordinary way in the Years of Hands, the years when a town’s own Tree is what people expect. It was not always so. People devout enough to want the origin still travel to the Awakening Tree, either to have a child Turned there or simply to stand under it. On Heskoren, the continent where that wave of living wood is still unfinished, and in any place where a graft has failed, the walk is a necessity and not only a devotion.

The devout call each grafted tree a Hand of the Mother. Anyone in the square can see the cut and the planting, and whether a mind is choosing through that wood remains the faith’s argument, which the horticulture does not close.

The graft is a rite, and it is also the work of keeping living wood. The tree-wardens cut a scion from the Awakening Tree or, in ordinary practice, from a healthy town Tree that is cutting on the origin’s behalf. The cutting travels in living earth, and it is planted with ceremony. The first time a carrying succeeded, someone took living wood from Thaeloren, or from a branch that came away in a hand, carried it as far as the wood can go in a day and still meet new ground green, set it into that ground, and it took. Everyday speech calls that taking the First Cut. What the college captured afterward was not the living wood, which it could not own, but the right to say who may cut next, and that right is a paper. The cutting had been a heresy before it was a permit. The clergy count their years from the taking itself, so the taking is Cut-year 0 and the present year is Cut-year 387.

A young Tree cannot Turn anyone yet. A scion that has just been planted needs years, a generation by the reckoning people actually use, before it is mature enough to hold a Leaf-Fall. While it grows, the new town leans on a neighbour’s Tree, and the children travel to the nearest town that can Turn them. That borrowing is where a lot of the small texture of the world comes from: rivalries between towns, customs that belong to the road, and the sentence people still say, “we Turned at Harrow’s Tree before we had our own.”

When Trees sicken and die

The wood is mortal, so a blighted or dying Tree is a real crisis for the town, because the town may lose the power to Turn its own children and have to fall back on a pilgrimage or on a neighbour. A Tree that has died is replaced only by a fresh graft, and then by the long wait while the new wood matures. A mature Tree is hard to move once it is in the ground. The practice is to graft a new scion, rather than to dig the old tree up and carry it.

A town with no Tree is what the frontier usually looks like. The place is too new, or too remote, or it has lost the Tree it had. Towns in that condition send their ten-year-olds onto the road to be Turned, and the journey is one of the ways the map marks its own edge.

The Leaf-Fall

The Leaf-Fall is the rite the rest of the world is built around. It is held in Turning-Week, the tenth-year solstice week, which is the High Solstice of midsummer, when the Trees hold their colour and the leaves fall.

Every child who has turned ten since the last solstice is brought by their family. The witness-circle, the people gathered to see that child, comes together, and a tree-warden of the town officiates. The First Seat is present only in a week when people have come on pilgrimage. The hour is a sacred rite and, at the same time, the largest festival the settlement holds all year, something like a christening and a graduation and a fair held in the same afternoon. In a village the witness-circle simply is the town. In a city the circle is a hearth, a group of people who already know the child, and the square is still full.

The children come to the Tree one at a time, or in the small cohort who share that year, and they stand where the canopy can reach them, and they wait. The Tree turns, and it lets fall whatever it is going to let fall. The rest of the town watches from the edge of the boughs.

A healthy Tree, with a child under it and the town watching, does one of two things, and the wardens do not write a third outcome into the book.

A colour falls, and a Condition is Given. One leaf, or more than one, in a colour that means something, drifts down and settles on the child. The colour is the name of the Condition. This is the outcome people expect, the one they call proper, and the one they celebrate. The child grows up already knowing what they will become, and the town trains them and guilds them toward that life.

Or the leaves hug the child, and there is no colour, and the child is Kept. Instead of a coloured fall, the ordinary leaves gather and wrap the child, a green embrace with no colour that names anything. The faith holds the hug to be a kindness the Tree chose, and the schism argues over that reading, which the faith has not closed.

The Leaf-Fall is warm, and it has weight, and it belongs to the whole town: a breath that the circle holds, every eye on one child, a parent who was Given this same colour years ago weeping when it falls again, or a parent who had quietly hoped the leaves would hug. The Tithe, the upkeep a Condition later asks of the person who carries it, belongs to the years after this afternoon. The shadow that belongs to the rite itself is a human one, a wrong word spoken over a fall, or a week that was missed.

Turning-Week in a city

A Gift can still be given in that one week, and not in some other week, and the Tree is still the centre. A city of tens of thousands does not grow a second rite to get through the number of children. It divides the witnesses into hearths, the groups of people who already know the child they have brought.

The stands run by hearth across the week. In the morning, the afternoon, and the eve, a quay-gang or a courtyard or a guild-stair or a lot takes its turn, eighty to two hundred people who already know the child, so that hundreds of ten-year-olds are never stood up together as one crowd nobody could read.

The warden Speaks. To Speak is to say aloud whether the Tree gave a colour or a hug, and to name the colour when there is one. The warden does not write those gifts onto a roll. The week-slate, the board kept for the week, only records which hearth stands at which bell. It is a festival schedule, the same kind of board that says who has the square for the fair.

The legal fact is that a hearth witnesses a child, and a crowd does not. When a desk far from the city asks who saw the standing, one pillar of the hearth carries the memory. The pillar stood in that hearth, and already carries one of three Conditions: a Long-Lived, an ageless keeper of memory; a Bound, who swore a contract in extremity and is still keeping its terms; or a Far-Voiced, whose voice carries a feeling exactly as far as they mean it to, and no farther.

Threnmaieth, the crown on Maiethorn that keeps a written roll of its people and calls the writing a way of keeping them whole, is the one place that writes the stand down. A clerk who copies the colours off a week-slate has begun a register of Conditions, and a register is a thing the hearths do not keep.

A village still watches the rite as one circle.

Reading the colours

The colour of the leaf that falls is how the town knows which Condition has been Given, and the way that reading is known is also what gives the faith a civic office. Ordinary people know the common colours. Everyone in an ordinary town can already name the deep-red leaf of the Long-Lived, and the storm-grey fall of the Two-Bodied, who carry a second animal self and still command it. The tree-wardens hold the reading that counts. They confirm it out loud at the ceremony, and they handle a fall that is rare, or subtle, or mixed: a colour almost nobody present has seen, or a fall that could honestly be read two ways. In a small town the warden is the one who Speaks. In a pilgrimage-town, or at the First Seat, a Speaker is the elder who holds the rare-colour texts and the last word on a mixed fall.

The Conditions that are only ever Given have colours that are clear and widely known, because those colours are only ever seen at a Tree. Three Conditions can also be Struck, which means a person can come to them later, away from the Tree, and those three can fall as colours too. They are the Far-Voiced; the Stilled, who can hold a moment still, a bleeding wound or a blade already swinging or a patient under the knife; and the Taken-In, a person the wild took partway into itself and gave back changed. A Far-Voiced who was Given and a Far-Voiced who was Struck share a nature and do not share a story. The Answered are Given only: a person whom one element answered, fire or water or earth and stone or air, and that element has gone on answering ever since, under a leaf of lamp-amber or brass.

Leaf-colour Condition Who can read it
deep red / wine Long-Lived folk-known (already proverbial)
storm-grey Two-Bodied folk-known (already proverbial)
lamp-amber / brass the Answered folk-known
sea-blue Far-Voiced folk-known (a Given blue-leaf child is trained; a Struck Far-Voiced has no leaf at all)
pale stone / marble-white the Stilled folk-known, and feared. The warden says it carefully
copper-green / verdigris the Taken-In folk-known. This green is metallic, distinct from the Tree’s own summer green and from the hug
white-fire / opal Phoenix clergy-known from texts. Almost no living town has seen it fall. A warden who names it at a ceremony has just made history (and a problem).

The Tree never Strikes, so the Returned and the Bound have no colour, and the Unbound has none either. A Returned is a person who died with something unfinished, and whose purpose got them walking again. The Bound come by the contract, not by a leaf. The Unbound is what a term-limited contract leaves behind when the term ends and the other party to that contract collects the piece the person named at the signing, so they walk away free of the terms and short of that piece, and that becoming chains off Bound instead of falling as a leaf of its own. The hug that marks the Kept is ordinary summer-green, and it carries no naming colour. That is why the leaf of the Taken-In must not be that same ordinary green.

A fall that is rare, or mixed, or already being argued, two colours at once, or a colour nobody in the square has seen, or a reading of Phoenix that someone wants to be wrong, is why the tree-wardens are a civic office and not only a devout one. White-fire is the leaf of a Phoenix, a person who dies down to ash and comes back a little further from the person they were, and there is only ever one of them alive in the world at a time, which is why a living town almost never sees that leaf, and why naming it is history and a problem together.

The Tree only Gives, or it Keeps. People who are Struck received a Condition through a later threshold, a drowning, an oath, or a death they survived, and that change happens away from the Tree, with no leaf and with no ceremony. Whether the faith still counts the Struck as the Mother’s own doing is the schism that is still live.

Questions a warden gets asked

These are the questions families actually bring to a warden, and the answers are the custom of the town. The door is still one week, the High Solstice week of the year a child turns ten. In the Walking Years the only Tree was the origin, so a tenth year was a journey or it was no Leaf-Fall at all, and the towns of the Years of Hands did not grow a second chance beside that narrow door. A healthy Tree, with a child stood under it, still gives a colour or a hug.

What they ask What you say What you do not
We missed the week. Fever, a shut pass, a boat that did not come. They are unTurned. The child never stood. Their week for a Gift is over. Next summer they may visit the square; they do not stand for a Gift. A Struck threshold can still come later. The costly mercy is the old one: house a nine-year-old through the winter near a sound Tree. Call them Kept. A Kept child was hugged while the town watched.
We will not stand. The Old Ways kept their own rites before the grafts arrived. The Isle keeps the Open Table as its own faith. Some refuse from fear, or from a quarrel. The Tree does not chase them. Same legal result as a miss: unTurned, and the week for a Gift is over. A warden may ask once. They do not put a rope on a child to make a Gift. Treat refusal as a failure of the wood.
Who brings an orphan? The town is the family. Kin first; then the household that feeds them; then the warden-hearth. That is the warden’s house on the square. An orphan who stands is witnessed like anyone. An orphan no one brings is a miss. A second leaf as consolation.
An adult who never Turned. They stay unTurned. They do not stand for a Gift at thirty. They can be vouched as the person the town raised. They can still be Struck. Some hearths file them as Kept to be kind. That kindness is sloppy law. A late appointment.
Can they stand again? Wrong colour wanted. Hug regretted. No. A completed standing — colour or hug, under a Tree the warden called sound — is once. You may correct a Speaking. That is the colour or the hug as the warden said it. You may not rerun a fall. Offer a second Leaf-Fall. The wood has never answered one.
Our Tree is sick this week. Do not stand them under unsound wood. Borrow a neighbour’s canopy this same week. A warden who lets a cohort stand under a Tree they know cannot Turn has spent the week. Those children are unTurned. Next year as a repair.
The child is already Struck. Bring them to be acknowledged, not for a Gift. The Tree does not lay a second Condition on the first. A tenth year that starts the life over.
Twins, or a fall nobody will name. Two children are two standings. A mixed fall is why the Speaking exists. Two Speakers both claiming the last word.
The warden named it wrong. Correct the Speaking. Do not stand the child again. The year people cite is the Wrong Green. A second Leaf-Fall.
White-fire fell. Or someone wants to say it did. A town-warden does not guess Phoenix. They send to the First Seat by runner. Naming white-fire is history, and a problem. Guess from a book in the square.
A child of the Open Table, from the Isle. A Yumboe from that isle, under our boughs. If they stand in their tenth-year week, the Tree does what it does. If the host will not bring them, the week can end. No warden is sent to Kumbaan to fetch a child. Kumbaan is the storm-walled isle. Wait for the argument to finish. The week does not wait.
The city cannot know every child. They stand by hearth, in named slots. The square is full. The memory is the street that brought them, plus one pillar who can carry it. The colours stay unwritten. A city register.

UnTurned is not the same thing as Kept. Kept means the leaves hugged the child and the town watched it happen. UnTurned means the child never stood. From the street the two lives can look alike, because neither one carries a Tithe and neither one carries a guild, and only the Kept life was witnessed at the Tree. Citizenship still depends on who saw you. A neighbour who is unTurned is vouched for as the child the town raised, and not as a colour, and not as a hug.

A failure in the rite means a standing was not completed, and the Tree has not produced a third outcome to cover the gap. While the Tree is healthy, the child is under the boughs, and the town is watching, a colour falls or the leaves close in a hug. A missed week, a refusal, or a week spent under wood that could not Turn leaves no Given. The later doors, the ways a person can still be Struck, are the whole of the mercy that remains. If a fire takes the square, or a bough comes down, or the child is pulled away before the fall, and the week still has days left and the Tree is sound, the standing is finished later in that same week. Once the week has gone, the town treats the child as a miss. When the Speaking fails, the precedent is the Wrong Green: the town corrects the word that was said, and it does not bargain with the wood for a different life.

A parent who asks what happens if the Tree simply does nothing is asking a question the hearths do not keep a form for. A skeptic will say that is because it is just a tree, and trees that Turn, Turn. A believer will say the Hand does not come to the square to shrug. The working clergy side with the book they have: two outcomes, or the child was not there.

The Leaf-Mother

Some people hold that the Leaf-Mother blessed the world with the Conditions, the gifts of a becoming beyond the life a person was born into, and that the Turning Trees are her hands reaching down to choose. On that account each Leaf-Fall, the town’s gathering when a child of ten stands at the solstice and a leaf falls or the leaves hug, is an act of a mother’s love. Many people hold this, and it remains a belief, because nobody in the world has proved it. The skeptics who decline it are sincere and full members of society, the faith having been built to keep a place for them. Everyday people call the faith the Motherfaith. The faith calls itself Maieth, and a devout square that says the name means a mother, quiet, who gives, and who does not come because someone called.

A gift-religion

The faith begins from gifts the world received, the Conditions, and from the gifts that still come at each solstice. Nobody here is being rescued from a fallen state. The long question is how a person lives worthy of a gift.

What makes you of the Motherfaith is what you do. You bring your children to the Tree, you tend your Tithe honestly, the upkeep a Condition asks of the person who carries it, and you keep the festival. That practice counts for far more than what you privately believe about who does the choosing. A devout believer and a quiet skeptic can stand at the same Leaf-Fall and both belong, because the practice is what binds and the belief is what the faith argues about.

The faithful speak of a mother who is benevolent, attentive, generous, and quiet: she gives, and they say she watches, and she does not thunder or command or ask to be feared. People come to her by trying not to waste what she hands them.

The Motherfaith is the dominant faith of the Turning lands, and the other faiths are lived beside it. To the people who hold her, she is their Mother.

The houses do not share one face for her. What they share is the wood. A pressed leaf kept in a chest is a common keepsake, and it is only a leaf, and it does not speak, and some hearths keep no image of her at all. The faith does not picture her standing at a drowning, or at an oath, or out in the deep wild, because it has not agreed that she is in those places, and that argument stays open. Some Long-Lived people, the ageless keepers of memory, keep a cup they call the Unspent. Among themselves they say the Cup We Made, because they will tell you they invented whatever is on the other side by pouring in memories they could no longer carry, and on a quay people say the Poured God, with the smile they keep for a rich uncle’s hobby. No town Tree is involved in it, no leaf falls for the cup, and a warden does not set that cup on the sill.

Doctrine (as the faithful hold it)

What follows is what the faithful hold. Nobody in the world has proved it.

In the beginning, they say, a person was only what they were born. That born half is a Kind, the people they were by birth, and nothing more. The Leaf-Mother’s gift was becoming: the capacity to be given something beyond birth, a Condition the world would need. They call that first gift the Giving. They say she first reached down at the Awakening Tree, and that every town Tree is a grafted Hand of the Mother, a living cut of that first Tree, planted so that no child is too far from her reach.

Doctrine holds that she chooses, and that she chooses well. The colour a child receives is chosen, looked-at, intended, and fitted to the child and to the town’s need. Believers point to gifts that fit too well to be accident. Skeptics call that hindsight.

The Tithe is the weight of a gift, and the faith does not read the cost as a punishment. Every Condition asks upkeep. The faith reads that cost as honest weight: a real gift has a real charge to carry, and tending it well is the ordinary devotion of a lifetime. “Tend what you’re given” is the closest thing the faith has to a first commandment.

To be Kept, hugged by the leaves and given no colour, is in the doctrine a gift of being left whole. The faithful do not call the hug an oversight. This is where the argument bites hardest, and the schism below is that bite.

She has no throne a person can visit, and no voice that answers because someone demanded an answer. The faithful say a person meets her at the Tree, in the turning of a life, and in the fittingness of things, and never by summoning her. They hold that the quiet is intended, because a mother lets her children live. The same quiet is what leaves room for honest doubt.

Practice

The Leaf-Fall is the central rite, a child’s tenth-year solstice Turning, and people keep it as sacrament, coming-of-age, and the town’s great festival in the same afternoon. The questions a warden actually gets, a missed week, a refusal, an orphan, a child who is already Struck, and whether anyone stands twice, belong with the Tree. The rite’s cited shadow is the Wrong Green. In Cut-year 248, at Harrow’s Green, a warden named a hug as copper-green, and the child spent two summers in a garden that had no gift to teach, until the correction came as a second word and the child was not stood under the Tree again.

The Tending is the ongoing, private devotion of paying a Tithe well. To tend a Condition honestly is, in this faith, to honour the gift. A Two-Bodied person, who carries a second animal self and still commands it, works in that other body. A Long-Lived person keeps the vigils and the learning their years require. The faith calls that life worship, lived as the upkeep itself.

The Turning-week festival is the solstice week around the Leaf-Falls. Towns hold markets and feasts, families reunite, and the year names its new Given and its new Kept. A colour fell on the new Given. The leaves hugged the new Kept. It is the emotional high point of the calendar, the week the year calls the High Solstice, and also Turning-Week.

The Struck receive a Condition away from the Tree, at a drowning they survived, an oath they swore, or a death they crossed, so the faith grew quiet rites to receive them afterward. A Struck person is brought to the Tree to be acknowledged, and folded into the community of the Given, rather than left as an anomaly. The Tree does not Strike, so this is not a Turning. How warmly a town does it is itself part of the argument.

Tree-tending is the civic and sacred care of the town’s Turning Tree: the watering, the watch against blight, and the planting of a new scion, a living cut carried in earth. The tree-wardens do that work. They are one order with offices inside it, not a set of rival chapters. They officiate the Leaf-Fall, and they hold the authoritative reading of the colours. Common colours are already folk-known. The wardens confirm them, and they rule on the rare, the subtle, and the mixed falls, which is why a town needs them as a civic office and not only as people who pray.

The First Seat is a college in the Motherwood about the Awakening Tree, the old wood around that grove, and it is not a throne. Pilgrims go there. The Seat authorizes graft-scions, whether the cut comes from the origin or from a healthy town Tree acting on the origin’s behalf. It confirms Road-hands, the people who carry a living cutting, and Speakers, the elders who hold the last word on a rare colour. It does not appoint every town-warden. A hearth is taken by apprenticeship, and the town that watched the new warden through a year is what confirms them.

The keeping of the order is ordinary and local. Towns house the warden-hearth, the warden’s house on the square, and the stipend is bread, wood, and a place, not a tax on Conditions. During Turning-Week the warden eats from the festival, the way the town feeds any office it needs that week. Cutting-leave, the paper that says who may take wood and for where, carries a fee the Seat describes as carrying-earth, the cost of the living soil the cutting travels in and of a Road-hand’s year. Pilgrimage keeps the Seat: offerings, lodging, and the devout who settle in the Motherwood. The wardens point a new Given toward the work the colour named. The halls that help a person meet a Tithe are other people’s work.

The live schism

The faith holds more than one reading. The central argument is sincere on every side, and no one has settled it, which is why the faith endures. It turns on three questions the doctrine cannot prove.

The first question is the Kept: if the Mother blesses everyone, why does the Tree hug so many children and give them no colour at all? The Tender reading is the majority, and it is the teaching the faith usually gives. The Kept are given wholeness, a real gift, chosen for them, and to be Kept is to be trusted to need nothing added. The Wanting reading is the minority. The Kept were passed over, loved but not chosen, and the doctrine of wholeness is a kindness the faithful tell them. This reading quietly stings, and it shapes how some Kept feel about the festival.

The second question is the Struck, who received a Condition the Tree never handed out. Did the Mother reach through the threshold too, or did something else give the gift? The Wide-Hand reading says she meets people at the drowning, the oath, and the death, and that the Tree is only her ordinary hand, so the Struck are fully hers. The Narrow-Hand reading says she gives only at the Tree, and that the Struck received their Condition by some other means, which is why this reading finds the Struck a little suspect. That suspicion is the seed of real social friction toward the Struck.

The third question is whether a mind chooses at all, and it is the line between believer and skeptic. Believers say the fittingness of the gifts, the care of the Kept, and the way the Struck feel received add up to a Someone. Skeptics say it is just what the Trees do, biology, or a phenomenon so old that it wears a face people gave it. The grafting is horticulture a person can watch, a cut of wood set into new ground, and a choosing mind is an inference they decline to make.

Because a person belongs by the rite they keep, a skeptic who tends their Tithe and brings their children to the Tree is a good member of the Motherfaith. Belief in the Mother is honoured, and it is not policed, so the skeptic can speak the doubt and remain that member. Every branch above is held in good faith, and no house is a villain. Being a skeptic costs nothing day to day, because the practice is what binds. The questions stay open because no one in the square can close them.

Two sayings

The Tender’s blessing is spoken over each child at the Leaf-Fall.

“What falls to you, wear well. What is kept from you, keep. The Hand that reaches is the Mother’s own — and the Mother does not reach twice by chance.”

The blessing is comfort, and it carries the ethic of tending the gift. Believers hear intent in it, skeptics hear a proverb about not asking the wood twice, and both can say the words.

A Kept child’s saying is folk, half a consolation and half a barb.

“The Tree that gives to all its neighbours held me instead. I have decided that is not the same as being forgotten.”

It takes the Tender reading of the Kept and makes it personal, and a little defiant. “I have decided” is a choice made against doubt, and not a certainty.

The Five Faiths

The Motherfaith is the dominant faith of the Turning lands, and it is not the only one. Five lived faiths each answer a different experience the Trees, or the lack of a Tree, actually produce, and what follows is how people live those answers, not a list of gods.

Faith Home A Condition is… Everyday name Own name
the Leaf-Mother everywhere the Trees stand; born on Maiethorn a gift chosen the Motherfaith Maieth
the Watching Maiethorn’s oldest districts a seeing, later named a gift the Watching Haelthael
the Fair Hand Strandoren’s ports and houses a bargain struck the Fair Hand Leddoren
the Old Ways Heskoren’s groves and doors the land making its own the Old Ways Vaeloren
the Open Table Kumbaan, the Sundering Isle a mainland hunger they never had the Open Table Ndeyaan

A Condition, in all of these arguments, is a becoming: something a person becomes, set beside the Kind they were born. The Watching, the Fair Hand, and the Old Ways live where the Trees stand, on Maiethorn, Strandoren, and Heskoren, so the friction is inside the settled world, among people who already live with the wood. The Open Table grew on Kumbaan (koom-BAHN) with no Tree and no Mother-name. Sailors call that place the Sundering Isle, and a storm-wall of weather, current, and reef keeps it, which is why the grafts never crossed.

Smaller household rites, quay-charms, and Kind-customs stay local, especially the household customs of the Kitsune, the Selkie, and the Tengu, peoples a person is born as. Those charms are not what the five faiths stand on. A household can keep a charm the next street has never heard of, and the five faiths are still the five.

The people who do the daily work are the tree-wardens, who keep the Motherfaith at the Tree; the Watchers, who keep the vigil; the Book-Hands, who witness a signing; the Door-Keepers, who walk the rivers, the stones, and the groves; the Table-Keepers, who keep the supper; and the Shore-Sitters of the isle, who sit the storm-beach and wait, and do not swim out. A fringe of the Long-Lived, the people whose aging has stopped, call themselves the Pourers and keep a cup they call the Poured God, and that cup is not a sixth faith.

The argument (what a becoming is)

Every faith in this world has to answer the same fact, that most people become something they were not born as, and the faiths do not agree on the verb for that becoming.

The people a Tree gives a colour are the Given, and even that name is already an argument: the Motherfaith says the child was chosen, the Watching at the same wood says the child was seen, the Fair Hand says the child was signed, and the Old Ways say the Tree is a late guest at a door the land already kept.

The Struck are the people who change later, at a threshold, often with no Tree nearby, and the faiths do not hear the same door. The Motherfaith is still arguing whether the Leaf-Mother reached that threshold, while the Watching says the threshold was always a place of seeing, the Fair Hand hears a later contract struck in extremity, and the Old Ways call this the oldest becoming, the land’s own children.

The Kept are the people who get the hug and no colour, and on the mainland that same hug has four readings: a gift of wholeness, a person passed over, no bargain taken, or a year the land had no door for you. The Open Table does not offer a reading of the hug, because on their account a Condition is a mainland hunger they never had.

The Tithe is the upkeep a becoming still asks, and the faiths read that same upkeep four ways: the Motherfaith calls it the honest weight of a gift, the Watching calls it the cost someone once paid, the Fair Hand calls it the term of the contract, and the Old Ways call it the land’s due.

None of these is a villain-theology. Each is a sincere answer to a seam people actually live with: gifts that fit, a reach that runs thin at the edge, the written terms a Bound person carries, the Struck who change with no Tree nearby, and a whole isle that never Turned, that never brought its children under a Tree to become. The Motherfaith’s own schism already taught the courtesy the others use. What you do at the rite is what binds, what you believe is what gets argued, and a household that keeps two practices is ordinary rather than a scandal.

How they live together

People belong by the rite they keep, and the creed can wait. Because the Motherfaith counts you by what you do at the Tree, a Watcher who brings their child, a Settler of the Fair Hand who stands as witness to the colour, and a Kin-speaker of the Old Ways who also walks the rivers, the hills, and the stones can all belong at the same Leaf-Fall. Doctrine fights, and the festival usually does not.

Each fight stays in its own land, inside a district or a port, and it does not become a march of one faith upon another.

On Maiethorn the fight is at the centre. The Watching and the Motherfaith share the same Trees and argue over the blessing spoken there. Threnmaieth, the crown that writes its people down, files the Watchers on the Threnhael (THREN-hayl), the roll whose name means the keeping-whole, as a known, counted dissent. The file calls that dissent the Grown-Over. What follows from the filing is pressure, not a pogrom.

On Strandoren the faith is worn light, so the fight is over the Bound and the books. The Bound are the people who chose a grant and named the terms of it. The Fair Hand and the Motherfaith compete for the same oath-keepers in the same port. Lestrand, the great merchant power of that coast, which people call the Ledger Coast, prices both and polices neither.

On Heskoren the fight is over the grove. The Old Ways were there before the grafts, the Trees set into older ground, and the Motherfaith burns hottest where the gift is scarcest. A dying Tree has two claimants. Vaethorn, the devout power of the Waiting Lands, makes the quarrel tender and sharp, not holy-war loud.

On the Sundering Isle the wall still holds. A Yumboe on the mainland, one of the good people born to that isle, is a guest at everyone else’s rite. They keep their supper, and they find the noon-day faiths, the mainland rites kept in the daylight, loud the way a guest who will not sit is loud. The quarrel is already in the port. A host counts a guest as family after two suppers, a clerk wants to know where the person was Turned, and a host will not spend a child’s tenth-year week on a Tree.

Most years what actually happens is a household keeping two practices. The hard edge is the hour when the two stop agreeing.

Pair The common blend The hard edge
Motherfaith + Watching The household keeps the same Tree and inherits which of the two blessings it speaks. Threnmaieth’s roll wants one name for what you are.
Motherfaith + Fair Hand The Leaf-Fall is a festival and a signing-watch, the Fair Hand standing witness to the terms, and the Tithe is paid as both tending and settling. Gift-language and debt-language contend over the same Bound soul.
Motherfaith + Old Ways People make a pilgrimage to a graft and still walk the old doors at the threshold. When a Tree sickens, the quarrel is who tends it, the warden or the door-keeper.
Any mainland + Open Table A shared supper is rare, and someone will say “no one is a stranger twice.” On the mainland a person belongs because a town watched them Turn. The Open Table says a person belongs after two suppers. A child of the table who reaches Turning-Week in Eolthael, the Turning-month of the High Solstice, is the hard case.

All five houses tell the Child at Four Doors, and the last line changes. That is how the world argues without a council.

The Leaf-Mother remains a belief in public life, and the other faiths stay beliefs with her. The Watching says it remembers a cost, and what that cost was the house will not agree, so the claim stays unsettled.

The Watching

The Watching is Maiethorn’s heartland heresy, an older Tree-faith the Motherfaith grew over, and the dissent sits at the centre rather than out on a frontier. They keep the Tree and refuse the Mother-name, holding that the colours fall because the Tree sees, and not because a she chooses.

In everyday speech a neighbour says the Watching. Their own name is Haelthael (hayl-THALE), from hael and thael, the Tree kept whole. They mean the Tree before anyone split it into a Mother and her hands. The Motherfaith’s soft name for them is the First Watching, and Threnmaieth’s file-name is the Grown-Over.

Shape of the faith

This is a witness-faith, and the founding fact is that the Tree looks, so a colour is a seeing made visible, and not a present wrapped in a leaf. To live well is to name what was seen, rather than to thank a giver you cannot prove.

Their practice is older than the Motherfaith’s. They stand at the same Leaf-Fall, and they will not say the Tender’s blessing, the line the warden speaks over the child, as the warden says it. The rite still binds them to the town, and the withheld word is the whole dissent.

They will not give the Tree a divine character, neither a mother nor a bargain-partner nor a land-spirit in a new dress, because for them it is the Tree. Naming it Maieth is, to them, the overlay, a comfort the sacred centre invented when the seeing needed a face.

You know them by the name they keep for the wood. They keep Thaeloren, the Tree that witnesses, and they refuse Hand of the Mother, so the wood is the same and the title is the schism.

Doctrine (as believed)

They share the Motherfaith’s picture of the Before, a beginning in which the world was Kind and Kind alone, people as they were born and nothing besides. They part company on what came next: the Tree, they say, was already there and already watching, the Giving came after that Watching, and the Mother-name came last, so that each layer is a story laid over a seeing.

“She chooses well” is, to them, a later sentence. Fittingness is what a witness produces: the Tree sees what you can carry and what the town will need, and the leaf matches the seeing. They call that intent, and they do not call it a mother’s. To a Watcher, the skeptics of the Motherfaith are almost right, and still too quick to call the Tree a phenomenon with no mind. There is a mind in the seeing, and it does not owe you a lap.

Haelthael teaching remembers a cost, and holds that the Giving was not free: something was spent, someone was lessened, and the Tree, or whatever stands behind it, does not reach twice by chance, because reaching costs. They will not name a Mother who pretends otherwise. What the cost was, they will not agree, though they agree the cost was real.

The Kept were seen: a hug and no colour is a seeing of wholeness, or a seeing that did not reach, and they argue this as fiercely as the Motherfaith does, without the consolation of a mother’s lap. The hug is still a witness, not an oversight, and not, they insist, a slight dressed as love.

The Struck were seen at a harder door, so a drowning, an oath, or a death is an older place of seeing, and the Tree is the ordinary one. The Watching does not need the Wide-Hand and Narrow-Hand split the Motherfaith keeps, the quarrel over how wide a giving hand reaches, because seeing was never confined to a grafted scion, a living cut of the origin planted in a town.

Practice

The Night Watch is kept the night before Turning-Week. Watchers keep a silent vigil at the town Tree. They speak no blessing and read no colour. They keep watch on the Tree all night, as they believe it watches the town.

The withheld blessing is what they do at the Leaf-Fall itself. They attend, because the practice still holds and their children still Turn, and when the warden says the Tender’s line a Watcher household speaks its own, quietly.

“What falls, was seen. What is kept, was seen. The Tree does not reach twice by chance.”

The cadence is the same as the Motherfaith’s blessing, and the Mother is not in it. Towns that have lived with both wordings for a long time barely notice the difference. Threnmaieth notices.

Name what you saw is the devotion after a Turning. A Watcher does not say “tend what you’re given.” They sit with the child and describe the fall: the colour, the way the leaf came, and what the year will ask. Devotion, for them, is accurate speech.

In Haelthael liturgy the origin Tree is only Thaeloren. “First Hand” is tolerated as poetry. “Hand of the Mother” is the overlay they will not say.

Watchers are not priests. They keep the Night Watch, they teach the withheld blessing, and, where a town will have it, they offer a second reading of a rare or mixed fall. That reading is a witness alongside the tree-warden. It is not a reading over the warden, and the warden’s word stays the town’s. In Threnmaieth they are a known column on the roll. The Watching has no mother-church and no seat in the Awakening Tree’s shadow, because that seat was grown over by the First Seat. Their oldest rooms are under older chapels, or in houses that never took a warden’s blessing on the door. What they keep as offices are the Night Watch and the withheld blessing.

The live schism

The Masked say the Mother is a later face the Witness learned to wear, or a name people needed and the Tree allowed. The reading sits close to the Motherfaith, and it is common in mixed families. A Masked Watcher will stand for the Tender’s blessing and add the withheld line under it.

The Bare Tree says there was never a she. The overlay is a comfort the sacred centre invented, and comfort is not the same thing as truth. This is the harder and smaller reading, and it is the one Threnmaieth files most carefully.

Both branches agree the Giving cost something, and they do not agree what: a wound in the Tree, a year the watching failed, or a someone who became the wood. This is the question they will not close. It is also the one the Motherfaith most wants left unasked.

An inscription on a door-beam

The inscription was cut on a door-beam, then recut, and found when a warden-chapel on Maiethorn was re-floored. The new beam faces the Tree. This face was turned to the stone.

We kept the watch before the name. The wood was already looking. If a mother came after, she came to a work begun. Do not thank the latecomer for the seeing.

It reads as heresy, stubborn and local, and it claims that the Tree is older than the Mother-name.

The Fair Hand

The Fair Hand is Strandoren’s fortune-and-contract faith. It has no catechism, and it distrusts anyone who offers one. What follows is assembled the way Settlers, the people who keep this faith, assemble what they hold: from working books, settled margins, and clauses copied often enough to become prayer. The faith reads a Condition not as a gift given but as a bargain struck. The world, on this account, is a ledger of deals. The Tithe is a term, not a devotion. When the book is closed you are even, and you do not owe gratitude forever. It is the direct rival to the Motherfaith’s gift-language, at home on the trade continent, and especially among the Bound.

In everyday speech the name is the Fair Hand. Their own written name is Leddoren (LEDD-or-en), from ledd and oren, the witnessed account. Along the Ledger Coast the slang is the Settling.
