Tithe-poverty and the safety net

Because the provided-for Tithes cost money, you can be too poor to stay whole. A Taken-In who cannot afford green, a Long-Lived with no access to anything new, a Far-Voiced with nowhere to vent: these people do not only suffer want. They slide toward the danger, into the wilting, the fade, or the involuntary Cry, a voice breaking out because it was not let out on purpose. Destitution here has a visible, dangerous face.

Who pays for that provision is the political question, and polities do not answer it the same way.

Where provision is treated as a public good, which is the Warm answer, the devout end of the world’s theology, the town keeps it the way it keeps roads and wells. There are town greenhouses, free venting-halls, and endowed libraries, because a town whose Conditioned stay whole is a town that stays safe and keeps working. The pious way of saying the same choice is that you help every person tend their gift.

Where provision is left as a private burden, harsher polities hand it to the individual and to the guild. The Tithe-poor fall. They become a real hazard to the people around them, and the same polities then police the fall instead of preventing it.

The cynical middle is leverage. The town, the guild, or the employer does provide the Tithe, and holds what it provides, so the furnisher can withhold it. How that lands on the stances is at the end of this chapter.

Labor: who does what

The Tithe and the vocation are usually the same shape, which is why a town’s jobs sound like its Conditions. How large each workforce is lives in The Conditions. What follows is the work, not a census.

The people who move things are the Two-Bodied, and they are the plurality, the largest share of any Condition. Herding, haulage, rescue, courier, and scouting sit on them, and so does the fighting when a war actually comes. The Condition runs in blood, so a family can be wolf-folk or hawk-folk straight through, and the trade comes down with the animal.

The food those herds and that haulage depend on is Taken-In work: farmers, foresters, herders, and wardens. The frontier runs on them because they thrive on living land. A city still needs their grain, so it keeps a working minority inside the walls, at the social arm’s length the next section describes. The distance is manners. It is not an empty workplace.

Once the goods are moving, someone has to be heard across the distance. Far-Voiced criers stand on the coasts, the roads, and the borders, and the same people perform, negotiate, and swear as witnesses when a court needs a feeling that cannot be faked. The relay is a live signal from coast to border. A medieval world would not otherwise have it, and it exists because the people posting it carry the voice.

The crafts that shape the materials are the Answered, guilded by the element they use in earnest. Ember is the smiths and the glasswrights, Tide the shipwrights and the dyers, Root the masons and the potters, Gale the sailmakers and the millers. When a fire breaks out, or a rescue needs those same hands, the guilds rotate into it.

Some of the work kills the living, so the Returned do it. Death cannot take them a second time until the Purpose is met, and the jobs are the plague ward, the mine after a collapse, the deep salvage, and the tending of the dead. Beside that, the Stilled do the work that needs a body held still: surgery, a riot-line, a demolition, a course of stone. They are licensed, and the guild disciplines them, because the Gaze is the hazard as well as the tool.

What has to be remembered, the archives and the notarial acts and the judgments and the banks, sits with the Long-Lived. They are few. If many more people never died, those chairs would stiffen and stop changing hands. Where a word has to hold, the Bound keep the oaths, the debts, and the treaties, and they stand as witnesses whose word is literally binding. The Unbound are in that same work. A released Bound is not a second workforce. They go back to whatever they did before, and they need other people if they are to keep at it.

A Phoenix is only a trace, and the economy does not employ them as a class of worker. They are a political symbol, not a trade. The Kept are the inversion of that whole ledger. They carry no Tithe, so there is no upkeep to fund, and they carry no Condition, so no Condition-guild claims them. They take ordinary work and move where the work is. Where the faithful pity them for missing a gift, the ledger calls them the least encumbered people in the world, a real freedom sitting under the slight.

Why Taken-In live in stone cities

Green costs money in a stone city, and the cities keep the Taken-In at arm’s length because the Taken-In thrive on the frontier. Both are true. Arm’s length is how the polite districts stand toward the bark and antler a Taken-In carries on the body. The lots are still staffed.

They are in the city for five ordinary reasons.

  1. They were Given here. A copper-green leaf, the Taken-In’s colour, fell at a city Tree. Family, work, and a hearth-witness are what keep them. Leaving the city would mean leaving the circle that saw them Turn.
  2. Grain and timber come in, and people come with them. Seasonal Taken-In work the quays and winter over, and some of them stay. They are the harvest-hands who do not go home in Hale-month, the spring month, also called Haelren.
  3. The lot is a job. The greens-keepers need Taken-In labor. The city imports that green-skill for the commons, and then will not sit the workers at the high table.
  4. The door can open in a city’s old green. Being lost and dying in a deep wild is the Struck path that makes a Taken-In. A walled grove, a lot at night, or a river-garden after a flood can open the same door. It is rare, and it is often enough to count.
  5. They cannot afford to leave. Green-poverty is a trap. You need the lot if you are to stay whole, the lot is gated, you work for the hours on it, and you never save the cart-fare home. That trap is the city’s book of the Slide, the illicit market in Tithe-goods. Week-keepers sell it, and the green is what they sell when the gate will not.

The Taken-In share of the whole world is in The Conditions. A stone city runs lower than that share. The Taken-In who are there concentrate on the lots, the orchards, the river-gardens, and the week-keeper’s pot, the private green that same trade rents by the week. There are enough of them to make a queue, enough for a wilt two streets off the lot, and enough for the Slide to have a customer. The frontier keeps the density and the honour. The city keeps the gate.

Banking and the deathless houses

The banks of the Turning do not die. These are the deathless houses. A Long-Lived founds the house and is still personally running it two centuries later, the same memory, the same word, and the same unbroken ledger. In a world of letters of credit and merchant houses, that continuity is the great advance a Condition makes in finance. A letter of credit is a written promise to pay, carried in place of a chest of coin. Three things follow.

The trusted note. A note from a deathless house is trusted almost as coin, because everyone knows the banker cannot forget a debt, cannot be quietly succeeded by a defaulting heir, and will personally answer for the paper in fifty years. Their paper circulates further than any crown’s, and it holds its value better. Other paper is trusted by how close it comes to that word. The nearest thing this world has to a standard that does not wear out is the word of a house that will not die.

The long instrument. Deathless houses lend and endow on horizons no mortal lender would risk: century loans, multi-generation trusts, and the patient financing of cathedrals, canals, and universities. The instruments are letters of credit and endowments. There is no stock exchange, and no company split into shares a crowd of strangers can buy.

The concentration risk. Wealth that never passes to an heir never disperses through inheritance. The great scattering that a death forces on every other fortune does not happen here. There are few of the deathless, and even so they can slowly gather an outsized share of the capital that stands still. Their small number is what keeps that share from becoming the whole of standing capital, and the economy has never fully resolved the gathering. An endowment does not undo it. The coin moves out, and the steering stays, so the influence concentrates even while the cash flows into institutions the same hands still direct.

Many of the houses began as road-houses in the Walking Years, the age when families still had to walk to Thaeloren. They were inns, beds, and century-credit for that road. The everyday name is still road-house. The cant, the working nickname, is brenhael (BREN-hael), “the hearth kept whole.” The lived version is a house still in the act of being an inn: the Held bed, a bed kept for a name that has not come, and a note a necessity-family pays on the home-walk, which is to say they eat now and pay when they walk home. When the walk stopped being required in the core, the lands nearest the Awakening Tree, the same Long-Lived still remembered every debtor, and the paper outlived the pilgrimage season. The inns became banks. Two fates of that memory are still standing, on opposite errands. The White Note House took the path of collecting on the old paper. The Third Hearth kept making the bed. The trusted note is an instrument from the Walking Years that outlived the road it was written for.

Inheritance and the problem of not dying

Inheritance law is bent by the deathless, and the bend is a grief as well as a rule. A Long-Lived’s children are not guaranteed to inherit the Condition. Most of them age and die while the parent does not. A deathless person therefore outlives most of the heirs, and the estate never enters the inheritance stream at all. A fortune that is never passed down still has to go somewhere.

The usual answer is that the deathless endow. They have no line of heirs waiting on the death, and their own Tithe needs a steady supply of novelty, new books, new scholarship, new things to learn. A Long-Lived characteristically funds the institutions that generate that knowledge: the libraries, the universities, the archives. The deathless banker becomes the deathless patron, and pays their own Tithe by building the places that feed it. It is also how they grieve, an endowment in the name of a child who died a century ago. It is not the same thing as letting the fortune go. An endowment converts coin into patronage that is permanent and directed. Because the founder does not die, the founder keeps the chair, names the scholars, and steers the institution for centuries. Endowment eases the concentration of coin, because liquid wealth flows out into public works, and it deepens the concentration of influence, because the same few deathless hands still guide the universities, the courts, and the archives their money built. Keeping the Long-Lived few does not end that lock-up. The lock-up changes shape, from hoarded coin to patronage that does not step down.

For everyone else, inheritance is ordinary, except in the Two-Bodied bloodlines, where the Condition, the family’s animal, and often the family’s trade descend together, so that a place in the guild and a Condition can be a single inheritance. The sharpest question the law still has open is economic at the root. The Given-Over is a Bound who contracted away so much of themselves that the counterparty effectively owns the person. That is the ultimate inheritance failure: an estate, and a self, absorbed by a creditor.

Center and periphery

The economy is not spread evenly, and the unevenness follows the same geography that shapes the law. Near the mature Trees, in the core, Conditions lie thick, the guilds are strong, and specialized Condition-work and the goods that come from it are what the core sells to everyone else. Out at the margins, on the frontier, the giving thins. More of the people there are generalist Kept, or Struck and untrained, and fewer of them are Given specialists.

The core exports the specialized work and the finished goods, Answered crafts, Stilled medicine, deathless-house credit, and it imports the raw staples. The frontier leans hardest on the Taken-In, who thrive there and are neighbours, and on Kept labor that can turn its hand to whatever the week needs. It exports food, timber, and raw materials, and it imports the specialists it cannot grow. Distance, spoilage, and the thin reach together make the friction real. They leave the frontier specialist-poor and self-reliant. Cities still keep a working minority of Taken-In behind a gate. They do not ship the Condition out of town.

The shadow economy

Every gate grows a market on the far side of it. The gates in this economy are Tithe-provision and vouching.

Illicit Tithe-supply. Where the legitimate provision is rationed, gated, or unaffordable, a shadow market fills the gap. The green it smuggles is for a Taken-In cut off from living land, and the customers of that urban book are the city-Given, the winter-stayers, and the people caught in the lot-hour trap. The same market keeps unlicensed venting-rooms, and it sells black-market novelty, rare texts and forbidden knowledge, to a Long-Lived who is starving for anything new. The customer is someone already sliding toward the wilting, the fade, or the involuntary Cry, which makes the trade both lucrative and cruel. In the street this trade is called the Slide. The same people are called week-keepers, because the sale is rented by the week.

Off-book contracts. The whole domain of the Bound has an underside: contracts sworn outside the honest tables, unregistered terms, and the predatory brokers who arrange them. That pipeline feeds the Given-Over. In the street this desk is called the Holding Desk. It sells clauses. It is not the Slide.

Sold vouching. Citizenship here is a place counting you as its own because a person will stand for you, rather than because a clerk has written your name down. The unvouched will buy a voucher, and a market exists in dubious character-witnesses. The one thing that cannot be faked is a Long-Lived’s memory, which is why an honest vouch from them is priceless and a corrupt one is catastrophic. In the street this market is called the Standing Trade. It sells a person who will stand. It is not the Slide.

The Slide sells the upkeep. The Holding Desk sells clauses. The Standing Trade sells a witness.

How polities vary (economic faces)

The rules of the Tithe are the same everywhere. Who actually receives what is politics. It follows the same three choices as the law: how gift-devout the polity is, how many healthy Trees it has, and how far the state reaches onto the person. Three stances keep recurring, and each has an economic face.

The Warm (high theology). A Warm polity treats Tithe-provision as a public good. It keeps town greenhouses, venting-halls and libraries that someone has endowed, and ranging-commons held in common, ground at the edge where the Two-Bodied can be their other selves. The Conditioned are kept whole at the town’s expense, because a whole populace is a safe and productive one, and because the faith says to tend every gift. The economic injustice is soft. The same help arrives with an expectation attached. You are helped to tend your gift, and you are quietly obligated to spend it as the community sees fit, until the subsidy shades into conscription, a requirement to spend the gift as the town decides.

The Watchful (governance at its extreme). A crown that writes its people down, as the Tallied Crown and the Worn Count do, turns the need of a Tithe into leverage. It provides, and it provides efficiently, even generously, and it holds what it provides. The green, the outlet, and the novelty all come through channels the crown controls and can withhold. Its deathless-house finance is superb and centuries-deep. The injustice is cold and precise. A population whose upkeep runs through the state is a population that cannot afford to refuse the state. It is the most complete control in the world, and it is dressed as care.

The Frontier (low reach). There is little formal infrastructure for the Tithe, and there are few specialists. People improvise a way to meet the need, or they go without. The freedom is real. There is no guild monopoly and no crown holding the Tithe, and the Taken-In are neighbours rather than curiosities. The harshness is also real. The provided-for who cannot pay their Tithe slide with no net, and untrained Struck people manage dangerous Conditions alone. At the edge the economy runs on barter and favors, cash-poor and land-rich.

A polity’s economy is set by where it stands on all three choices at once. A devout frontier runs commons-minded charity with almost no infrastructure to fund it. A secular Tree-rich republic has deep markets and thin welfare. A Watchful-and-pious core turns generous provision into the tightest hold in the world.

Daily Life

Most families in the Turning are ordinary, and that is the first thing to understand about them. Two people marry. Some of the household carry a Condition, the change that arrives across a life, and some do not. The children have not Turned yet, and will not until their tenth year. A Kind is what a person is by birth, the ancestry they arrived in, and a Condition stacks onto that Kind. It can arrive years later. A Tithe is the upkeep a Condition keeps requiring, and it shows up in a house as a cost, a noise, or a door left waiting. A wife born a Selkie, one of the seal-people, a husband Returned from a drowning, a Kept grandmother, three children who are simply children so far: this is not a remarkable household. It is the household. Because nearly every family is mixed in that way, mixed families are not a category anyone thinks about. There is no unmixed household to marry away from, so nobody treats the mix as a departure, and nobody keeps a separate name for it.

Family, the whole spectrum

Family life spreads along a range, and the spread itself is the point.

At the warm, mundane end, which is most families, a Condition is a texture of the household the way a trade or a temperament is. A Two-Bodied parent’s other self has a name, and the children know it. A child says, “That’s Bramble, mother’s otter,” and grows up with that other self as much a part of the family as a pet that is also a person. A Far-Voiced household is a loud one, because the Tithe means feeling must be aired each day. You do not get to sulk quietly in a home with a Far-Voiced in it, and families learn to treat the evening’s singing, or weeping, or laughing, as ordinary weather. A Taken-In parent keeps the windows open and the rooms green. These are quirks rather than tragedies, the small daily accommodations of living with people who are also in the middle of what they have become.

In the middle, the Tithe becomes a shared family labor. Where a Condition is provided-for, kept whole by something the household has to furnish, keeping a family member whole is a household expense and a household duty. The green for the Taken-In, the books for the Long-Lived, the outlet for the Far-Voiced. Families organize around it the way a household organizes around a member’s chronic need, mostly without drama, sometimes with strain, and with the quiet knowledge that to let a loved one’s Tithe lapse is to watch them slide toward the harm that Tithe was holding back. A family too poor to furnish a Tithe carries a particular grief. They can see exactly what their kin needs, and they cannot buy it.

At the aching end sits the marriage ordinary life keeps returning to: loving someone whose span of years is not yours. Chief among these is marrying a Long-Lived. Their aging simply stops. Their spouse’s does not. A Long-Lived can have children and a full family, but the Condition is not reliably inherited. Most children age and die like anyone, so a Long-Lived does not build a deathless dynasty. They outlive it. They watch a spouse grow old across a marriage that stays, on one side, unchanged. They bury their children. The old saying is that the cost of the Long-Lived is measured in funerals, and it is a cost paid inside the family, at the dinner table, over decades. A Long-Lived who has done this once faces the choice their whole existence turns on. They can stop, live on alone, and keep no more households. Or they can begin again, marry again, love again, and outlive that family too. Neither choice is cowardly, and neither is free. The grief lives in the most ordinary place there is, which is a marriage.

A few threads run through that range, and each of them is a way a house already knows its own people.

A Long-Lived never crosses another’s home threshold uninvited. It is held as the deepest good manners, the mark of someone safe to let in. Inside a family this softens into something tender. To be welcomed across a Long-Lived’s own threshold, or to welcome them across yours without a thought, is a real intimacy. A door held open is how this world says you are mine and I am yours. A door refused is felt more than a Long-Lived will ever say.

A person who died and Returned comes home, and contrary to what an outsider expects, they are not cold. They are calm, deliberate, unafraid, and quietly respected, and their loved ones get them back. The chill comes only if the Purpose lapses. The Purpose is the unfinished thing that holds them here, and a Returned who neglects it runs cold. The living can feel the wrongness at a touch. So a Returned’s family learns a hard and intimate literacy. You can tell, by an embrace, whether the one you love is tending what holds them here. A warm embrace means they are well. A cold one is a family emergency dressed as a hug.

Two-Bodied bloodlines are family lines. The Condition runs in blood, and children of a Two-Bodied parent usually Turn the same animal, so wolf-folk, hawk-folk, and otter-folk are real extended families. The family animal, the Condition, and often the family trade descend as a single inheritance. Marrying into such a line is marrying into a shape your children will likely wear.

Every parent lives the same open question until the child’s tenth year: what will they become, or will they be Kept? In a devout home a parent will say the Mother will give what the child can carry. In an anxious one the decade is quiet dread, or ambition. Parents who carry a heritable Condition, Two-Bodied especially, can half-guess. Most cannot. The Leaf-Fall, the rite inside Turning-Week when the child stands under the Tree, is therefore not only the civic hour of the year but the emotional hinge of a family’s life, the day you finally meet who your child has been becoming all along. In the Walking Years, when a Giving still required the walk to Thaeloren, the Awakening Tree, the question had a prior, which was whether the household could get there at all. A household that could walk only one child still lives in the present as two siblings, one Given at the origin and one UnTurned, who never stood under a Tree. Folk still call that UnTurned child Kept. The law does not.

Mixed-Kind children are allowed. Two mainland Kinds may sit in one body, the way the rules already allow a mixed ancestry, and a fox-and-seal child, Kitsune and Selkie together, is as ordinary as a Returned husband. Nobody files the marriage. Nobody calls it marrying out. The live question is whose kitchen the summer before they Turn, not whether the marriage was permitted. Yumboe, the people of the Sundering Isle, are the exception. A Yumboe at the table needs the GM’s leave, because they are mythic-rare off the isle, and if one is seated they are the full Kind, never a mix. A child of a Yumboe and a mainlander is a full Yumboe, under that same leave, or the mainland Kind, with at most a story people tell about the child. There is never a half.

Medicine: miraculous, and strange to outside eyes

Medicine in the Turning is astonishing for a late-medieval world, a world of guilds and bone and herb with no anaesthetic worth the name, and it is astonishing for one reason. The work a Condition makes possible shows up hardest at the sickbed and the deathbed. Two Conditions turn a clinic into something a world of this technology should not have. To anyone standing outside it, the room holds wonder and wrongness together.

The Stilled are the surgeons. A stiller’s Gaze arrests motion. It holds a wound from bleeding, slows a poison’s spread through the blood, and keeps a patient perfectly still under the knife without holding them down. It does not petrify, and it does not harm. It simply stops what is moving, for a beat. In a world that cannot halt a hemorrhage any other way, this is the difference between a survivable operation and a death. The best surgeons in the world are Stilled, and a great infirmary is built around them. Sit in that room as an outsider and watch what it is. A surgeon’s flat, patient gaze freezes the blood in the vein on command, and the surgeon works fast because the Grey is filling as they work. The Grey is the stillness the Gaze leaves in the surgeon, the clock of their Tithe, and a Grey left full locks their own limb to stone. They drill and spar between patients to burn it off. The most gifted healers in the world are also the most tightly licensed and quietly feared. The same gaze that saves you on the table can, misused, hold a person helpless, and it is the one the law watches hardest. Wonder and dread, one person, one room.

The Returned do the work that kills the living. Plague wards, mine collapses, the recovery of bodies from places the living cannot safely go, and the tending of the dead: this is Returned work, done by those death cannot take a second time until their Purpose is met. A Turning mortuary is staffed by the Returned, people who have been dead, calmly and well. A plague ward that would empty a town’s living physicians is walked by Returned who are unshaken by rot and contagion. To an outsider this is ghoulish. Inside, it is simply respected. The Returned are the reason a plague does not take the doctors too, and everyone knows it. There is a real tenderness in it as well. No one speaks for the dead, or tends them, as gently as someone who has been dead.

The rest of medicine is ordinary, and ordinarily unequal. Midwives, bonesetters, herbalists, and the Answered’s craft turned to apothecary and instrument-making do the everyday care. More of the population carries a useful becoming, so that everyday care is better staffed than a town of this technology would otherwise manage. The care that makes the world exceptional is not evenly available. The great Stilled infirmaries and the deathless-endowed hospitals stand in the rich, Tree-dense core. A frontier town makes do with a travelling stiller if it is lucky, and with cloth, a rope, and a prayer if it is not. The deepest inequity is the one the economy already names. You can be too poor to stay whole, and the medicine that treats a lapsing Condition is the medicine the poor can least reach. The wonder is real. So is the queue outside it.

Living in a Turning town: city design

A city here is shaped by a fact no other world’s city has to build for. Most of its adults have an upkeep, and some of those upkeeps are dangerous or expensive to meet. So the town builds for the Tithe the way it builds for water and waste, as civic infrastructure, visible and load-bearing.

Every town is organized around its Turning Tree. It is the civic and sacred heart, the site of the year’s most-attended week, the thing the oldest quarter grew up around. You can read a town’s age and standing in its Tree. A mature grafted Tree, grown from a cutting of an older one, means an old town where the giving runs thick. A young Tree, or none, means a new settlement or a frontier one. Geography and the street plan both point back to it. Older uses sit in the same square, a stone, an upper room, a road that ends at the boughs. If you want one of those squares under your feet, Harrow’s Green is the neighbour’s canopy on Heskoren’s live front, and new towns still say they Turned at Harrow’s Tree before they had their own. The three hamlets past the ford can see that green from the water, and they still have to send their ten-year-olds on. Further out, the Third Hearth is the road-house on the Near Mile that stayed an inn, the bed still made, and Ornsael is the well-town on the Rain-Shadow, where the drink that made people stop is leaving. When the question is a whole polity rather than one square, the seats are Eolvaeth in the Waiting Lands, Orentel on the Ledger Coast, and Maiethlir under the Tallied Crown.

A village watches a Turning as one circle. A city of tens of thousands does not pretend to be one. Turning-Week is still the civic festival, and the legal witness is the hearth that brought the child, the street or the quay-gang or the courtyard. The square is full. The memory is nested.

Where the polity treats provision as a public good, the town furnishes it in the open, and these buildings are as ordinary in the street as a well or a market cross. They are wells, not granaries. Grain still feeds the city. The lots and the halls keep a minority whole, and they keep a Cry, a Far-Voiced voice breaking loose, out of the market.

Everyday speech calls the venting-hall the ael-hall, pronounced AYL, “the airing.” It is part concert hall and part a place to let the voice out, and it often is the town’s performance venue as well. In Vaethorn, the Waiting Lands, the same building is the gift-hall. On Lestrand, the Ledger Coast, it is the release-house, and it is also the playhouse. In Threnmaieth, the Tallied Crown, it is the counted hall.

The greens are the potted groves and the garden-commons, the living plants a Taken-In in the city rests on so they do not go to seed indoors. Everyday speech just says the greens. A devout town in the Waiting Lands calls the same ground the Mother’s green, after the Mother the devout name, and holds it in common. On the Ledger Coast it is the leaf-lot, rented by the season. Under the Tallied Crown it is the tended green, because the crown is who furnishes it.

The long-house of books is the endowed library. It feeds a Long-Lived’s need to learn something genuinely new, and a Long-Lived is often the person who built it. In the Waiting Lands that gift is called the deathless gift, because the patron does not die. On the Ledger Coast the money set aside is the endowment, or simply the house. The Tallied Crown calls the shelves the crown archive, and the books sit with the crown.

Out at the edge, the ranging is the commons where the Two-Bodied can be their other selves. The Waiting Lands call it the wild-leave, which is leave to go out into the wild. The Ledger Coast calls it the beast-yard and hires the yard. The Tallied Crown calls it the ranging-roll, because someone writes down who went.

The night-watch and the ward-watch are part of the same street. They hold a person until morning, and at a gate they ask three things: a name, the last hearth, and who stands. They are not police sent after a Condition.

The work that can harm a bystander sits where such work always sits, at the margins. Stilled infirmaries and Answered workshops, fire and forge and tide, are guild-quartered and set slightly apart. The Returned’s mortuaries and plague-work sit at the town’s edge, near the dead. They sit there for the same reason a tannery sits downwind, and not from disgust.

Ordinary houses bend quietly to what the people in them have become. Windows open, and rooms stay green, for a Taken-In guest. An evening’s rhythm is built around a Far-Voiced’s vent. A threshold is a place a Long-Lived waits to be asked across. You can read the household in the house.

Core and frontier show in how much of that provision is there at all. Dense, Tree-rich towns are thick with it. Frontier settlements have little of it and improvise. How much of a town’s Tithe-provision is public, private, or simply missing tells you where that town sits.

How polities vary (domestic faces)

Everyday life varies on the same three choices as the law and the economy: how gift-devout the place is, how many healthy Trees it has, and how far the state reaches into a house. Three stances recur.

The Warm (high theology). In a Warm house the gift-theology is simply how the family talks. A child’s Turning is a joyous sacrament, a mixed household is read as blessings compounded, the Tithe is furnished in the open, and the sick are tended as people whose gifts must be kept whole. The soft injustice reaches the same hearth. The Kept child is pitied for being passed over, marrying “beneath your gift” is quietly frowned on, and the family is expected to spend its members’ Conditions as the community sees fit, so the love and the pressure arrive in the same kindness.

The Watchful (governance at its extreme). A crown that keeps a roll of persons, as the Tallied Crown and the Worn Count do, does not stop at the door. Marriages of heritable Conditions may be noticed and then encouraged or discouraged, a child’s Turning is an event the state records, and the medicine that furnishes a Tithe runs through channels the crown controls. The cold injustice is that domestic surveillance. A household whose upkeep and bloodline are both on file cannot easily refuse the crown anything.

The Frontier (low reach). Infrastructure, medicine, and ceremony all run thin, so families improvise their own Tithe-provision or do without, and a travelling stiller is a rare blessing. The Taken-In, whom core cities keep at arm’s length, are neighbours and kin here, the backbone of the place. No one polices your marriage or your gift. A lapsing Condition may have no infirmary to reach, and an untrained Struck child, someone the change came to outside a guild, may have no guild to catch them. The feeling runs warm. The net under a lapse is thin.

A place’s daily texture is set by all three choices at once. A devout frontier holds joyous Turnings with almost no infirmary behind them. A secular Tree-rich republic has superb medicine and a marriage market that shrugs at theology. A Watchful-and-pious core turns the sacrament of a child’s Turning into a state census with a hymn over it.

When the town buries

A funeral is the hour a street has a body to carry. It is a walk, and then a meal, and then a door. It is not a Turning. Nobody asks the Tree what the dead person was, and nobody stands the body under the branches for a colour.

The body is washed in the house, often by someone who is Returned, because that labour is already their street. The family still chooses the cloth. Then the neighbours carry the body. In a town with a Tree, the carry goes past the canopy, along the street the person used when they were alive, and the body is not stood under the boughs. A tree-warden may walk with the house. If the house wants a name said, the warden says Maieth, the short name the devout use for the Leaf-Mother, and says it the way a neighbour would. If the house has asked for silence, the warden walks without speaking. Both of those walks are the same office.

Neighbours bring food to the door, and the door stays open through the meal. The person who is going to sleep in the house that night is the one who shuts it, or else the person the house has asked.

A Long-Lived who loved the dead waits on the step until someone says come in. That waiting is already how a household treats a deathless life, a life long enough that the funerals in it have to be counted, and this hour is one of them. It is still a door and a loaf.

Because a mixed house is the usual house, the meal is mixed, and each person does their own small rite at their own bowl. Nobody stops the eating to argue which name ought to come first. That argument can have the time after the dishes. A Motherfaith sibling says Maieth over their own bowl and means the life that has ended. A sibling of the Watching does not thank a giver. They talk about the dead as they were at the stall in Gift-month, the summer month after Turning-Week, when the colours have settled: the coat, the argument, the way they counted change.

If the dead kept a book, a Settler of the Fair Hand closes it on the table, where the room can see the last line, and does not write a new one. A kin-speaker of the Old Ways sets a little of the meal at the threshold, and if the dead kept those ways, the rest of the food goes to the door once the street has finished. Ancestors in that rite are kin who stayed in the ground. A return is a different matter, a Returned person still living a neighbour’s life, and you do not summon one. The food at the threshold is the funeral. It is not a calling.

Nobody Speaks a fall. To Speak, at a living child’s Leaf-Fall, is to say aloud whether the Tree gave a colour or a hug. Speaking a fall over the dead would mean naming a colour as if the Tree were being asked to answer, and the room does not do it. A neighbour who tries is walked outside by whoever is nearest the pot.

On a dock, if the dead person worked the water at Orentel, the gang carries the box along the quay. The box does not go under Tallo, the quay’s name for its Tree, to be read. Some of the gang say “fair wind, fair term,” because that is the sentence they already have for a leaving. Some of them will not say it, because they keep that sentence for a hull that is still going out. Both of those things happen in the same hour, and the gang does not stop the carry to settle which is right. If there is a book, it is closed where the gang can see that it has been closed. Salt sits on the Tree’s roots in Eolthael, Turning-month, the month of the High Solstice. People say it is the tide, and the tide does not reach the rise. Orentel will not say why the salt is there. The salt is not part of this hour.

Eolvaeth does not send off to a Tree-town to borrow a warden it does not have. If the warden is already in the vale, that warden may walk with the house. If the town sent its children somewhere else to Turn that summer, the town buries its dead with the people who stayed. The pot that feeds the mourners is the gift-hall’s, and the food goes to the door the dead person kept. A wet leaf lies on the spring, or too many, or none. The leaf is the spring’s business. It is not a funeral token. They will not say why it is there.

At Ndenjoo the body is carried above the tide, and the hall does not lay a second empty plate for the dead. The dead person’s own cup is set in the place that was already laid. It sits there for one night, and then it goes back onto the shelf. Whether anyone speaks a name is the argument the valley already knows how to have, and that argument waits until the dishes are done. The shore does not come up the hill to invent a rite on the sand.

The guest-meal

The bowl is set down before anyone asks the guest who they are. That order travels from town to town. Everything after the bowl is the stance the street was already keeping.

In Maiethlir, in a kitchen on a thaw-street, there is bread and there are greens, and the river is loud enough that people can talk over it. The guest is a walker come from the vale, with a letter and with wet shoes. They sit, and they eat, and only then does someone ask, “Of where?” The guest says the vale. Nobody asks what colour they are, or whether any leaf fell for them at all. The host says Maieth over the host’s own bowl, and does not hand that name to the guest to say. A Watcher in the same kitchen tells the guest what is in the pot, greens and a bone and too much salt, and then stops. A Settler at the end of the bench does not open a book. The only thing waiting to be settled is the letter, and the letter can wait until the shoes are dry.

At Orentel the first bread is eaten standing, at a barrel, where the crane can be seen. If you sit down before that bread, you are claiming a berth you have not paid for. After the bread, if no paper is open, there is a chair, and they ask which berth the guest holds. The guest has none, and the guest still eats. If a filing house has a paper open, the house-name is spoken before anyone offers the chair. A house-name is an old given name that stuck to a family line, that place’s own word, and it is not a surname brought in from somewhere else. While the paper is open, a clerk gets the house first and then the given name. Shut the paper, and the quay goes back to asking where you are from. The bowl does not wait for the house to finish its paper. A book-hand who wants the guest’s affairs written in ink is told, by the person who cut the bread, to come back and do that writing on the quay in the morning.

The guest who turns up in Eolvaeth is often the visit turned around: a clerk from the core who came to see a week and found a pot. If the house is thin, that clerk is fed out of the gift-hall. Nobody promises the guest that the wood will speak. If the clerk asks about the leaf on the spring, someone passes the bread instead of answering. The leaf stays unexplained, and they will not say why. A walker who arrived with a cohort, the group the town sent on to another Tree, eats with that cohort. The town does not lay a separate table for people who stood somewhere else this summer.

On the first night at Ndenjoo, the guest does not serve the food, and does not sit in the place that is set back from the board. That place is already kept. On the second night a plate is put into the guest’s hands to carry, and someone says the sentence the hall already lives by. The words of that sentence belong to the hall. What this hour has is the plate. That second supper is how the hall counts you as kin on the isle. It does not become a last hearth you can name to a mainland watch, and it does not become papers. On the one night of the moon sailors call Yoltal, the hall eats the heel of the loaf first. Every other night the heel is last, or it goes to the goats. A guest who asks why is given more bread. They will not say why.

If someone asks what the guest is before the bowl has been set down, the room goes quiet. The person nearest the pot puts the bowl down anyway. Talk may start again when the guest takes a second bite, or it may not start again at all. There is no speech kept in reserve to repair the asking. A host who wants a doctrine can have one after the dishes, taken from whichever faith that host already keeps.

What a house keeps

When a town needs work done, it hires a person. The work people expect from a made thing is already someone’s job. An Answered coaxes stone, water, fire, or air, and then goes home. A Stilled holds a body still for a knife. A mill-hand sets the stones, a hull-wright walks a hull, and a road-mend leaves a shovel in the bank. Those are people. A Clank is a Kind, a person born a Clank, who mends flood-walls, hulls, mills, and lofts alongside everyone else who does that work. A made thing is a thing, and a Clank is a person.

Most towns do not have one. If a scene has a thing that keeps working with nobody in it, a crane left running, a mill someone swears turns with nobody at the stones, or a figure of clay, then it has a maker and a problem. The maker is a person, or was one. The problem is why the thing is still doing the work: the stop broke, the maker left a debt unfinished, or a story got ahead of the mechanism. Name both before the scene goes on. It has no Kind, no Condition, and no hearth, and it owes no Tithe. It has no domain, because a domain is a job a person does. If the work needs doing, send the person whose job it is. A town without that problem does not keep one on a shelf.

Ordinary kit is whatever that ground already needed, clothing and tools, and it is not a ladder of better kit. Nothing here is rarer than the next town’s version of the same need. A coat from this list keeps the weather off. It is not armor unless the wearer is also wearing armor. If someone fights with one of the tools, it counts as the smallest one-handed weapon in the rules, and the town that made it adds nothing.

Place What they keep Why it is there
Rain-Wall shelves, the passes above Lirorn An oiled wool coat The shelf is wet and cold, and a quay shirt does not finish the walk.
Orentel’s quays A short hook, and a coat waxed against brine The quay is lines, crates, and salt. The hook pulls. The coat is for the spray.
A young graft on the Heskoren live front A pruning knife, and a wind cloak The wood is new and the weather is not. The knife is a tender’s tool, and it is not the One Knife.
Rain-Shadow herds, toward the Dry Stair and Ornsael A goat-hair blanket, and a water-skin The days are dry and the well is shared. The blanket is the herd’s hair, felted.
Kumbaan halls and shallows A peat cloak, and a short knife for mussels Smoke, rain, and the rocks. The cloak is for the hall and the terrace, and it does not cross the storm-wall.
Mother-core orchards Beeswax They keep it for the hives, and for the halls that are owed wax when the blossom fails.

Motherwood is not on this list. A scion, a cutting of a Turning Tree carried for planting, is a warden’s cargo, not a material a person buys. The Spent Leaf and the Closed Lamp are not craft stock.

The pruning knife is not the blade people mean when they say “the knife.” One house on the Near Mile hangs a kitchen knife on a ribbon beside a scorch on an old pot-ring. The people in the house know which summer that was. It was the Closing, the war that ended when the riders went home, and they do not turn out for it. The Low Wall is another stone, from another dig, and a knife-ribbon left at that wall was left in error. Strangers call the Near Mile knife the nameless knife, because they want the first blade to have a handle they can buy. The house will not sell it as that. It is their kitchen knife. The summer is theirs, and the scorch is on their pot. A person can take it down and hold it. In a fight it is a small one-handed blade, the smallest such weapon in the rules, and the ribbon adds nothing. The single blade people mean when they say the knife has not been produced. Nobody has named who made the First Cut.

Tithe-Infrastructure and Guilds

People call this work the furnishing, or simply the greens and the halls. There is no church-name set over the whole of it. In the Waiting Lands, which write themselves Vaethorn, the same work is the gift-works. On the Ledger Coast, written Lestrand, it is the provision. Under the Tallied Crown, written Threnmaieth, the clerks file it as the counted channel.

What the sector does is keep people whole enough, in public, and then stop at the gate. A Condition is a change a person comes to carry. A Tithe is the upkeep that change keeps demanding, the living ground or the hour or the new page a person has to have if the change is going to stay livable. The furnishing is the town’s way of meeting that upkeep until the share runs out. After the share, the Slide will still sell a week. What the Slide rents is not falling, one week of green or of an outlet or of a new page, and the week is measured so the person does not quite get free.

The greens-keepers and the hall-keepers are parts of this sector. They keep a lot or an hour, and they are not houses with colleges of their own. The Stillers and the element-guilds remain craft-guilds. They stamp a licence where a use can hurt someone standing nearby. The Intake is the shed that does not face the street. A person newly Struck, changed outside the childhood ceremony and not yet safe to stand next to, is caught there before the town reaches for a rope.

Shape of the sector

Furnishing and ticketing are two jobs. A town may put both under one roof, and they stay two jobs even then. Furnishing is the share of upkeep: a bed of living dirt, a scheduled hour, a library that is open. Ticketing is the licence for a hazardous act. The product of the official door is a person who can walk away until tomorrow. The Slide’s product is a person who cannot. The town is glad of both. On an ordinary day the guilds pretend not to know the week-keepers next door. When an official gate closes on purpose, or a wilt or a Cry can be walked from that gate to the room that still opens, the pretence is over, because the two doors are then serving the same street, and the town has to say so.

A ticket names a competence, the practiced skill, and not the Condition itself. The people who might be asked for one are a large minority, about three in ten, the Stilled, the Far-Voiced, and the Answered, if they practise the use that can hurt a bystander. The papers actually issued are fewer than that, and fewer again on a frontier where a rope is as likely as a stool. Three guilds keep the papers, and they keep no shared list. A stiller cannot ask the element-guilds for every Answered person in the city. The state watches the charter, the guild’s leave to operate, and it cannot ask for a list of this city’s Far-Voiced. The arrangement makes its own friction. Guilds guard their monopolies. A ticket can start to be treated as a thing the guild holds, and an unlicensed practitioner threatens the charter as much as the street.

There is no Furnishing Seat, no college set over the other towns. A town keeps its own lot and its own hall. A deathless house, a house of people who do not die of age, endows its own stacks of books. Nothing in this sector tells a far commons how to water a bed.

Who furnishes what

Each gate has a shape of enough, a moment when it closes, and a place the need goes when the gate has shut. The official door does not follow you past that line.

Gate Form of enough Closes when Where the need goes
Green, the greens-keepers A night or an hour on living dirt, for a Taken-In person, someone the wild has taken partway into itself, who wilts without living ground. The bed-slate is a list of plants. The share is gone. They will not walk three streets. A cousin’s pot. They do not say the cousin’s name. That private pot, once it is rented, is the Slide.
Outlet, the hall-keepers A scheduled Cry, a boards-hour, or a sweep-hour, the hour a person can still afford when a bench is beyond them. The Voice-ticket sits on the same stool. A Cry is a Far-Voiced feeling breaking into everyone in earshot. It is a blow, not a command. The lamps. A missed hour is a missed hour. A room that still shuts. They do not say the room’s name.
Novelty A long-house of books, where a deathless chair still sits. What it furnishes is something genuinely new, which is the upkeep of a Long-Lived person, someone who does not die of age and who fades without it. Closing. They will not carry a rumour to a fade shut in a room. A junior who extends a page. That junior has started a week.
Unbound warmth Almost none. An Unbound person is what a finished contract leaves behind, free of the Terms and missing the piece the contract took, and the upkeep is connection. Family, an attic, or a paid sitting is what there is. The sector has no hour to close. None. The sector cannot buy being known.
Bound Terms An honest table, and the Book-Hands, the clerks who close a civic year. A Bound person swore a contract and is still under its Terms. This is not a body-ticket. The Whisper, the contract’s voice, cannot command another person’s will. The year closes. The Terms do not. The Holding Desk, the back room that will write a next term when the honest stamp has already closed.
Returned purpose Cannot be furnished. A Returned person died with a purpose unfinished and came back to it. A purpose is not a share the sector can hand over, and no employer can supply a vengeance, a vow, or a person still to find. — None.
Two-Bodied ranging Civic land, and no ticket. A Two-Bodied person carries a second, animal body, and the upkeep is time spent as that animal. — None.

The three tickets are for danger to others only. The person holds the paper. The craft issues it.

What Who holds paper Who does not
The Stilled, a personal Gaze-ticket. The Gaze is the look that holds a moment still. Anyone who Gazes in public, including surgeons, riot-lines, and demolition. Most stillers hold one, because the vocation is the Gaze. The Stillers stamp it. It is the strictest ticket, because the same look can, misused, leave a person helpless in a fight. A Stilled person who never Gazes, which is rare, though the guild still wants that person in the yard.
Far-Voiced, a Voice-ticket and a hall-hour. Those who Cry in a crowd or keep a scheduled hour: criers, performers, and sworn witnesses. The hall-keepers stamp the competence and sell the hour at the same desk. A field-voice who vents at the hedge. The hall-slate is a list of hours, not of every blue-leaf in the city. Blue-leaf is the ordinary name for the leaf a Far-Voiced child draws.
The Answered, a shop charter and a journeyman-mark. An Answered person is someone an element answered, and goes on answering. Those who let an element speak in a crowded yard. The element-guilds, the Crae, charter the door, and journeymen sit under that charter. A Tide-Answered person on their own boat, under a master’s eye. They answer to the shop. The shop does not keep a person-file.
Bound, a table, not a body-ticket. No licence is issued for the body. The honest table hears the Terms. A Bound person is not counted among the licensed.
No ticket. — Two-Bodied, Long-Lived, Returned, the Taken-In, the Unbound, Phoenix, and all the Kept. Phoenix, a single person the town cannot mistake for anyone else, is a political problem and not a licence. The Kept are the people a Tree hugged and left without a Condition. Most people hold no ticket. They are simply neighbours.

The Intake is the shared shed of those three ticket-yards. It catches a raw Struck person before anything happens in public, and the work has succeeded when nothing is heard of it afterwards.

Fellowships

A mill, a hull, and a road each have people who keep them through a season, and those people are the fellowships. The work is the ordinary keeping of that mill, that hull, or that road, and it does not licence a body. The licences already written stay where they are: the Stillers stamp a Gaze, the element-guilds stamp an element, the hall-keepers stamp a Voice-ticket, and the Intake catches a raw Struck person before the town reaches for a rope. A mill-share, a hull-wright, and a road-mend do not stamp any of those. They will not rent a week, which is the Slide’s rental, or refinance a Term, which is the paper the Holding Desk refinances when the honest stamp has closed, or sell a standing, which is the witness the Standing Trade sells, a person paid to say they were there when a town was not.

A Gale-Answered miller, an Answered person whose element is the wind, can hold an element-guild ticket for that wind and still owe a share of grain. The ticket is the hazardous act, letting the element speak. The share is the season of work. A Tide-Answered wright can hold a ticket for the water and still be the person who walks the hull. A Root-Answered mender can hold a ticket for the stone and still be the person with the shovel. In each yard the fellowship is the season, and the ticket is only the act.

You are of a fellowship when you have kept the thing through a season and someone of it will say so. There is no Seat set over the other towns, and no apprenticeship a crown confirms. The fellowship does not ask what Kind a person was born, the ancestry they arrived with, and it does not keep a chapter of any born people. Kumbaan, the Sundering Isle beyond the storm-wall of weather, current, and reef, does not keep these three. No graft ever crossed to that isle, so there is no race to share, no quay that classes a hull, and no Mile to mend. They will not follow a Taken-In person home. That walk belongs to the greens-keepers. There is no town where the fellowship is the government, and there is no boss to send for.

The mill-share. A miller takes a share of the grain that comes through the mill, and the fellowship is the people who will say whose race this is, the mill-race that turns the stones, and whose share of that grain is owed.

At the Mill-hold the miller is not the person the square turns to, and the share is still taken. When the culvert is opened to keep water off the Hand, that town’s Turning Tree, the race drops, and a mill-hand is already there with a count of lost turns. They do not Speak a colour, which would be naming a leaf in the square, and they do not carry a scion. A scion is living wood cut to plant a Tree, and that cart belongs to a Road-hand.

A Gale-house may coax the wind at a mill. If the person is Answered and lets the element speak, so that the wind answers the hands rather than the room, the coaxing is a ticket. The stones, the sacks, and the share belong to this fellowship even when nobody in the mill is Answered.

When the race is drawn down, the mill-share sets the stones and leaves one measure of last year’s grain on the lip until the water comes back. They will not say why.

Threnmaieth would like that measure on a roll of persons. The mill-share keeps it with the grain. The Walled Book, the closed house that ranks the people who live inside its walls, can give those people a turn of work at a mill. That turn is the Book’s assignment of a person. It is not a share of the grain.

The hull-wrights. They know whether a hull will take water, and they look at the bend, the caulk, and the line to know it.

The Hinge Shore decides whether a hull is a pilgrim, a pot, or cargo, and the Book-Hands stamp the paper that records the class. A Tide-Answered person may work the bend under an element-guild ticket. The hull-wrights do not classify the cargo, do not set the Hush-rate, the single charge on a crossing of the Old Crossing, and do not sell a witness who will say I was there. The Standing Trade sells that witness. This fellowship sells a hull that floats.

On the Down-Bank there is no hull yet. A traveler who rehearses a hull-class at an inn is early, and a wright who starts the classification there has left the craft and begun the Hinge Shore’s job. At Denlad a tied hull is a hull waiting out weather. The wright will not call it a hold and will not charge a house-share for the tying. At Orentel the fellowship sits under the crane. It is not the White Note House, and it does not keep the berth.

Netstrand charters hulls. The charter is a crossing, and the wright is the person who will still walk the hull after the quote is written.

Before a new hull takes water, the hull-wrights walk it once empty, from stem to stern, and do not speak. They will not say why.

The road-mend. They fill a hole, clear a ford, and shore a culvert. The stretches they keep are the Near Mile, the inland walk through the Motherland, the spur that stops at Nelath, and the days along the Down-Bank.

They are not Road-hands. A Road-hand carries living wood, and a mender carries a shovel. They do not ask a traveler for a name, a last hearth, and who stands for them. Those questions belong to the watch, which holds a person until morning and does not keep the answers past dawn.

A person on a named walk is still vouched as a walker by the road, which means the road itself is what says they may walk it, and the mend is why the road is still there to walk. At Nelath the road ends at the boughs, so the mend stops with it. They do not cut the thorns back to make the spur go on. The town already decided where the road ends.

The Walled Book can give a turn on the road to a person who lives inside its walls. A mender on that page still knows the work. The assignment is the Book’s.

At the first ford after a town, they leave the shovel standing in the bank overnight after a mend. They will not say why.

The work people hire

When the work needs doing, people hire a craft. They do not enroll in a school of magic to get it.

A Daggerheart domain card is a job the town already pays someone to do, and the nine domains below are those jobs. The cards stay on the SRD, and this chapter does not copy them, because a class on a sheet is how the table plays the jobs. A domain card does not Turn anyone, which means it does not make a person into a Condition. If the same person has both, each one does what its own card says: the Tithe ticks only from the Condition, and the domain card still does what the SRD printed. A licence is still a licence. None of those papers comes off a domain card, and the fellowships still do not stamp a body.

Domain The job
Arcana Shaping heat, water, stone, air, or a light a workshop already charges for, the same family of work as an Answered coax. The card is the craft. The Condition is the element that answered a person for life.
Blade A weapon in the hand, a watch holding someone until morning, a pruning knife or a kitchen knife, or a cohort walking children to a sound Hand, a sound Tree.
Bone Knowing where to stand, who is tired, and which bank will go, which is reading a fight the way a road-mend reads a ford.
Codex Paper, minutes, a copy, and a count, the work of a Book-hand’s table. Reading a page is not Speaking a colour.
Grace A guest-meal, a factor’s terms, or a voice that asks. The hazardous Cry stays on the hall-keepers’ ticket. This job is the ask, not that Cry.
Midnight A shut door, a night’s work, or a trade that does not want a square. The Slide keeps its own note for that trade.
Sage Ground, herd, weather, and the bark of a young graft, which is a greens-keeper’s eye. The Taken-In remain their own card.
Splendor The room after harm, the wash and the light and the pot and the table once a stiller’s gaze is done. Phoenix fire stays with Phoenix.
Valor Standing a gap, whether that is a flood-wall or a child walked to a sound Hand. The watch, and the cohort it sends, is the civic hold.

An Answered person who also carries an Arcana card has a Tithe and a craft, and what it means for that person to be idle is already said with the Answered: an element left unused will speak whether or not the shop is paying. A Kept person with the same card has the craft, and no element that lets go in a crowded room. The town can tell those two people apart by the work, and by whether the workshop has a plan for a day off.

At Leaf-Fall, the week the door is open and a child can stand under a Tree, a warden says the colour, or says that the child was held. The square hears what the leaf did. That sentence is the Speaking. It is not a spell, and it does not use a Spellcast trait, the trait a spell would call on. Hope does not buy a colour. A warden cannot Speak a person into a Condition who is not standing under a sound Tree in the week the door is open. When a colour is misspoken, it is corrected, and the week is not run again.

The long-house (novelty without a new order)

A Long-Lived house that has endowed a library is already this sector. What that house furnishes is something genuinely new. The money goes out into the stacks, and a deathless member of the house still sits the chair and names the scholars, which is how an endowment keeps the steering after the coin has left. The Pourers, a circle of Long-Lived who meet at a shelf in a deathless library, keep one such shelf on the Ledger Coast. Staff are often the Kept, people with no Tithe of their own, able to fetch and to stay. What the house will not furnish is a page at a time to a person who cannot walk in. They will not carry a rumour to a fade shut in a room. A junior who extends a page, the way a clerk extends a novelty subscription one more week, has started the Slide’s week beside the long-house.

The gate (the sector’s shared courtesy)

Every official door stops at a line the town has agreed to call enough. The greens-keeper keeps the lot, and does not walk the room where someone is already wilting. The hall-keeper keeps the hour, and does not open the side door after the lamps for a voice that missed its slate. The long-house is open to a person who can walk in, and it will not carry news to a Long-Lived shut in a room. The ticket-house trains the child who was Given the colour, and stamps the adult who has become competent. The raw Struck person is the Intake’s problem. The guild is glad to forget the shed if the catching-year, the in-house word for that week, stays quiet.

The Slide begins where that line is. The two houses can meet, and they do not merge. A hall that runs late on purpose is already arguing with a week-rent that still opens. The worst of it is a public wilt or a Cry in the market that the official door caused by closing.

The other houses touch the gate without becoming it. A tree-warden points a newly Given child at a lot or a hall, and does not licence anyone. The lot and the hall decide who gets the bed or the hour. A Book-hand’s term may assume a greens-share, or an hour on the seventh day. If the lot or the slate is full, the term is unpayable that day, and the book records it as owing. The Holding Desk is not this sector. A Bound person’s civic year may assume a hall. The desk downstairs does not furnish one. A Taken-In door-keeper, one of the people who keep the older doors a later Strike can come through, may live on a lot. The courtesy of that door does not give anyone a bed.

Under the Tallied Crown the hall and the green are the channel, the share the roll can open or shut. Videm (VEE-dem), the channel-clerk, runs the counted hall and the slate that is supposed to match the tended green, and will say the channel held while someone three streets off is already wilting. Sirtal (SEER-tal), the warrant-hand, writes the warrant that withholds the share until a name sits still. A lot that still has beds, and a share Sirtal will not open, are the same street.

What follows is a closing-notice, nailed to a lot-gate and, in the same hand, to a hall door. The back of the sheet is last week’s notice, not taken down.

Share is enough. Hour is enough. After close we do not walk the rooms. After the lamps we do not open the side door. If you have already wilted, the lot is still the lot — come when we open. If you have already cried in the street, the hall is still the hall — come at open, not now. If you cannot wait, we do not know a pot. We do not know a room. The town is glad. File that as weather if you must. It is a door.

The keepers do know a cousin’s pot, and they do know a room that still shuts. The notice says they do not, so that neither the lot nor the hall is blamed for what the pot and the room do. The town is glad of both, the official gate and the week that opens when the gate has shut.

How they live in the three corners

In the Waiting Lands the works are commons-minded, and the purse is thin. A cousin’s field stands in when the lot is short. You were helped, so the valley expects you to spend the gift as it asks, and when the share fails the Slide is a private pot they call the last pot, and also gift-credit.

On the Ledger Coast the provision is posted and charged by the season. You can be priced out of staying whole, and after the fee fails the Slide is week-rent.

Under the Tallied Crown the crown furnishes, and the crown holds. Videm holds the channel. The Slide is the late week that channel will not admit failed. Videm knows the week is there, and Sirtal files the leak as the person’s own lapse.

Kumbaan, the Sundering Isle, has no greenhouse and no ael-hall. A wreck walked uphill is a guest. The storm-wall is weather, current, and reef, and a graft never crossed it.

A bed-list is plants, a hall-slate is hours, and a guild-roll names the practitioners of a dangerous art. Only two crowns write persons and the gifts they carry on the same paper. Threnmaieth calls its roll holy and names it the Threnhael. Trenledd, the Worn Count, keeps a roll of persons too, and does not call that roll holy. Road-hands carry living wood, greens-keepers keep the soil, hall-keepers keep an hour, and the ticket-houses keep a licence.

The Greens-Keepers

Greens-keepers keep the garden-commons, the greens, and a leaf-lot, so that a Taken-In person in a stone town has living ground to lie on and does not wilt on a parlour floor. They are a jurisdiction of the furnishing, not a house with a college of its own. They keep the lot, and they do not go looking for anyone who is not at the gate.

Everyday people say greens-keepers, or lot-keepers. In the liturgy they are the Saelhael (SAEL-hael). Sael is sowing, the first green, said “sayl,” and hael is whole, said “hayl,” so the name is the sown-whole. The Waiting Lands’ second word is Mother’s-green hands. The Ledger Coast says lot-keepers, as ordinary as saying gardener. The Tallied Crown files them as the Tended.

Shape of the house

The house is the lot. A town has a strip along the wall, or pots in a yard, or, in the Waiting Lands, a cousin’s field held in common. Whoever waters it, and says who sleeps on which bed tonight, is the house. There is no Green Seat over other towns.

A share gives a night on living dirt, a season on a bed, or a commons-hour. The person should leave able to work. Someone who cannot leave is the Slide’s work, a private pot after the share fails. The keepers will not follow you home with that pot, and they will not open the gate again because the wilt has started in a room they do not walk to.

A bed-slate is a list of plants, rows and tired beds. A person’s name gets onto it because that person is on a bed, not because the lot has started a roll of people. In Threnmaieth the crown already has another list. Videm, who holds the counted channel, wants the beds to match that channel. The lot will not invent a bed to close someone else’s book.

If you meet one

You meet them with dirt under the nails, a key to a gate in a wall, and a slate of rows, and if you are let far enough in you meet last year’s leaf already buried under a new bed. Ask where a Taken-In person sleeps when the rooms are stone. A stone town cannot keep its Taken-In without a lot. Green is free on a farm, and in the city it costs a gate.

Who comes, and when

A Taken-In person who works in town comes because the rooms are stone and the Tithe is due. The keeper gives the share the lot has, a bed or a night or an hour, and writes the bed if anything is written. They will not walk the three streets to the room where the wilt has already started.

A Book-hand comes when a settling assumes a greens-share. The keeper honours the term if there is a bed, and marks the slate full if there is not, so the book becomes owing and the lot does not tell a lie to close it. A crown-clerk in Threnmaieth comes because the tended green is supposed to match the channel. The keepers give the beds they have. They will not pretend a wilt off the lot is not happening, and they will not walk to it.

Almost no one else comes for the share. The week that is not a queue is watering, and turning the rows the slate already names. Grain feeds the town by another door. This gate is the living ground that keeps an exposed person off a parlour floor.

An ordinary week

They open the gate, and that opening is the kindness. A Taken-In person lies down on living ground until the tokens fill, the count of the upkeep coming back up, and then leaves, after which the bed is turned and the next row is watered. Last year’s commons-leaf is buried under a new bed. No one will explain the leaf to a guest. A first-year who asks is told, by whoever is on the gate, that this is how the lot remembers.

When the queue is longer than the wilt, they still open for the share they have, and they close when the share is gone. They know a cousin still has a pot. They do not say the cousin’s name. A child who carries the water can name that cousin. The slate cannot, and the notice on the gate says the lot does not know a pot, so the lot is not blamed for what the pot does.

They do not steal a scion, the living wood a Road-hand carries to plant a Tree, and they do not send a lot to Kumbaan. What they give, they call a share.

Who may keep a lot

The house does not ask what Kind a person was born. You are of the house when you can keep a bed, when the lot is still alive in the dry month, and when the town still sends its Taken-In to you.

How they live in the three corners

In the Waiting Lands, where they are called Mother’s-green hands, the commons is a cousin’s field. They will say they are tending a gift. The quiet obligation is the one the valley keeps: you were laid on the Mother’s green, so you will spend the green as the valley asks. When the field fails, the last pot does the Slide’s work, and they will still call it tending.

On the Ledger Coast, where they are called lot-keepers, the leaf-lot is posted by the season, with coin on the gate. A Taken-In person who cannot pay the season is priced out of this lot. The lot that still opens after the fee has failed is doing the Slide’s week-rent.

Under the Tallied Crown they are filed as the Tended. The crown furnishes the tended green and can withhold it, and the beds are supposed to match the channel. A wilt off the lot is a leak the roll does not want to file. The keepers look like gardeners. What the crown can shut off is the water.

Kumbaan has no greens-keepers, and no lot is sent there.

The gate

Whoever furnishes a provided-for Tithe holds power over the person who needs it. The greens-keepers hold that power and refuse to carry it past the wall. The refusal is the kindness, because they will not own you, and it is the cruelty, because they will not walk three streets. The town is glad either way, because a person who wilts quietly off the lot is not a public hazard. A devout town can say the gift was offered, a Lestrand quay can say the season was posted, and the Tallied Crown can say the channel held.

The need for living land is the Tithe. People built the gate. A lot can be full of beds and still have a queue, and the keepers are then choosing who sleeps on stone.

A bed-slate

The slate inside the gate is plants, which rows are taken and which beds are tired. The words the town is meant to read are the closing-notice nailed on the gate itself, the same sheet a hall door wears in the same hand. Last week’s notice is still on the back.

Share is enough. Hour is enough. After close we do not walk the rooms. After the lamps we do not open the side door. If you have already wilted, the lot is still the lot — come when we open. If you have already cried in the street, the hall is still the hall — come at open, not now. If you cannot wait, we do not know a pot. We do not know a room. The town is glad. File that as weather if you must. It is a door.

The notice is a commons keeping itself to the share, and a little cold about it. The keepers do know a cousin’s pot. The child with the water can name the cousin. The slate cannot, and the leaf under the new bed is not on the notice at all.

The Hall-Keepers

Hall-keepers keep the official outlet and the Far-Voiced ticket in the same building. A Far-Voiced person needs both the scheduled hour and the licence. In the ael-hall, the airing, from ael, to let feeling out, they empty a voice on that schedule, and the building is the town’s playhouse. They furnish enough voice that a person can walk until tomorrow. After the lamps, a room that still shuts belongs to the Slide, and it is not this hall’s side door.

Hall-keepers, or ael-hands, is what people say in every register, from the street to a docket. There is no church-name over them. The Waiting Lands’ second word is gift-hall folk. The Ledger Coast says release-hands, as ordinary as saying box-office. The Tallied Crown files them as counted-hall clerks.

They sell you an hour in which you may feel in earnest, and they will not open after the lamps.

Shape of the house

One building does two jobs. The hall furnishes the outlet, and it stamps the Voice-ticket. The keeper who says your hour is the third is the keeper who says you may stand in a crowded room. The hour is enough: a song, a weeping, a relay-call, a laugh that empties the chest, feeling on purpose where a neighbour paid to hear it. The person should leave emptied and able to work. This house wants you gone until tomorrow.

Each town keeps its own hall, and no seat over the other towns writes to it for leave.

If you meet one

You can tell them by the ink or the chalk on a finger, by the slate of hours, by the stool at the door where the ticket is stamped, and by the one bench nobody sweeps. Ask where a voice can be loud without becoming a Cry in the market. A town with Far-Voiced people and no hall leaves a Book-hand writing owing, and leaves the street waiting for the feeling to land where everyone can hear it.

Who comes, and when

A Given child, after the sea-blue leaf, is apprenticed here. The voice has to be trained before it is a hazard, in breath and projection and venting on purpose, and the ticket comes when the town can stand next to them. The hall does not Speak the colour. The warden already did that.

A working Far-Voiced person, a performer or a crier or a sworn witness, often pays the Tithe by the vocation itself. The hall gives them the stage, the relay-post, or the stand, and stamps the year if the ticket is due, and it will not invent a crisis so they can vent off the slate. A person who has lost that honest stage, posted somewhere isolated or set to dull labor, can buy or be granted a scheduled hour, be emptied, and be sent out. The hall will not open after the lamps. A room that still takes a voice after that belongs to the Slide, and the week it sells is never quite enough for the person to get free.

A Struck Far-Voiced person, raw from the drowning that brings the voice later and untrained, is handed to the Intake. If the Cry is already in the room, a hall-keeper may sit the first hour with the shed. The hall will not stamp a ticket on a raw voice, and it will not leave them in the market.

A Book-hand whose settling assumes a seventh-day hour is honoured when the slate has a hole, and marked full when it does not. Greyhull’s release-house will take that seventh day when the term names it. The hall will not pretend a full house has a bench. In the eighth week, when the passage-money fails, the slip can still be fair, and the person can still owe a book that does not close.

Anyone who came for a play is sold a bench. The working voices pay their Tithe as the show. The hall will not stop a performance to process a ticket. The show is the Tithe for the people on the boards, and a night out for the people who paid to hear it.

An ordinary week

Morning is the slate, with the hours named, the relay-posts listed, a child’s breath-lesson in the cold hall, and the ticket-desk a stool by the door. Evening is the house, feeling in earnest and on purpose, where a neighbour paid to hear it. One seat is never swept. The line people use for it is, “That’s the first Cry’s seat.” No one will explain which Cry.

When a voice misses its hour, the keeper does not open the side door. They know a room that still shuts, and they do not say the room’s name. A raw Struck person is the Intake’s, and the hall will not stamp that ticket. They do not run a mission-hall on Kumbaan.

Who may keep a hall

The stool does not ask what Kind a person was born. You are of the house by practice, by who can keep the hour, and by whether the town still comes when the slate says it will.

How they live in the three corners
