The danger is a lapsing Condition with no infirmary near enough to reach, and a faith that consoles what it cannot cure, a quiet cruelty in which scarcity of the gift shades into a doctrine that the people who went without were unworthy of it.

Geography and climate

The country is rugged and various, with highland spines, upland moors, deep forests, and long river-runs down to a wild coast. The weather is bigger here than on the Old World pair, the winters are harder, and more of the ground is still untamed. These spines are not the Rain-Wall. That range is Maiethorn’s, and it does a different job. Tengu ridge-towns and Fox-of-the-Snows hearths sit on the heights, the Fox-of-the-Wilds live in the deeper woods, and Selkie families hold the wild coast. A dense hearth is a family’s livelihood on that ground. It is not a state of that Kind.

Settlement clusters wherever a graft has taken. A healthy Tree is the seed of a town, and the map of Heskoren’s civilization is a map of its surviving Trees. Between those towns lies wild that no power claims, thinly held marches, and long roads from one Tree to the next. Harrow’s Green sits above the Rise-water. Downstream is the ford of Brenod, Vaelun, and Ornath. The Seat will not learn those three names, so it keeps calling the place by the water. A day’s walk from Vaelun, sometimes two, takes you into the Yield, the country of Vaelhesk, and not back along that stream. There you find the First Bowl, a guest-grove in an old green, not a second Harrow’s.

The frontier coast is the east coast. It faces the West Water back toward Strandoren, and that crossing is the lifeline for trade and for new grafts. Eolvaeth is a vale behind this coast. It is a place people walk to in order to wait, not one of the towns where a new graft has just taken.

The slate-shore is the west coast, in Ornled. Sanbreo’s beach faces the last capes and, far beyond them, the storm-wall. A hull that wants a beach here comes round the capes. Heskoren’s westernmost capes are the closest settled land to the Isle, and the source of many people who have seen the storm-wall even if they never crossed it.

The climate is cooler, wetter, and wilder than Maiethorn or Strandoren. The Leaf-Fall is timed to the solstice everywhere, and here it is a hard-won event of a decade rather than a certainty that comes round every year.

Reach

The reach is thin. The grafts are young, scattered, and prone to sickening, and the three pillars are stretched thin, with few Long-Lived to remember a neighbour and few Bound to vouch for one, so citizenship-by-witness is fragile. The unvouched Struck are a constant, aching problem, and the frontier meets that problem with faith where there is little machinery. Kept and Struck are both common, many children stay UnTurned, and the specialist care other continents take for granted is scarce. People here put the thinness down to distance and history. The Ages chapter calls the unfinished carrying the Grafting, and it is this decade’s work, not a closed age.

The wood reached Heskoren in Cut-years 200–387, and the work is still incomplete. After Strandoren’s coasts, cuttings died on the Long Mile. Each new Turning Tree had to grow up before it could supply the next town, and the queue planted the town that could pay. That gap is a history of distance and of a queue. Vaethorn will preach that the wait means the people were unworthy. The years do not agree. Where the Old Ways hold a planting, the first meal is the host-right. A planting without that meal is a claiming. Harrow’s Green is the canopy the neighbours can see and use. The Three Hamlets Past the Ford — Brenod, Vaelun, and Ornath — are still walking their children to a Tree this year.

Powers

Vaethorn, the Waiting Lands (theology high · reach low · governance low) is the frontier’s touchstone. The faith is ardent, the Trees are thin, and there is almost no state. It is a warm, poor, half-lawless pilgrim edge, and its ruling mood is waiting: waiting for a graft to take, and waiting for a gift that may not come. Its injustice is a guilt, scarcity read as unworthiness. Its seat is Eolvaeth, a vale on the pilgrim edge, inland of the coast that faces Strandoren. People walk here to wait. Saelvaeth’s march lies on another road.

Ornled, the Outer Ledger, is the secular frontier: the same thin Trees as the waiting country, and no congregation to tend them. Its town is Sanbreo, on the slate-shore of Heskoren’s west coast, its beach facing the last capes and the storm-wall. It is on the brink of a small city, and the slate is kept there. A hull that wants the beach pays a beach-fee. A hymn is not what the town sells.

Vaelhesk, the Far Yield, keeps the Old Ways’ host-rights. The first meal at a planting is the law they keep. The land itself is the seat, and there is no city. The First Bowl is the guest-grove, where a stranger is fed.

Saelvaeth, the Sown Waiting, is the march on the live edge, where new grafts are taking. The march-voice stands at Natai, west of Harrow’s Green, in the country between Sanbreo and that grove. The days to either are not recorded. Harrow’s Green is a grove-town in this march’s country, and it lies in the power’s orbit without being the seat. People Turn under its canopy. The hamlets’ ford is the crossing Brenod, Vaelun, and Ornath use.

The four powers are fewer, poorer, and more scattered than the powers of the old continents. Wild country with no power of its own fills the space between them.

Faith

Two faiths stand in tension here, and the friction belongs to the frontier itself.

The Motherfaith burns hottest here. It is a theology of longing and pilgrimage that grew up around the scarce gift, around the Trees that sicken and the children who wait.

The Old Ways (Vaeloren) are an animist and ancestor faith that predates the grafts. Their own sentence is, “The Mother’s reach is new here. We had our own ways before her Trees came.” They revere the Struck, and the Taken-In, people the wild took partway into itself and gave back changed, as the land’s own children, and they resent the Motherfaith as a latecomer. The grievance has real theological standing.

The Sundering Isle: Kumbaan

(koom-BAHN, “the hidden home.” Sailors say the Sundering Isle or the Sunder. Outsiders name the barrier. The Yumboes name the hearth.)

The Sundering Isle sits off the edge of the reach entirely. It is the one land the grafts never reached, and dead wood is not a Tree. Where Heskoren is thin, the Isle is empty of the Trees the rest of the world is built around, and its people become what they are by their own path, outside the Leaf-Fall altogether. Nobody on the mainland knows how that becoming works. The storm-wall has wrecked most of the people who tried the crossing, so that in Maiethorn, Strandoren, and Heskoren alike a Yumboe is a figure from a sailor’s tale: pearly-skinned, silver-haired, “the good people from across the drowning sea.” Some of the stories are even true.

Kumbaan is an ordinary home, warm and hospitable, that happens to be nearly impossible to reach. The Yumboes are not strange to themselves, only to a world that has never met them. They are a hill-people who love a feast, served by hands you cannot see, and the rest of the world thinks they are a legend.

Geography and climate

The storm-wall is a near-permanent girdle of violent weather, treacherous currents, and reef, and it is the reason the Isle stays sundered. Ships that try the crossing are wrecked, turned back, or simply never heard from again. There may be a season, or a way, in which the wall thins, and nobody knows which, or whether. The wall is not a ferry, and it is not shut for good.

The Paps are the hill country, the Isle’s defining landform. The Isle is rolling green hills, honeycombed beneath with the dwellings the Yumboes actually live in. They live within the hills and come out by moonlight. What you see by day is pasture, terrace, and standing-stone, and the life of the place is below.

The climate is mild, wet, and moonlit, a temperate maritime island under the storm-wall’s cloud. In the Isle’s own tellings it is famous for its bright nights, because the people are nocturnal and moonlight is the light they do the day by.

The Isle is small, the one small continent of the four, an island you can walk and that its own people know in full, which is the opposite of Heskoren’s trackless vastness.

You do not book a passage here. A hull out of Netstrand may try, because that coast is where the far crossing gets quoted, and a quote is not a date. Shore-sitters do not swim out and do not keep a rescue boat. If you live, you are on the sand or you are not, a shore-sitter decides that you are alive, the living are walked uphill, and the first night is a guest’s night in a hall. At the second meal a table-keeper decides whether you are kin. That belonging holds on the isle, and a mainland watch will not take it as papers. The hall a sailor comes into is Ndenjoo, the Feeding Hill. Njunda keeps the table. The sand below that hall is Soonke’s stretch, and Soonke is the person who sits it.

Reach

The reach is near-none. There is no Tree on the Isle, and there never was a graft, because the grafts never crossed the storm-wall, so the count for this isle in the First Cut’s years is never. Sailors tell of pots that went into the water, and those pots were dead wood that never took as Trees. The Yumboes do not Turn at a Tree, and whatever they become, they become otherwise.

People: the Yumboes

The Isle is the homeland of the Yumboes, who call themselves Bakhna Rakhna, “the good people.” They are pearly-white-skinned and silver-haired, they live in the hills, and they keep the moonlit hours. They are famously hospitable to a stranger, whether the stranger was born on the Isle or came off a wreck.

They live beneath the hills, come out by moonlight, and hold great feasts served by hands and feet you can see but bodies you cannot. That service at the table is the image the mainland repeats whenever it tells the isle. They are native to Kumbaan and rare beyond it, because the storm-wall keeps them home, so the few who do cross become the source of every legend the mainland tells. Their tongue and their faith are their own, and they owe the Leaf-Mother nothing.

Faith

The Open Table (Ndeyaan) is the Yumboes’ own cosmology. It grew in isolation, and it owes nothing to the Motherfaith. Their old accounts bind the good people up with the ancestors and the dead, and the tales told on the mainland call them “the spirits of the dead.” They are a living people, with a faith of hill, moon, hospitality, and the staying-kin, which is what they call the ancestors and the dead kept with the living, and they are not ghosts. The Table-Keepers keep the hall, and the Shore-Sitters keep the sand.

The Reckoning of the Year

The Turning keeps time by the sun. The Leaf-Fall, the week when the Trees turn their colour and the year’s ten-year-olds stand under them, falls at a solstice, so the count is also how people know when children Turn, when the great festival falls, and how a world with mechanical clocks and no printing press numbers its days. The sky here is enough to run the rite and to date a debt.

The sky

There is one sun, and on the mainland one moon, on a familiar monthly round that is enough for nights and for tides. Kumbaan keeps twelve named moons and does not owe that mainland round a translation. They are the same sky, counted differently. There are four true seasons, and the winters are real. People stand on one ground. The storm-wall is weather, current, and reef, and it is not a door. The hills at Ndenjoo are hills people live in. A Tree is a tree on this ground, and a person who has become is still standing on this ground. The Low Wall, the Seeing-Ring, and the Dry Stair are older stone on this same ground, not a ruined heaven you can walk into. People reach a place by walking or by sail. What a faith calls a door, people keep as a practice, a meal, a return, or a hymn.

The fact that matters for the rite is the solstice, because that is when the Trees turn.

At the High Solstice, the longest day, a Tree’s shadow at noon sits almost on its own roots. Supper happens in light that should have been gone, and Turning-Week is that whole week of light. A storm can soak the crowd. The weather does not extend the week or move it off the sun’s day. On the Rain-Wall the sun clears a shelf it leaves in shadow in the Deep, and the snow-line looks further off than it is. On the Old Crossing the day is long, and a squall in Hale-month, when the land is supposed to be sound and the roads are full, can still take the sail. On Heskoren the same long light falls on a canopy, a bog, or neither, depending on the fold. People argue about what the light did. They are not arguing about a map of stars. Believers say the Mother timed her choosing to the year’s hinge, and skeptics say a tree answers light, but both stand in the same noon and see the same short shadow.

At the Deep Solstice the sun is a guest. It rises late, stays low, and is soon gone, so the work moves to the hearth and the roads shorten to daylight. The mainland moon is the light you actually use, when cloud allows, and the deathless houses finish closing their accounts in this dark. A clear Deep night shows the moon and a great many unnamed lights. People do not farm by those lights. They farm by the months.

At Ndenjoo, on a bright night, the moon is the daylight, and you can carry a bowl across the hill-yard without a lamp. The storm-wall is a darker ring around that brightness, reef-thunder under the cloud at the edge and the hill itself lit. The bright moon washes the small lights out, so a person here does not steer by a field of named stars. They say which moon it is. Njunda, who keeps the hall’s table, will say the moon’s name. There is no Leaf-Fall in that sky, and no Tree to throw a noon shadow. The long mainland day is a sailor’s story here. The bright night is the ordinary one.

The Leaf-Fall happens at the solstice because that is when the Trees turn their colour and choose. The sun reaches its turning, and so do the children. The devout and the skeptics share that calendar.

The Turning Year

The year hinges on two solstices, and those two dates are the fixed anchors everyone can see.

The Deep Solstice, at midwinter, is the longest night, the low of the year and its turning point. The season around it belongs to the hearth, to endowment-giving, and to the deathless houses’ closing of their accounts.

The High Solstice, at midsummer, is the longest day, and it is the Turning. This is the great one: the solstice when the Trees turn and the year’s ten-year-olds meet the Leaf-Fall.

The High Solstice is warm, safe to travel and to gather, and full of light. A child’s Turning is a joyous festival, so midsummer suits it, and that same warmth makes the pilgrimage to Thaeloren a summer road.

Turning-Week

The Leaf-Fall is not a single day. It runs through Turning-Week, the week that brackets the High Solstice, when the Trees hold their colour and the choosing is done. Every child who has turned ten since the last High Solstice Turns during this week, or misses it. The town gathers, the tree-wardens officiate, and the week is at once the holiest rite and the biggest fair of the year, part christening, part graduation, and part festival. A city nests that witness among the people who already know the child. A village stands as one circle. The year of a person’s Turning becomes a lifelong marker of age and of cohort, which is what people mean when they say, “We Turned the same summer.”

Months and weeks

The calendar is plainly countable. Twelve months follow the moon’s cycle, arranged as four seasons of three months each, hinged on the two solstices, with the two equinoxes between them kept as the lesser markers. The week is the working unit of the guild towns: guild-weeks, market-days, and the mechanical clock-towers of the trade cities striking the hours. There is no printing press, so clergy and clerks keep the calendars by hand, which is one reason the tree-wardens and the Tallied Crown’s clerks hold a quiet power. They are the ones who keep the dates.

The twelve Maiethren months

The liturgical names are Maiethren, the old speech of Maiethorn. Beside them sits the worn common-tongue form, the way Lestrand says the same month. The name a person uses shows the stance they are taking. The table is counted from the Deep Solstice, as an astronomical order. The argument about which day opens the year comes after it.

# Season Liturgical Says Worn / common Holds
1 Winter Nethael (neth-AYL) “the night made whole” Nethel / the Deep the Deep Solstice
2 Winter Brenorn (bren-ORN) “hearth-land” Brennor / Hearth-month midwinter hush; deathless account-closing finishes
3 Winter to Spring Liren (LEER-en) “the thaw’s speech” Liren / the Thaw water runs again
4 Spring Saelorn (SAY-lorn) “sowing-land” Salorn / Seed-month first green
5 Spring Haelren (HAYL-ren) “hale-speech” Hailren / Hale-month the land sound
6 Summer Eolthael (ay-ohl-THALE) “the Tree’s hinge” Yoltal / Turning-month the High Solstice · Turning-Week
7 Summer Vaelorn (VAY-lorn) “gift-land” Valorn / Gift-month after-Turning; the colours settle
8 Summer Leddorn (led-ORN) “reckoning-land” Leddorn / Ledger-month late-summer markets, contract-terms
9 Autumn Ornvael (ORN-vayl) “the land’s yield” Ornvale / Harvest bringing-in

When the year starts: three new-year days by stance

The devout and the clergy begin the year at Eolthael, because for them the Turning is the hinge that matters. Lestrand and the deathless houses begin it at Nethael, because midwinter is when the books close. In Vaethorn the pulpit follows the clergy, and the fields follow the last summer a local Tree actually managed a fall, so a child “turns the year” from that summer. The twelve names do not change. Any of the three days can open the year, and any of the three can open a dispute about what year a debt belongs to. A debt can be late on one count and early on another, and people will argue which day began it.

Kumbaan’s moons

The Yumboes of Kumbaan do not use the mainland table. They keep twelve named moons, a lunar count that owes the solstice nothing:

Yaaba · Ndibi · Sambiyo · Waandi · Lunji · Saalo · Soonke · Nkoosa · Ndenjoo · Yendo · Njili · Mbela

Saalo is a moon, and Seed-month is a mainland month. A mainlander who points up in Saalo and calls it Seed-month has put the moon in the wrong quarter of the year. Njunda will say the moon’s name. The hall will not correct the chart. It corrects the visitor by still being on its own moon when the mainlander’s month has moved on. Soonke, in that list, is one of the twelve moons. The sand below Ndenjoo is also called Soonke, because Soonke is the person who sits that stretch.

How years are numbered

Months name a season inside the year, and years have no universal number. The count written on a debt is a theology, the same argument as which day opens the year, turned now toward history. The Ages chapter keeps the full count.

The First Seat and the devout clerks count Cut-years from the First Cut, the first time living wood was successfully cut and carried. In the liturgy that count is the Eoloren-count. The present year is Cut-year 387.

Lestrand and the deathless houses count from a house-founding or from the issue of a note. A clerk of the White Note writes the present year as “the 307th summer of the White Note.” The famous problem of turning one count into the other is the archival 200th. Cut-year 280 was that house’s 200th summer, and Ledan, the Long-Lived clerk who still writes its quay-desk, asked the First Seat which number a hundred-year loan should carry, because the bank, the borrower’s town, and the Seat were not counting the same summer. The house still converts its years the way that query did. The Ages chapter keeps the letter.

Threnmaieth writes the Cut-years and also a crown-count taken from the Two Papers. The papers fall in Cut-year 67, and the present is Crown-year 320.

Vaethorn counts from the year the local graft took. People there say, “the year our graft took,” which is the same local-fall logic as the way they start the year.

The Watching refuse the Cut-count entirely. Kumbaan keeps its moons and owes the ages nothing.

The Awakening Tree is old beyond reliable dating. There is no year the world began, and no year she appeared.

How it is lived along the gradient

One sun, one moon, and the two solstices make the count the same sky on the mainland. People live it differently as the wood thins, from a country where Turning-Week is an institution to the one country that has no Trees.

On Maiethorn, where the reach is full, Turning-Week is a near-certainty and a vast institution. The Trees stand dense and healthy, the core runs higher on the Given than the world as a whole, and the pilgrimage to Thaeloren crests at the High Solstice. When that walk was required, it was the Walking Years. The Near Mile is the inland trip on Maiethorn, days to a couple of weeks. The Ages chapter tells those years.

On Strandoren, where the reach is high, the solstice is kept, and it is as much a commercial hinge as a sacred one. The fairs, the contract-terms, and the deathless houses’ own reckoning all turn on it. The Salt Walk was the berth that made Eolthael. Miss the last crossing, and you missed the year.

On Heskoren, where the reach is thin, Turning-Week is a hard-won event of a decade. A child may travel days to the nearest Turning Tree, or wait years for a graft to take. The solstice still arrives, and the gift may not fall. Whole districts are still on the Long Mile, weeks or months to a Tree that can Turn them.

On Kumbaan, where there is no reach, the Yumboes keep the moon and not the solstice. Their reckoning is nocturnal and lunar, and it owes the Trees nothing, because they have none. They are the one people in the world whose calendar has no Leaf-Fall in it. A mainlander who lines a moon up with a Maiethren month is wrong in the same direction every time, and the hall will not correct the chart.

What the year feels like

The year is kept by stance and argued by faith, and the two do different work. A place sets how long people talk and what they repeat. A person’s faith sets which words they will not say. That is why someone of the Watching can eat on a dock, and why a follower of the Fair Hand can stand in a pious square. Each street chooses the words. Each street also keeps one habit, and the people who keep it will not explain it.

In a devout town, and in any square that puts the name back when a sentence dropped it, the year people feel begins in Eolthael, whatever a clerk’s tablet started earlier. On an ordinary market morning, people carrying baskets stop when a tree-warden steps onto the Tree’s roots, and they start again when the warden steps off. Someone of the Watching will not say “Maieth,” and will still wait. The wood is the wood. Someone of the Fair Hand, passing through, will not wait, and the square notices without stopping them. In Maiethlir a clerk may be copying a slate of bells in the same hour, and the hymn is still first when Rithim, the Speaker, can make it first. The Core-thaw runs louder the week before Leaf-Fall than it did in Hale-month. Maiethlir will not say why.

On a dock, and on any quay that lets the th go, the year the account books feel begins at the Deep Solstice, when the notes are closed. Turning-month is a fair laid on top of that closing, and it is not the start of the quay’s own count. All year, a clear is a no-colour, a child the Tree hugged and gave no Condition, and the quay says the word the way it says a berth that just opened. A crane-crew will hire a clear. Nobody on this water calls a clear a sadness. Even a house that never kept a book will count coins into the other person’s hand, not onto the barrel, when the one they owe is watching. A book-hand calls that worship. The gang calls it how you fail to start a fight. They only collide when a child in the tenth year is present. In Eolthael, salt crusts the roots of the Trees, and on Orentel’s rise the tide does not reach the salt. Orentel will not say why.

In a waiting town, and in any town whose sentence does not close the week, people date a child from the last summer the local wood actually spoke. The pulpit may say Eolthael. The field says the last real fall. They do not spend the good flour on a promise that the wood will speak again. A guest gets the common pot. If the wood spoke last year, Turning-Week gets the better loaf. If it did not, the week gets the pot too. Some houses walk the old doors at a flood or at the ice and leave food, and they do not call that a second Turning. A wet leaf lies on the spring, or too many, or none. Eolvaeth will not say why. At Harrow’s Green, in a year when the wood will speak, people say “the wood” first, and the neighbour after that. If their own wood will not speak, the sentence in the street is “Not this week,” and they name the neighbour’s town when they have to send the children on.

At Ndenjoo the year is moons. Noon is when the hall is asleep, so a tool you need at noon waits, or you stay quiet enough that the sleepers stay asleep. A mainlander who lines a moon up with a Maiethren month is wrong in the same direction every time, and the hall will not correct the chart. On one night of the moon sailors call Yoltal, the hall eats the heel of the loaf first. Every other night the heel is last, or it goes to the goats. The valley says the hands like the crust when the mainland is loud. Njunda will not correct that, and will not say it is the reason. They will not say why. A guest who asks is given more bread.

Turning-Week, as a town spends it, is baskets, bells, a berth, and a loaf. The leaf-colours, and the questions a warden gets asked, belong to the rite at the Tree.

In Maiethlir the stalls go up under the town Tree on the first morning, and the hearths stand to the bell in the morning, again in the afternoon, and again at eve. The public slate names the street and the hour. The colour a child received stays off that slate. Rithim speaks the word of the fall aloud even when the square already knows the common fall, and the next errand waits until the people who stood have stepped off the root. A Watcher household stands with their child and says their own line, quietly, and Maieth is not in it. A follower of the Fair Hand stands at the edge with a book held shut. Before the fair eats, someone in from the road may set a bowl at the root and go back to a stall. The square lets the bowl sit. Setting it down is not the standing.

On Orentel’s quay they say “the fall” on the crane, and they call the wood Tallo, though a charter that is open still carries the long name. The standings follow the quay-gang, the people who already know the child, and they happen at the tide that gang can spare. A clear gets the same shout the quay uses when a berth opens. Salt crusts the roots, and the quay will not explain it. In the same days the book-hands settle a year’s term where the gang can see. If a Bound’s oath-day falls in the week, the oath is recited and marked, and the warden still speaks. The quay calls the Mother “the old rite,” and it does not put the th back into the word to be polite.

In Eolvaeth the town fills before the week arrives. In Hale-month the camp-streets double, and when Eolthael comes the town faces the canopy it has, which some years speaks and some years does not. If the wood will call a fall, the town stands small and the gift-hall pot is open. A hug is not dressed as a prize, and a sermon may still pity the person who received one. The pot does not wait for the sermon to finish. If the wood will not speak, people in the street say “Not this week,” and a cohort may be sent toward a luckier Tree. The spring has a wet leaf, or too many, or none, and the town will not explain it. In those same days some houses walk the old doors, leave food, and do not ask for a colour.

The hill on Kumbaan keeps its moons through the week the mainland calls Turning-Week, so no child is stood up and no one asks for a colour. A guest who brought a tenth-year is fed, and nobody offers the path to a Tree, because there is no Tree in the valley. The loaf comes heel-first, and they will not explain the heel. The shore does not come up the path to make a rite, and the sand stays the sand.

Climate, Ecology, and Travel

This chapter names the water and the stone, says how a week feels in each band of weather, and says how long a walk takes. Say the everyday name. A devout speaker keeps the th in the land-names around the water. On a dock, that th wears off. Clerks enjoy the long old form. Dates here are in Cut-years, counted from the First Cut, the first time living wood was successfully cut and carried. The Ages chapter keeps that count.

The year is familiar enough to farm by and strange enough to argue over. Maiethorn and Strandoren, the Old World pair, keep four seasons and the twelve shared month-names. The Rain-Wall, the range down the middle of Maiethorn, can make that same month a flood on one face and a dry well on the other. Heskoren gets a shorter kindness between frosts. Kumbaan keeps its own moons and lives inside the storm-wall. A month tells people what work should be possible. A season tells them what the land actually did. A late frost can put winter into Seed-month, and three clear weeks can put the harvest into Ledger-month. Clerks still date the note by the month. Farmers date the year by what survived.

Named water, range, and rivers

Everyday What it is Who says something else
the Old Crossing the busy water between Maiethorn and Strandoren, narrow enough to be one argument and old enough to be the oldest trade route Lestrand: the crossing. Vaethorn: the waiting-water. Sailors: the Crossing. Threnmaieth wants the name on a roll.
the West Water the wider sea between Strandoren and Heskoren already the Night Shore’s word for this sea. The Hush’s west-water clause lives on it.
the Rain-Wall Maiethorn’s central range, wet on one side and dry on the other Lirorn-folk: the Thaw-Wall. Clerks: the Divide.
the Noon Pass the old high road over the Rain-Wall. It lost its stone in Cut-year 233. the courier’s noon-pass. The water-line is still on the stone.
the Shelf-gate the pass Narol of the Pass took after the Break, when the old high road was no longer the way Threnmaieth named it the new one. Lirorn charges Break-rate.
the Core-thaw the river Maiethlir sits on clerks file the rise as snowmelt. Watchers will not.
the Well-wash seasonal water in the Rain-Shadow, east of the range dry most years; a bad thaw leaves silt
the Rise-water the stream from Harrow’s Green down to the hamlets’ ford the Seat still says the ford
the Chart-run Strandoren’s interior river, running out to Orentel’s estuary Lestrand files it as inland tickets that have reached salt

the Old Crossing. This is the oldest trade route in the world. It is narrow enough that a fair-weather hull makes it in a handful of days, and busy enough that a late storm in Hale-month, when the land is supposed to be sound, can hold a family past Turning-Week. Miss that week, and the child stays UnTurned, having reached no Tree in the year they turned ten. The Hinge Shore is Maiethorn’s face on this water. Orentel is Strandoren’s face. The Salt Walk, the old way a Shore-lands child reached a Turning, was this water first and the Near Mile inland after that, the walk on Maiethorn to Thaeloren.

People call Maiethorn and Strandoren the Old World pair because the water is old and close, and because it made the two continents into one argument. They do not call the water “inner.” What happened on it has dates. The Grey Summer, in Cut-year 171, was a fever that tied the quays. It began as a cough in packed holds, it killed across the Given, the Struck, and the Kept, and it left grafts unwatered when their tenders fell. It was a fever. The Stilled are people whose upkeep is exertion, and the Grey they work back out is the stillness that fills the body when the work stops. The Grey Summer was neither that stillness nor a punishment laid on anyone’s Condition. The Hinge Hush, in Cut-year 304, is the peace still charged as the Hush-rate. From Cut-year 299 to 304 the two shores fought over who set the price. The hush is a rate, a clause for the far water, and a refusal to name a winner.

the West Water. This sea is wider than the Crossing. It is the water-leg of the Long Mile, the long way on from Strandoren toward a Tree on Heskoren, and that road takes weeks. A pot of living cuttings has a harder berth here than on the Old Crossing. Netstrand quotes the far crossing on this water, and Braetu is the harbour where that quote is written. Heskoren’s frontier coast, its east coast, faces the same sea back toward Strandoren. Heskoren’s west coast, the slate-shore, faces the last capes, and beyond them the storm-wall.

The Hush’s west-water clause lives on this sea, and it says who may do what once a hull leaves the Crossing. Netstrand quotes the far crossing. Saelvaeth may take a pot of cuttings without a waiting-due, the charge Vaethorn would have written before the wood could move, while Vaethorn may bless a landing and may not levy it, and Ornled collects a beach-fee at Sanbreo when a hull wants the beach. Vaelhesk is not on the clause, because a first meal set for a guest is not a landing-due. Kumbaan is not on this water either. Sailors tell of a pot that went into the storm and was wrecked, and no graft took. No house on this water sells a passage to the isle.

the Rain-Wall. This is a highland spine down the middle of Maiethorn. Weather on the west face is wet and runs through four seasons. The leeward east is the Rain-Shadow, which is why Saelthael sows at wells, and why Lirorn can levy a thaw as if the melt were a tax. Fox-of-the-Snows and Tengu hearths sit densest on the high snow. That is terrain, families on the ground the weather made, not a flag and not a nation of one born people. Heskoren’s highland spines are a different weather. They are not this range.

Two passes cross the spine. The Noon Pass is the old high road. In the Thaw-Break of Cut-year 233 a water-line was left over its ribbon-notch, and the road up to the pass was gone for two summers. Children still rub that line for luck, and ridge-folk rub it because the water was real. The toll does not tell a lowlander which rubbing is the prayer. The Shelf-gate is the road that was left once the old stone sat under that line. Narol of the Pass took the thaw-toll when the old holder’s stone was under the water, and Narol is dead, so the household that inherited the toll still levies it. Threnmaieth wanted the new pass counted, and Lirorn charged them for the water anyway. The Shelf-gate is the road people use now.

Four rivers. The Core-thaw is snowmelt off the Rain-Wall’s west face, running toward the Old Crossing. Maiethlir sat down where the water had slowed enough to hold a Turning Tree, a day’s living-earth from the Motherwood, which is as far as a cutting could be carried in a day and still be planted. The town is on the river road, not on Orenbren’s Near Mile. Clerks file the spring rise as snowmelt. The river runs louder the week before Leaf-Fall, and Maiethlir is where that louder week is known. Watchers do not file it. Rithim, the Speaker, raises their voice over the water, and the town will not say why the week is louder. In a high Liren, when the thaw is already up, the lodging-road meets a near branch of the same river. The line “Eolthael, the summer the ford ran high” is this water in a bad year, and it is not a fifth river. Below Maiethlir the same water is the Down-Bank, the days a traveller is already going to spend on the way to the Hinge Shore. It is not a second river. In the Thaw-Break the Core-thaw took a month of melt in seven days.

The Well-wash is a seasonal run east of the range. In a kind Liren it is a river, and in a cruel one it is a line of silt. Towns cluster at wells because this water cannot be a civic certainty. Larbril is where the west road meets that wash, short of the pass. Ornsael drinks a well, not the wash, farther into the dry, with open country between it and Larbril, and the wash is why the well matters. The town sits inland. Between a river-week and a silt-week, the day-wash shows for an afternoon, water enough to look like a camp. A traveller from the core sees a silver in the dust and treats it as a ford, and by morning it is a stain. Saelthael already knows this, which is why the towns sit at wells. Ornsael’s problem is a well dropping, not that shine. The Dry Stair climbs above a different well-town, and it is not a river-shrine. Sometimes a bright thread of water runs uphill of the last rain, lasts an hour, and is gone. Well-keepers say the rock remembers a wet year, and travellers from the core say the map is wrong. Nobody on the bank will say which of those is true.

The Rise-water is a low stream off Harrow’s rise. Downstream it becomes the hamlets’ ford, the crossing of Brenod, Vaelun, and Ornath. The Seat still says the ford, because the Seat will not learn those three names. In clear weather the hamlets can see Harrow’s canopy from the water, a dark on the far slope. There is no stone on the waiting side, and the cup still goes on the ford-rock. Natai, the march-town, stands on other ground, west of Harrow’s Green, between Sanbreo and that grove, and not on this ford.

The Chart-run is Strandoren’s interior river-plain, running out to Orentel’s estuary. The coasts took their Trees by sea. The inland country waited on a cart and on this river together. Lunbra sits on the wealthy stretch, and that is where the roll is kept. Food sold on the Salt Quay comes from this plain, from the catch of the Crossing, and from whatever the hinge pays to have brought across.

Climate bands

A week in each band feels like this. Choose the band, read the month, and then let the weather turn once. A whole week of identical weather should feel notable. Weather is usually an inconvenience before it is a danger: the queue at the dry shed, the cart sharing a rock, the neighbour whose cistern failed. Turning-Week stays the week around the High Solstice. A storm, a fever, a blocked pass, or a late hull does not move it.

Band Where Weather
Crossing-shore both faces of the Old Crossing mild, wet-temperate; a Hale-month storm can decide a Salt Walk
Mother-core Maiethorn west of the Rain-Wall four true seasons in old sacred country; winters that make the High Solstice mean something
Rain-Wall / Thaw-Wall Lirorn snow, shelves, and a thaw the towns keep as a civic year
Rain-Shadow Saelthael, east of the range dry hills, wells, and either the Well-wash or nothing
Shore-lands Strandoren coasts and the Chart-run maritime, indented, the sea used as the highway
Night Shore Netstrand open ocean, west-weather, watches kept for hulls that do not arrive
Sundered upland Heskoren cooler, wilder, harder winters; settled country is a map of the Trees that survived
Storm-wall / Kumbaan the Sundering Isle mild and wet under cloud, bright nights, and the wall itself is the climate

On the Crossing-shore the week opens under low cloud and mild rain, and the turn is a clear tide-day or a fast squall, which in Hale-month is the squall. Berths close before the roads do, so a Salt Walk family can lose Turning-Week without ever being far inland. The Mother-core opens on weather you would know as four seasons, and the turn is a river rising, a bright drying wind, or a cold night that does not belong to its month. Mills keep moving, while the grafts, the orchards, and the crowded greens all want the same drink.

The Rain-Wall opens with snow on the high shelves and melt or cold rain below, and the turn locks the path or unlocks all of it at once. In Liren the Shelf-gate may already be a lake before a traveller reaches the toll. The Rain-Shadow opens clear, cool, and dusty, and the turn is a hard shower, a blow of dust, or no change at all, so the wells fail before the roads do. The Well-wash may run for a day and still leave no drink a town can count on.

The Shore-lands open in salt mist and a working tide, and the turn is sun enough to unload, estuary rain enough to flood, or a gale along the coast. A leaf-lot, the rented plot of living green a stone town keeps for people who have to rest among plants, can be burned by brine and drenched by fresh water in the same month. The Night Shore opens on an open-ocean wind, and the front arrives as hard rain, a sudden lull, and then a second wind, until missing hulls become a kind of local weather. A Far-Voiced warning, from a person who has to put the feeling of the voice somewhere, can cross when the hull cannot.

The Sundered upland opens as cold rain below, sleet on the ridges, and sun in one vale while the next is still in cloud, so a healthy pocket can be bringing in a harvest while the next valley loses its roof, its road, or its young graft. On Kumbaan the inside of the island is mild and wet under cloud, and the edge is reef-thunder. The turn is a bright night within the wall, or a squall that reaches inland as steady rain. The crossing remains a chance, and it is never a timetable.

Maiethorn

Maiethorn holds four of the eight bands, and a traveller can go from salt drizzle to old forest, cross a pass that floods like a lake, and reach a well-town measuring dust, without leaving the Motherland. The deep difference is water. Towns in the core drain it, Lirorn waits to levy the thaw the range lets go, Ornsael divides what the wells hold, and every living graft wants a share.

West of the Rain-Wall the country keeps four true seasons, and the winters are real, which is why the High Solstice means something. A core week is two wet days, one bright break, and then a river on the rise. Grafts take in the old sacred country and in the Motherwood because generations have built drains, cistern turns, and a rule about keeping animals off the roots. The core’s food is bread, peas, cabbage, and orchard fruit, with pork or river fish when the week allows. In the core, the greens a Tithe asks for, the living plants a Taken-In person has to keep near, are commons and garden lots. Stilled infirmaries and Returned plague-work cluster in the rich core because that is where the chairs and the endowments are. The Mill-hold is the caution in that plenty: the mill-race stayed full, and the town’s Tree stood in the overflow. Stored grain did not water it.

On the range, last year’s snow is this year’s civic year. A Wall week freezes at night and melts by noon. Lirorn levies the thaw, the pass, and the high road, because the weather has made that road scarce. A thaw-week can turn the Shelf-gate into a lake. The Thaw-Break was that arrangement failing at once, a month of melt in seven days, and the west road stayed closed for two summers. People still remember which notch holds the water-line. The lower shelves eat barley, roots, and hard cheese. Hay is wealth, because the animals of winter eat the summer that was cut.

East of the Wall the week is dry wind until one hard shower fails to fill the well. The food is millet or barley, lentils, onions, and goat cheese if the herd came in. A Taken-In Tithe’s living green is cheap on a terrace and expensive if the well is dropping, because the same bucket is the food, the plants, and the Tree’s drink. Two-Bodied people, who have another self in a real animal body, range the dry hills at night. Returned work sits downwind of the drink. People on the pass tell of a travelling stiller, a Stilled person whose upkeep is hard use of the body and who can hold a wound. The dry country has no stillers’ college. At Ornsael the well-rope is knotted at last year’s water-line, and this year’s knot is wet even when the water stands below it. Ornsael will not say why.

On the Old Crossing face the weather is the berth. The week is mild rain, with a squall in Hale-month that decides a Salt Walk. Far-Voiced warnings are how a dock hears weather it cannot yet see. They do not steer the ship. Selkie hearths are common on the quays. The Hinge Shore says what the hull is carrying before anyone across the water prices it. The food on that shore is herring, mussels, and rye bread.

Strandoren

Strandoren is maritime country. A week can begin with three working tides, lose two days to fog, and end with every crane tied down. The sea softens the cold and refuses to be predicted. Hard frost is less reliable here than in Maiethorn’s core, which makes the winter wet rather than kind: rot, mud, smoke, and bad bedding do more harm than deep snow. People eat rye or wheat bread, beans, cabbage, apples, and eel or herring, with mussels and cockles when the tide is safe, and oat pottage when the fleet stays tied.

The coasts received the wood first. The Chart-run carried it inland, and the river also carries another district’s weather downstream, so a quay can flood under a clear local sky. Food on the Salt Quay is this plain, the Crossing’s catch, and whatever the hinge pays to bring across. Tithe-provision here is a market. You buy a hall-hour, a lot-night, a novelty page. The Taken-In who live in the stone cities are a working minority on lots, orchards, and river-gardens. They work at a polite distance, and the lots are in use. Brine in a lot is a failure of that provision. A west wind lays salt on leaves that were green at dawn, a rise on the Chart-run or a squall off the Crossing soaks those same leaves with fresh water, and a Taken-In person resting in the lot feels the scald and the rot as one week while the granary uphill still has bread. That split is the estuary’s weather. Guilds count the flood, because a flood has a witness, and the salt-burn is quieter and often the one that takes the green. Sometimes a lot salts on a windless morning, when the estuary is flat and nobody filed a gale. The tender washes the leaves and will not say where the salt was in the air.

Separate from that lot, salt lies on the roots of mature coastal Trees above any storm line. Orentel’s Tree on the rise is the case people know, on ground the tide does not reach. Tenders wash the roots with fresh water, the factors file the salt below the rise and decline to file this, and Orentel will not say why.

The Night Shore watches for hulls that do not arrive. A west-weather week begins as a long low swell, spends a false lull arguing whether anyone should sail, and finishes in a second wind that can break a berth or bring in wreckage with no crew in it. Chart-crews and the rightful owners meet at whatever the water brought. Prestige and necessity use the same water and do not pay the same rate.

A Hale-month storm on the Old Crossing can turn a Salt Walk into a missed year. Denlad is the inlet about a day’s sail short of Orentel’s estuary, a village with its own Tree on a low rise, and you can miss the week from there without ever seeing a crane. These spans are fair weather. A storm rewrites them. A later fever is not a second Grey Summer. People say “Grey” when they are frightened, and a clerk decides whether the comparison changes a rate.

Heskoren

Heskoren is one broad band with several weathers inside it: cool coast, rough moor, wooded vale, high spine, and long river country. Winters run harder than on the Old World pair, and the kind season between frosts is shorter. A clear day is when the roofs, the hay, the carts, the witnesses, and the people tending a graft all try to move at once. A usual week is cold rain in a vale, sleet on a ridge, one brilliant dry day, and then a hard frost. On the west coast a long swell can keep the next hull outside while the shore spends those clear hours. The food is oat mash, rye bread, peas, cabbage, turnips, hard cheese, and smoked fish, with berries and nuts when the season allows. A first-meal bread at the First Bowl is a little sour.

The continent is not empty wilderness. It is worked pockets around surviving Trees, and older hearths that predate them, with country between that is too wet, too steep, too cold, or simply too far to hold densely. Young grafts face wind, thin soil, and a queue written in the Motherwood. A Taken-In person’s upkeep is the living land itself, until a bad winter, a quarantine, or a dead planting cuts them off from it. Two-Bodied people range, scout, and herd, and a town can start treating a family’s range as if it were public stock. Returned work the far sheds, the flood, and the dead, and a useful danger is not automatically the Purpose they chose. Stilled medicine is one tired stiller, or a rope. The high country is not Maiethorn’s Rain-Wall. It has no thaw-levy and no Shelf-gate. Tengu and Fox-of-the-Snows hearths are denser on the heights because of the ground and the history, and a mixed hearth uses the same winter stores.

On a clear day a canopy shows on the next ridge, and the road does not. Someone says the wood spoke this week. Someone else says the colour is last year’s leaves. Neither of them has walked it. Tunral is that kind of gap, a kitchen and a mile-post coastward of Harrow’s Green, about a week along a road with no sight of the canopy. Huval, who keeps the post, sets a bowl outside at dusk on the side away from Harrow’s, and will not say why. The bowl is not a first meal, and it is not a shrine. Harrow’s Green is what the far green is, on the weeks the road allows. The hamlets are the rare case where the canopy is a sightline and a ford, not a rumour. On some clear days the green is there at dawn and gone by noon, with no cloud. Travellers blame haze, ridge-folk do not bother to blame it, and nobody measures it.

The live front is Saelvaeth’s luck, which is why Harrow’s Green is the grove the neighbours can see, with the Rise-water running from that rise down to the hamlets’ ford. Natai, the march-town, stands west of the grove between Sanbreo and Harrow’s, on its own ground, and the days between them are not recorded. Harrow’s square is the grove-town’s own ground, so a complaint can name Natai while the canopy the hamlets can see is still Harrow’s. Vaethorn waits in a vale with no view of that canopy, and the people there do not want the view. Ornled has the same thin wood and keeps no congregation, with the slate kept at Sanbreo on the west-coast slate-shore. Vaelhesk is old greens, the land is the seat, and there is no city on it. Between mile-shrines the next stone is a rumour, though empty road-houses still make a bed for the people who did not go home.

After the first hard snow around some young Trees, a narrow melt runs back along the road by which the graft first arrived. It can lie on the shaded side while the open square stays white. People call it the old-road melt only when they need to give directions. Packed earth, a buried stone, or a tender’s morning walk can account for any one example. No account covers enough of them to end the conversation. The melt does not point toward the next town, and it does not promise a Tree will take there.

Kumbaan

Kumbaan is mild, wet, and cloudy, and it turns bright by night when the storm-wall opens a view of the moon. The wall is the wind, the current, the reef, and the surf working together at the edge of the island. It is not weather happening somewhere past the last beach. Inside, the same weather arrives diminished and still persistent: cloud, rain, salt carried farther inland than a guest expects, and a low thunder that can keep going under a hill sky that looks calm. A week is mild rain under low cloud, one bright moonlit night, reef-thunder with no local wind, and then a squall that closes the shallows and soaks the peat. People eat barley broth, oats, beans, peas, cabbage, turnips, onions, and goat milk or cheese. The shore adds mussels, limpets, fish, and seaweed, with berries and nuts in season. Fuel is peat, and what a wreck sometimes gives the hall.

There is no Tree here, and no graft crossed. A slip planted on the isle would die. Dead wood never became a Tree. A wrecked mainland pot is rot, fuel if anyone will burn it, and the discomfort of knowing why it was carried. Islanders date a rain, a birth, a debt, or a second sitting by the moon, and they describe the season by its work: ditches full, terraces open, shallows closed, peat drying, goats brought in. A mainlander can call a week springlike and be understood. They cannot convert the calendar by picking whichever mainland month has similar rain.

The hills, which people call the Paps, carry pasture and terrace-gardens on the surface. Halls, stores, and the rooms where people sleep through the day lie under the turf. Rain runs down every mistake in a terrace wall. Goats are common, and they undo a repair the moment it is finished. Large draught animals are uncommon on ground this steep. People, goats, small carts on the good paths, and unseen hands carry most of the loads. Those hands can hold a basket, lift a light net, fetch a line, gather limpets within reach, and bring the wet baskets in before the rain. They do not conjure food, they do not harvest a valley at once, they do not swim the wall, and they do not make a lean year generous by themselves. A great table after a poor harvest means the hearths contributed, the stores were opened, or the meal is thinner than the serving makes it look.

There is no ferry, and no ticket you can buy. Shore-sitters know a moon when the wall thins, the wreck-moons and the weeks after a rumour of a crossing, and that knowledge is weather. Nobody sells it as a sailing date. A quiet shore does not mean the outer reef is passable, and a violent night can still put a living wreck on the sand. Most ships wreck, turn back, or are never heard from again. Shore-sitters do not swim out, and they do not keep a rescue boat. They decide whether you are alive after the sea has already decided.

If you live, the landing goes in this order, and it does not skip. You are on the sand, or you are not, and a wreck that never makes the beach has not landed. A shore-sitter decides whether you are alive. The living get water and a blanket, and they are not asked their Kind or their colour. The dead go above the tide. The living are walked uphill, and the first night you spend as a guest begins at a hall, not on the sand. At the second meal a table-keeper decides whether you are kin, and the guest is told, “no one is a stranger twice.” That belonging holds on the isle. It does not travel back to a mainland watch. Before you sail, a Strandoren quay still wants a road-word, the name of someone at your last hearth who will stand for you. On the isle the watch’s three questions, your name, your last hearth, and who stands for you, are not asked.

The way back is the same wall, and the sitters do not send anyone home. You wait for a thinning, or you take a hull that will try. A Yumboe who wants off the isle sits the same sand from the other want. If you eat, eat what is set in front of you, and sleep the day if you can. Do not plant a Tree, do not file the hill in a clerk’s book, and do not swim the wall. Do not repeat “no one is a stranger twice” at home as a saying you can spend. It is said to a guest at the table, and it is not a pass. Guest-right on the isle is the table, not a token you carry home to show a watch.

The hall a sailor comes into is Ndenjoo, which sailors call the Feeding Hill. Njunda keeps the table. The sand on that stretch is called Soonke, and Soonke is the person who sits it. The lamp on the path does not call ships.

On some nights later remembered as a thinning, peat smoke from the hill vents lies seaward while the grass and the rain move inland. Shore-sitters notice it after the wreck or the sail. They do not use it to call one beforehand. A bad vent or a crossed gust can explain the smoke for any single hall. The smoke stays an observation, and it is not a crossing calendar.

Travel times

The unit is a day’s walk, the interval a mile-shrine on the old roads already marks. A horse takes the same road and spares the blisters. A ship takes the water those walks already name. It does not invent a different country.

Walk What it was Fair-weather band
Near Mile Maiethorn inland to Thaeloren 3–12 days (a couple of weeks at the long end)
Salt Walk Old Crossing, then the Near Mile 3–5 days’ sail plus the inland days; typically 1–3 weeks
Long Mile West Water, then Heskoren inland weeks to months; figure 6–12 weeks for a coast-to-grove attempt

Kumbaan is not on that table. No walk has crossed the storm-wall.

From To How Fair weather
Thaeloren Rothallo (people still say the Inner Close) walk 1 day
Thaeloren Maiethlir river road along the Core-thaw 1–2 days
Thaeloren the Third Hearth Near Mile 3 days
Third Hearth Brenthael Near Mile 1 day further out
Brenthael the Mill-hold Near Mile 2 days further out (Raillath, the ordinary halt, sits in this stretch, a day from each)
Brenthael Raillath Near Mile 1 day further out
Raillath the Mill-hold Near Mile 1 day further out
Near Mile, a day short of the Third Hearth Nelath the spur, and then it stops 1 day
Thaeloren the Low Wall off the present Mile 1–2 days (not inside the Close)
Thaeloren Hinge Shore quays (Votaer is the port) Core-thaw and the west-road 8–12 days
Thaeloren Ornsael west-road over the Shelf-gate, or the Noon Pass if you want the water-line 10–14 days
Hinge Shore quay Orentel Old Crossing 3–5 days’ sail
Orentel Denlad a side inlet toward the Hinge Shore, short of the estuary about 1 day’s sail
Orentel Lunbra Chart-run 4–8 days
Orentel Braetu coasting, to the Night Shore 8–14 days
Braetu Heskoren frontier coast West Water 2–4 weeks
Heskoren coast Eolvaeth inland vale 1–2 weeks
Eolvaeth Harrow’s Green live-front roads 2–3 weeks (Eolvaeth cannot see Harrow’s, and does not want to)
Harrow’s Green Tunral live-front road, coastward, no sight of the canopy about a week
Harrow’s Green the Three Hamlets Past the Ford the Rise-water hours to 1 day (the canopy is a dark on the far slope)
Harrow’s Green Natai west, between Harrow’s Green and Sanbreo; not on the ford not recorded
Vaelun the First Bowl vale track into the Yield, away from Harrow’s 1–2 days
Maiethlir Seinbrun off the Down-Bank; north of Maiethlir on the atlas more than 1 day (the first day below the Down Gate does not reach it); the rest is not recorded
Thaeloren Tasain the west road, below the Shelf-gate; south of Thaeloren on the atlas not recorded
Tasain Larbril the west road over the Shelf-gate; Larbril is east of the Rain-Wall, on the dry side, where the road meets the Well-wash not recorded
Maiethlir the Seeing-Ring a hill in the old Watching country, north-east of Maiethlir; the atlas sheets do not mark it not recorded; the climb up the hill takes a morning
Orentel Raitin the road inland; south-west of Orentel on the atlas not recorded
Orentel Naenor coasting; south-west of Orentel and south of Raitin on the atlas not recorded
Any mainland quay Kumbaan storm-wall not a timetable

Where a row says not recorded, the seat gives a place and a direction and does not give a time. The directions come from the atlas sheets. Larbril lies on the dry-side road toward Ornsael, short of the pass, and the counted days in the table are the days to the well, not a separate count for Larbril. Raillath is a halt, a few hearths and a shrine with water, and it is not Nelath. Nelath is the spur where the walk stops.

A Hale-month storm on the Old Crossing can turn a Salt Walk into a missed year. A thaw-week on the Rain-Wall can turn the Shelf-gate into a lake, and the Thaw-Break closed roads for two summers. The table is weather, not a promise.

The Closed Seat was an origin-gate on the grove. Hildal’s Retreat shut its walls one day’s walk from the Motherwood, inside Orenbren’s lodging-country, and that city is Rothallo, which people still call the Inner Close. The book kept there is the Walled Book, and it belongs to the grove’s country, not to the shore. Fifteen powers stand. Rothallo sits inside Orenbren as one of them, and it is not a sixteenth. The Hinge Shore is the coast of a different war. Its peace is the Hinge Hush, still charged as the Hush-rate. Rothallo’s wall and the Hinge Shore’s quay keep their own names.

What a house keeps in the field

An ox ploughs, hauls timber, and pulls a cart. The herds are on the core farms, the Chart-run plain, and the broad vales of Heskoren. A breeding animal is worth more to a house than a week’s wages, so people are more afraid of losing the ox than of the ox itself. The ox will not take a ford when the water is over the axle, and then it stops, so a driver who knows the animal waits, or finds the shallow, or unloads. Whipping it through is how a house loses the season. On a ford that is already shallow, the driver still gets down and leads, and they will not say why. A Two-Bodied person in an ox’s body is a person. This animal is an ox, and it is not on a guild roll.

A goat gives milk, meat, hide, and dung, and it browses scrub other stock will not take. The herds are on the Rain-Shadow, the rough ground of Heskoren, and the terraces of Kumbaan. A house that loses the herd loses the cheese and the wall’s upkeep in the same week. The house is afraid of the goat in two places: a terrace wall knocked loose, which is a season of soil in the wrong yard, and a well-share argument when the herd comes in and the coping is already crowded. The goat is not afraid of the wall. The goat is doing the job the scrub offered. A Two-Bodied person in a goat’s body is a person. This animal is a goat, and it is not breeding stock for a guild.

A dog herds, guards a door, and keeps a quay or a hall honest about who is coming in. Farms, quays, halls, and road-houses keep them. The dog knows the way the house uses, and the house trusts the stop. The dog is afraid of floodwater and refuses a flooded path, so handlers who know the dog stop with it. A driver who drags it through is arguing with the animal about the water, and the animal has already read the path. A granary cat, on the same kind of work, marks spoilage, and that is a different animal. A Two-Bodied person in a dog’s body is a person. This animal is a dog.

Horses, mules, sheep, cattle, pigs, geese, and bees are livelihoods in the same way, on the ground that can feed them. They enter a scene as property, food, labour, or loss. The adversaries of a wild road are a different matter from a house’s stock.

Maps

East is Maiethorn, where the wood is oldest. West of that heart the grafts are still arriving on Heskoren, and past the storm-wall is Kumbaan, where the count of Trees is none. The names of the water and the stone are in Climate, Ecology, and Travel. What the lands are is in The Four Continents. These sheets show where a named place sits. If a painted roof and a sentence in this book disagree, follow the sentence.

There are two kinds of drawing, and they are not the same thing. The schematic is the placement: west is left, east is right, and if you read it from the left you are walking the reach backward, from none, through thin, through high, and at last to full. Kumbaan, the storm-wall, Heskoren, the West Water, Strandoren, the Old Crossing, and Maiethorn sit in that order, and the coastlines on it are a sketch, not a measured survey. The pictures in this chapter are the labeled paintings. They carry the same four landmasses and the same west-is-left rule, and they are still paintings. The relative positions stay. A later page may turn the compass. What has to hold is who sits next to whom, and how far.

World map

The picture is the labeled world painting. West is left, and the labels are the ones painted on that sheet: four landmasses, the Old Crossing, the West Water, the Rain-Wall, the four rivers, the Noon Pass, and the Shelf-gate. The fifteen powers are regions of ground. No surveyed border is painted. If a painted roof and a sentence here disagree, follow the sentence. An isle with no name in these notes is paint.

Rothallo is the mark inside Orenbren, one day’s walk from the wood. People still say the Inner Close. That name is this city, and the city is the capital. On the regional sheets the painted mark is still the small walled square. No sheet paints a star on a capital. Maiethlir and Orentel are each marked once.

Capitals, large cities, and important towns are marked where the notes already place them. Vaelhesk is the land. It has no settlement dot. Harrow’s Green is a grove-town, not a capital. Ornsael is a well-town, not a capital. The First Seat stands in the wood, and no sheet marks it. No date is written on the Tree. There is no graft on Kumbaan, and none took on the isle.

On the drawing, three older stones are small marks: the Low Wall, the Seeing-Ring, and the Dry Stair. They are found stone from before the Walking Years, on this same ground. The Seeing-Ring is on a hill north-east of Maiethlir. The painted sheets do not mark it. The Ages chapter tells that stretch.

Natai sits west of Harrow’s Green, between Sanbreo and that grove, on ground of its own. The hamlets’ ford is a different crossing. Larbril is where the west road meets the Well-wash, short of the pass, west of Ornsael’s well. Ornsael is farther into the dry, at a well. Open country lies between it and Larbril, and the town sits inland. Where the paint and a sentence in this book disagree, follow the sentence.

Continent maps

Maiethorn, east. The labeled continent painting is the picture.

The Mother-core lies west of the Rain-Wall. Thaeloren is the canopy-ring in the old growth, the Tree the later cuttings came from. Rothallo is the walled mark one day out. People still say the Inner Close, and the city is the capital, still painted at the scale of that small square. Maiethlir sits where the Core-thaw slows. Seinbrun stands off that river, north of Maiethlir. The Seeing-Ring’s hill is north-east of Maiethlir and is not painted. The Third Hearth is a road-house three days out. Lirorn is the range. The name of the divide is the Rain-Wall, and Lirorn calls it the Thaw-Wall. The Noon Pass is the older high notch, the one with the water-line. The Shelf-gate is the lower road, the one taken after the Break. Tasain is in the valley below that gate, on the wet side, south of Thaeloren. Saelthael is the dry east. Larbril is the meeting of the west road and the Well-wash, east of the range and short of the pass. Ornsael is the well-town farther along that road into the dry, with open country between the two, and the town sits inland. The Hinge Shore is Maiethorn’s face on the Old Crossing. Votaer is the port on that shore.

Strandoren, middle. The labeled continent painting is the picture.

Orentel is a plain dot at the eastern estuary, not a star. The Chart-run crosses the interior to that estuary. Lunbra is on the run, upriver of the salt. Raitin stands on the river behind the premier coast, south-west of Orentel. Trenledd and Netstrand are written as areas of ground, and no border is painted around them. Naenor is on the south coast, south-west of Orentel and south of Raitin, on water of its own, apart from the Chart-run and apart from the West Water. Braetu is the harbour on the Night Shore. Six charter-towns sit around Raitin. This sheet does not name them, and it does not mark them. Denlad, the inlet about a day’s sail short of the estuary, has no sheet of its own.

Heskoren, west of the West Water. The labeled continent painting is the picture.

West is left. The west coast is the slate-shore, in Ornled, facing the last capes and the storm-wall. The sea on the right of the sheet, the Strandoren side, is the West Water, off Heskoren’s east coast. Eolvaeth is the pilgrim-town in the waiting vale, and the vale has no view of Harrow’s. Sanbreo is the slate-shore town on the west coast, the mark that names Ornled’s seat, and its beach faces west. Harrow’s Green is a plain grove-town on the live-front rise. Natai is the march west of that grove, between Sanbreo and Harrow’s, on ground of its own. The hamlets sit on different ground past the Rise-water crossing: Brenod, Vaelun, and Ornath. Their ford is that crossing. Harrow’s square is the grove-town’s own ground. Vaelhesk is old greens, and it has no settlement dot. Tunral, a kitchen and a post coastward of Harrow’s with no sight of the canopy, has no sheet of its own.

Kumbaan, behind the storm-wall. The labeled continent painting is the picture. There is no settlement dot and no graft.

It is one isle, and the name sits on the hill-country with no point marker. The storm-wall is weather around the isle: cloud, current, and reef. The sheet shows no graft, no city, no harbour, no safe channel, and no Tree. Ndenjoo is a hill-hall. Njunda keeps its table, and that is a person, not a second mark. The sheet gives the hall no flag. Nothing on the isle is a graft.

The overlays

Each painted region keeps the names the ground already had.

The world sheet is the painting at the start of this chapter. It runs the same west-to-east line: Kumbaan, the storm-wall, Heskoren, the West Water, Strandoren, the Old Crossing, Maiethorn, the Rain-Wall. The sea-names sit in the water. Vaelhesk has no dot on this sheet either. Maiethlir and Orentel are marked once here.

The Old Crossing. Orentel is on the Strandoren estuary. The Hinge Shore is named as a stretch of the Maiethorn coast, and Votaer is the port on that coast. The Hush-rate is the charge for the crossing.

The Sacred Core. Thaeloren’s canopy-ring. The First Seat, in the wood, has no separate mark. Rothallo is the walled square one day out. Seinbrun is off the Core-thaw, north of Maiethlir. The Third Hearth is three days out. Maiethlir is the counted city on the Core-thaw road.

The Rain-Wall. The range is the Rain-Wall. The Noon Pass and the Shelf-gate are notches in the range. Tasain is the town in the valley below the Shelf-gate. Tengu and Fox-of-the-Snows hearths sit on the snow, inside Lirorn.

The Rain-Shadow. The dry east, painted as weather. Larbril is on the west road, short of the pass. Ornsael is on the well, farther into the dry, with open country between them. The Well-wash is seasonal water. The Dry Stair is a site on a different rise. The well-town at its shoulder has no name in these notes.

The Chart-run. The river to Orentel’s estuary. The first quay is the old landing. The White Note is one desk-house on the third quay, north side. It keeps the notes, and it is not a crown. Lunbra is upriver of the salt. Other towns in the filed country have no names on this sheet.

The West Water. The open ocean, in the blue. The Night Shore is the west-and-south face, named as a shore. Braetu is the harbour. This sheet does not mark the unlit berth.

The live front. Harrow’s is a grove-town on the rise. The march’s seat is Natai, west of this grove, and this sheet is not Natai’s square. The Rise-water runs to the ford. Brenod, Vaelun, and Ornath are three small hearths past the crossing.

The waiting vale. Eolvaeth is a pilgrim-town at the gift-hall. The spring is a pool. This sheet does not draw Harrow’s canopy.

Square and seat maps

Closer sheets exist for the seats and the town squares that already have streets. They are the same places as the notes. A closer sheet of a city is that city. Rothallo’s gate is the same square gatehouse as the city: beds outside, the Book inside. Larbril’s Well-wash is a silt-line, and the road there is the west road. Vaelhesk has no sheet. Raillath, Denlad, and Tunral are on the travel table, and they have no sheet of their own. The Third Hearth, the three hamlets, and the First Bowl are painted on the regional sheets above, not as cities of their own.

Three old walks are still roads.

The Near Mile is the inland stones toward Thaeloren. Some of them now end at a Turning Tree. Nelath’s spur is one road that stops, and Raillath is the halt that does not.

The Salt Walk is the Old Crossing, then the Near Mile. The Hush-rate is charged on the hinge. Votaer sorts the hull. Orentel prices the berth. Denlad is the inlet where a family can still miss the week.

The Long Mile is the West Water, then Heskoren mud. Empty road-houses still make the bed. Braetu quotes the far run.

The travel times are in Climate, Ecology, and Travel. A day’s walk is the interval a mile-shrine marks.

Closer paintings of the seats and town squares that have them follow. West is left on each.

Rothallo, the walled capital. People still say the Inner Close.

The gate is the same square gatehouse, with the beds outside and the Book inside.

Seinbrun, Maiethvael’s capital.

Larbril, where the west road meets the Well-wash.

Harrow’s Green, the grove-town on the live front. Natai is the march’s seat.

Book VIThe Ages

The Ages

People in this world do not live in a fourth age stacked on three earlier ones. They keep two clocks at the same time, and the clock a person reaches for tells you where that person stands.

The first clock is personal, and a family keeps it the way it keeps a grandparent’s stories. It counts how you were Turned. Turning is what the Awakening Tree does for a child in the tenth year: a Condition, a change that comes to a person rather than a people they were born as, can be Given, or the Tree can hug the child and leave them without one. A colour at that giving means a Condition. A hug means no colour, and a person left with none is called Kept, and also UnTurned. Did you walk to Thaeloren, the Awakening Tree itself, or to a neighbour who had already made that walk, or did you stand under a town graft, a cutting of that Tree planted at home and grown as the same plant? An ordinary family will tell you they are a Hands-house, Hands being those planted town Trees, and that grandmother still talks of the road. A Long-Lived person, whose aging has stopped and who forgets nothing they have witnessed, who says “I walked” is saying when they were young, because the Long-Lived live long enough that the walk can have been their own childhood.

The second clock is geographic, and it has not finished. The Grafting is the carrying of living wood outward from the origin, Hand by Hand, and it is not a golden age that opened and then closed. The wood started at the Awakening Tree, filled Maiethorn, crossed the sea to Strandoren, and is still arriving on Heskoren, which people also call the Sundered Reach. Kumbaan, the Sundering Isle, stands entirely off that spread. Where the wood is still thin, that thinness is not a scar history left behind. It is the front of a process that has not finished.

Both clocks sit on a preface that was never given an age-name, Before the Walk. The Tree was already there. People were already born into Kinds, the peoples a person is from birth and does not become later, and some were already Struck, which is a Condition arriving later at a threshold such as a drowning, an oath, or a death, before anyone had called the Tree a mother. No count that is being honest begins with the Tree.

This was not a civilizing mission, and the Walking Years were not a golden age of pilgrimage that the grafts then improved. The Walking Years were the work of getting a child to one Tree in time, across weeks of road and water, and that work killed children. The Grafting was horticulture, the cutting and planting of living wood, and people sanctified it afterward. The First Seat, the college of tree-wardens at the Awakening Tree, now tells both the walk and the grafts as the Mother’s will travelling. Folk memory is less tidy, and holds the romance and the graves in the same sentence.

The ages at a glance

Everyday Liturgical Says What it is
Preface Before the Walk (mostly unnamed) · the Watching keep the Before — The Awakening Tree already stood. People were already born into Kinds, already becoming at doors, and already seeing, and nobody had called the Tree a mother. The time is left uncounted on purpose.
Count of how you Turned, old default the Walking Years Brenvaeth (BREN-vaeth) “the hearth gone to waiting” You walked to Thaeloren or you stayed UnTurned for want of the trip. The far lands ran heavy with the UnTurned, and with people who were Struck later.
The hinge the First Cut Eoloren (EOL-or-en) “the witnessed hinge” Someone cut living wood and the cutting took. Who cut it is argued. That it happened is not.
Count of where the wood has reached the Grafting (a process, not an age you leave) — The carrying of living wood, Hand by Hand. It is still unfinished on Heskoren, the Sundered Reach, and it never crossed the storm-wall.
Count of how you Turned, new default the Years of Hands Ornthael (ORN-thael) “Tree-land” A town Tree is the ordinary way to Turn. Pilgrimage remains, as devotion, as prestige, or as a necessity wherever a graft has failed.

The pair of liturgical names turns inside out the name the Road-hands use for the work of carrying wood, and the Road-hands are the tree-wardens who walk that wood. In the Old Tongue, Thaelvaeth means “the Tree gone to the waiting,” which is wood carried out to the hearths. Brenvaeth (BREN-vaeth) means “the hearth gone to the waiting,” which is people walking in to the Tree. Eoloren (EOL-or-en) is the liturgical name of the cut, and Ornthael (ORN-thael) is the liturgical name of the years when a town has its own Tree. The Grafting is the moment the world stopped sending hearths to the Tree and started sending the Tree to hearths.

A history in order

This section tells the history in order, from before anyone counted years to the present. The years are given the way the First Seat and the devout clerks count them, from the First Cut, the first time a piece cut from the Awakening Tree was planted in another town and grew. That year is Cut-year 0, and the present year is Cut-year 387. Many people count another way, and “How years are numbered,” below, says who they are. The later sections of this chapter tell each part at length. What follows here is the order of events, and what each one left behind.

Before anyone counted years

Before anyone counted years, the Awakening Tree already stood on Maiethorn, in the country now called the Sacred Core. It was the only tree in the world a child could be Turned under, and nobody planted it in any summer that anyone remembers.

People were already born into their Kinds. Some were already Struck into a Condition at a threshold, far from the Tree and with nobody to witness it. Under the Tree, children in their tenth year were already brought at the solstice and either Given a colour or hugged. Nobody knows how long any of that had been going on.

The Watching, the faith that keeps a night of attention and will not start history at a mother’s name, call this time the Before. They teach that the Tree was already watching people before anyone called it a mother. The Old Ways on Heskoren, a long way from Maiethorn, say their people were already being Struck at the places they call doors, a drowning, a grove, or a stone, before any road to the Tree existed. Kumbaan is not part of this history. Its people have their own past, and they do not count it by the Tree.

Nobody wrote down a king, a war, or a founding from this time. A few stone places from it survive, and three of them are described near the end of this section. More of the thin preface is in “Before the Walk.”

The years of the walk

The time before the First Cut is called the Walking Years. Nobody knows when it started, because it started when families began to organize the trip to the Tree, and nobody wrote that year down. The road, the inns, the graves, and the gate are told at length in “The Walking Years.”

In those years there was one Tree to Turn under, and one week in which to do it.
