Laevila looks like the neighbour who stayed, flour on the cuff and no mark of any office, and you know them because someone said ask the old room, or because you saw them under the Tree the night before Turning-Week with no lamp.

What they want is Senithi (seh-NITH-ee)’s name good for a marriage. Senithi is their grandchild, Given a colour at the Leaf-Fall and of the same house, and a marriage is priced on a line that lists the wrong grandmother. The hidden face still has that grandmother under her own name. Laevila wants it read once, in a room a clerk will accept as a witness, not as theology but as a name a tablet will swallow. They will not Speak, and they will not say Two-Bodied if what they saw was two colours, though they will say the two colours. Rithim Speaks in the same square. They eat together after the Night Watch. Rithim will not say the line the clerk is waiting to copy, and Laevila will not say the Mother, the name a Watcher leaves out of the blessing. That is as close as peace gets on this street. The chapel wardens leave a plate during Turning-Week, and that plate is courtesy, not a wage. They cannot confirm a colour, and they cannot unsay the recut. They can sit beside the Speaker and say the second colour aloud, so it stays spoken in the square and the clerk cannot quietly drop it.

Tesara — Orentel

Tesara (teh-SAH-rah) sits the stillers’ shed that does not face the street, the catching-year, which is the week a newly Struck person is kept somewhere quiet before the town reaches for a rope. A key is kept off the slate, so if the week goes well, nobody hears of it, and they will not stamp a ticket this week. A ticket is the licence that lets one of the Stilled use the gaze where the town can see it. There is no family to put first. A neighbour says Tesara, and a stranger gets Tesara of Orentel. Years back Tesara was Struck, a Condition met at a later threshold rather than at the childhood leaf, and what they carry is a Gaze, the stilling look, taken raw in a week somebody else sat. The paying floor does not write that down. Tesara remembers the door, and that memory is why they are the one the floor can spare. They think the work is first aid. You catch the person, you steady them, and you hand them on to the year the guild would actually train.

What they want is Valen stamped with a real ticket, not left on a slip that can be burned. Valen was stone on the third night, a Struck member of the Stilled, the kind who survived being turned to stone, stood for by a sister and by an N. who would not give a family name. The week is almost over, and the face of the ticket is still empty, because the slip is written on the inside of a blank and Tesara will not stamp the outside this week. A burned slip is how a quiet week disappears. The paying floor wants the master back, because a quiet catching-year is a week the theatre lost. They cannot overrule a quay-watch, and they cannot stamp a ticket this week. They can keep a master in the shed one more night, and they can fail to burn a slip. If Valen lives and still has no ticket, Mataero is who they will need, because occupancy will not say Struck. Rosire used to bring water downwind of the shed, and is not on the floor this Hale-month. Tesara has not been told why.

Named wants in the three seats

Wants sit on people. An institution can furnish a bed, a pot, or a paper, or withhold them. The want stays with the person.

Eolvaeth. Vaethod wants Saelid’s stall to keep its winter customers, because in a year when a cohort is sent away the camp-streets that buy the bread go empty. Nedaen (neh-DAYN), one of the Taken-In, the people the wild took partway into itself and gave back, keeps the commons around the Tree and wants the gift-hall pot to feed their child through Ledger-month. Mother’s green is enough until it is not. Heiral (HAY-ral) is Kept and lives on the camp-street. They want a marriage witnessed without being pitied as Mother-kept. They will take a neighbour’s word, and they will not take a sermon. Daron (DAR-on) is Returned, a person who died with something unfinished and is still walking because of it, and they keep the far shed. They want a specific corpse named so a grain-debt dies with it. The family will not come downwind to do it.

Orentel. Mataero wants Sorel off the White Note’s century-paper, and they think a clean loft-slate will buy that. Sorim wants berths 1–4 to stay held through Hale-month, the spring month when the land is counted sound. Their house-share is the hold-fee, the fee for keeping the berth, and not the wool. Tesara wants Valen stamped before the paying floor takes the master back. Lasole (lah-SO-leh) rents a leaf-lot on the rise and wants the credit extended one season. The lot will not follow them home, and home is a loft if it did. Didel (dih-DEL) of Hallowquay is Selkie, sea-born, one of the skin-kin, and works haulage. They want a kin-berth for a skin-kin wedding in Eolthael. Sorim has held berths 1–4 for a First-Hand year, a berth kept for the prestige walk to the origin, and Didel cannot hold those.

Maiethlir. Rithim wants Valein unfiled. The verso already knows how to write unmarked. Laevila wants Senithi’s name read off the hidden face of a recut beam, once, in a room a clerk will accept as a witness. Vehaela (veh-HAY-lah) came down from Lirorn’s thin snow with two children and wants an uncounted loft for one winter. The extra-mile street still has rooms the roll has not found. Baerith (BAY-rith) is Far-Voiced, a voice that carries exactly as far and as true as the singer means it to, and they sing the counted hour. They want the crown to stop cutting green on the street where their sister keeps a pot. To be cut off is framed as a lapse, and what it is, is a household going hungry.

The squares touch by paper, beds, pots, and one week in Eolthael, and the crossings are not a party. A household Vaethod sent last thin year sometimes eats now on a necessity-note from the White Note, a paper for a household in need. Mataero files the loft, and Vaethod does not know the house-year, the count that house keeps for itself. Sorim’s berth 5 is earth. The pot, a young tree in the container it travels in, is going toward a luckier Hand. Haelin will sleep the Road-hand, the warden walking with that wood, if the wood arrives. That is the live front, not a reunion. Rithim Speaks the colour, and Laevila describes the other colour in the same square, the same morning. They already share a street, and they do not say the same thing. Tesara’s week, if it is not burned at the end of it, becomes a person who later needs a loft or a berth. Mataero will hear occupancy, and Sorim will hear a hold they cannot invent. Thilim still holds a far-cape name the White Note does not have. A court that wants a Cut-year set beside a house-year writes inland and to the quay. The two answers will not match, and the two desks do not travel to deliver them. Reimaethe lives in a rise-room Mataero lets, and has given four years of memory into the Pourers’ cup. Hithaen arrived in the gift-hall with no list behind them. Vaethod can tell a person who came to wait from a clerk who came to write, and has not yet decided which this is. Rosire works a ticket-infirmary downwind of Tesara’s shed when they are in Orentel. This Hale-month they are not there, and Tesara has not been told why.

Other people of note

These are not a second court. They are the people already doing the work in squares that needed one more pair of hands.

Person Square The job The ordinary want
Njunda Ndenjoo table-keeper Nolas gone as kin, extra place still laid
Ledan the White Note House quay-desk founding-name spoken once
Theisva · Lesna · Bovaer Ornsael well-gang a share that lasts Hale-month
Tora · Nethiro · Baelon the three hamlets past the ford three kitchens send, or refuse, or not take the other road
Talen · Milsun · Thurrei the Mill-hold drain and slate a mill that still turns; a week that still has room
Delvor · Vilraet · Brudu the First Bowl bowl, Speaking, old planting sit before colour; a Struck housed; morning water
Meirim Brenthael neighbour-warden the Third Hearth’s stone down; room for the Mill-hold’s week
Raetoth · Lithsur Nelath stone and scar the mile stays in the square; the name goes back on the day
Lonteith Raillath the halt the column drinks and does not stay
Relmun Denlad the post a tide that is not a hold
Huval Tunral the night’s kitchen a true distance, and no invented colour
Nurreith the Low Wall one summer’s shovel the labour off the garden; the chip was the other quarry
Soonke · Saalo Ndenjoo sand and valley sit, or leave wreck off the hill; Waandi found
Thuda the Low Wall garden-end innkeep labour off the garden

Theisva (THAYS-vah) keeps Ornsael’s share, Lesna (LES-nah) the planting, and Bovaer (bo-VAIR) the west road, and the share is the want that has to last Hale-month. Tora (TOR-ah) of Brenod sends the child and walks the witness home. Nethiro (neth-EE-ro) of Vaelun may refuse the neighbour’s week. Baelon (BAY-lon) of Ornath has looked at the other road and has not taken it. Lonteith (LON-tayth) keeps the halt at Raillath, a day’s post on the Near Mile between Brenthael and the Mill-hold, fills a cup for a column that is passing, and will not chalk a bed, because hosting the week would make the halt a second Brenthael. Relmun (REL-mun) keeps the cove post at Denlad, a day’s sail short of Orentel, says a name aloud because chalk will not stick to the wet post, and will not call a hull that tied up in a blow a hold. Huval (HOO-val) feeds the night at Tunral, on the road toward Harrow’s and not under a canopy, will not invent a colour for a child who is ten, and at dusk sets a bowl outside on the side away from Harrow’s. The bowl is not a first meal, and it is not a shrine, and Huval will not say why.

Haelin (HAY-lin) keeps Harrow’s Green, the live front this cast points at, and wants the stone moved before Leaf-Fall so the crowd can stand, with the water still on it until then. They name a colour only when they are sure of it. Last Eolthael something white happened at that canopy, and Haelin did not Speak it. Tora is on the square when the stone is to be moved, because the next column still drinks there, and because a colour that was never named aloud cannot be walked home as a witnessing.

Maiethorn’s seats. These are people at Maiethorn’s seats, each with an ordinary want. A neighbour says the given name, and at Rothallo a clerk says the house first. A Given pilgrim is a person who received the becoming at the childhood Turning, and is on the road as that person. Tasain’s levy is the toll Narol’s household still collects, and Narol of the Pass is dead.

Person Square The job The ordinary want
Vuthbraen Seinbrun the furnished hall the pot still open to a house that left the hymn
Breillai Seinbrun outside the hymn a green and a bed without the net
Raermu Seinbrun the medicine basket a stiller’s hour for a Kept child
Brimaen Rothallo a stall inside the walls the key through Turning-Week. House Lanbru.
Breolnir Rothallo the sleep-line at the gate a Given pilgrim written as sleep. House Tethnae.
Methei Rothallo a turn of work on the outer beds the turn ends at dark and is not set again. House Sithlaen.
Brormei Larbril the meeting of road and wash the west road still a road when the wash is silt
Tumair Votaer the hull’s docket one class for a hull that is also a pilgrim
Lertho Votaer the Hush-rate the rate taken as a rate

Delamem and Talnin stay with the Walled Book, and Hithaen is another Given heir, already in Eolvaeth.

Strandoren’s seats. These are people at Strandoren’s seats, each with an ordinary want. A neighbour says the given name, and at Lunbra a clerk says the house first. Orentel was already seated above, Denlad stays Relmun, and the White Note stays Ledan.

Person Square The job The ordinary want
Turvo Raitin the shared notes a cleared note the next hearth will still stand
Nubo Raitin the gap between hearths a vouching that holds past the hall
Sulnu Raitin the ticket to the river stair a ticket that still means something at the water
Derdil Naenor the signing-watch a term that closes without making a gift a debt
Vamar Lunbra a column of the roll the row under the house that was said. House Melro. Not the crown.
Mursur Braetu the far quote, and a lamp the dark berth left without a house

Heskoren’s seat. There is one person in this table, because Sanbreo has no new person and Vaelhesk has no new person, and the land stays the seat. A neighbour says the given name.

Person Square The job The ordinary want
Dumu Natai the march-voice a shout that lands at that gate, and not on Haelin’s square

Ledan (LED-an) still writes the White Note quay-desk. They are Long-Lived, and the Cut-year 280 conversion-query, the question of how to turn one count of years into another, is theirs. They will convert a house-year, or a Cut-year, or a court’s third date, if you say which. They will not invent a berth, and they will not invent a hull. What they want is the founding-name on the north bed spoken once, aloud, so they can stop being the only memory of it, and they will not speak it first. The six pivots stay Vaethod, Rithim, Mataero, Thilim, Laevila, and Tesara. Ledan is the desk a session can sit at when the paper has to be in the room, and not a seventh pivot.

Four people a campaign can start from. They are four separate people, not a crew, and they do not travel as one.

Reimaethe (RYE-may-theh) is Long-Lived on the rise in Orentel, of the rise and of no house. Every Long-Lived person is asked once to join the Pourers, the circle that sets a year of memory into a cup, and Reimaethe said yes. A member gives one year at a time, each on its own night, with a drop of blood as the record, because a Long-Lived already reads memory in blood. The year goes into the cup and is gone from the member’s memory, the papers from that year go onto the shelf, and the circle counts the member one year younger. The circle says the cup holds a god it made, and the Unspent is the presence in it, a small household presence that stores what it is given and does not make plans. The circle asks five years in all. Reimaethe has given four, and a member may stop before any year, while the years already given stay in the cup. They want to stop before the fifth, and they want their papers back, thin as that copy is, because the papers are all the circle returns. They want Mataero to keep writing let and not why. Neighbours call the practice a rich uncle’s hobby, and they do not look like a hobby. A second cup sits next to the first. They have not asked to drink from it, because asking would already cost them something with the circle.

Hithaen (hith-AYN) arrived in Eolvaeth’s gift-hall this Hale-month with no list behind them and a name they will not put on a wall. They are Given, and somewhere behind the walls that are still standing, families that have stayed Kept for generations are still a class, and a child Given at Leaf-Fall can fall out of that line, which is what happened to Hithaen. The house is Brethlumal (breth-LU-mal). The line cast them out and kept the name on them. They will not say it, and they will not take of Eolvaeth. They want a life that is not a wall-pass, a life of being let through the wall, and on worse nights they want the name back, which is not the same want. They are not Talnin, and they are not Methei. Vaethod has not decided whether Hithaen came to wait or to be counted. What is left of the arrangement they walked out of is the Walled Book, the Inner Close inside Orenbren, political rank and not a church. This is one person eating alms in a vale that has no list, which is why they walked here.

Taeren (TAY-ren) is of Brenod, not of Harrow’s and not of a capital, and there is no house to put first. They are a hush, the filing word for a white-fire the clerks will not let become a civic fact, and a child who stood at the neighbour’s canopy when something white happened. The wider world knows there should be a Phoenix, the one person the stories are about, and it has not seen one in a generation, while doctrine says there cannot be two. If a white-fire is Spoken while a sanctuary still holds the Phoenix, the clerks file it as a mis-Speaking or as a hush. Last Eolthael Taeren stood at Harrow’s Green. Something white happened, and Haelin did not Speak it. A colour that was never named aloud cannot be walked home as a witnessing, so Taeren is still in the square when the Hale-month crowds arrive, with the tenth year just behind them and heat in the hands they do not show. They ask ordinary questions, about bread and about whether the week is over and about why an old hymn uses a name they do not own, and they do not know why a fire answers them when someone says an old name. The public sentence about a Phoenix is still that there is one, and this chapter does not change it.

Rosire (ro-SEER-eh) is of Orentel, with no house, and this Hale-month they are sleeping in an upper room at Harrow’s Green. They once held a post in a house they do not name. They opened a door they were not scheduled to open, and someone walked out through it. Rosire walked the other way, took the ticket-yard work of bringing water at Tesara’s shed, and does not use the byname from before that floor. They are not on Tesara’s water this week. They walked inland with the person who walked out. They want that person, and any child a fire might answer, not to become a story, and they want themselves not sent for. They look infirmary-tired, with grey under the nails from other people’s stone, and travel stays out of their talk.

A neighbour still gets the given name. Raetoth, Lithsur, Lonteith, Relmun, Huval, and Nurreith are given names the places already use, and a stranger hears of Nelath, of Raillath, of Denlad, of Tunral, or of the garden-end. None of them has a house. Maiethlir writes a house before the given name: Laevila and Senithi are Thalonve, Rithim is Nirsei, Valein is that same house left unwritten, and Baerith is Rairtei. Vehaela is of Lirorn, and has not taken a house. Eolvaeth asks of where? Vaethod, Saelid, Heiral, Nedaen, and Daron are of the town, or of the street they already stand on. Hithaen will not take of Eolvaeth. Orentel asks of where? as well. The quay does not file a family. The White Note is a house only while the paper is open, and then it is the desk. Valen is of Orentel, and Didel is of Hallowquay. Thilim is of the Held bed, Taeren is of Brenod, and Njunda is the given name, which is the whole of the name.

The six pivots stay the six. Reimaethe, Hithaen, Taeren, and Rosire stay four separate people.

Book IXAt the Table

Playing in the Turning

Follow this page, in this order, when you make a character and when you start play. The stories and the laws live in their own chapters. This page is the sequence at the table, so it tells you what to do and where the fuller ruling sits, and it does not become a second copy of those chapters.

Tone. The people of this world are neighbours and colleagues, and most of what a session spends its time on is ordinary life, with a real danger underneath it. A Tithe, the upkeep a Condition card asks of the person who carries it, never takes the player character over. Keep the frightening part rare.

Making a character

You run this once, in this order, and you do not invent a second way to build a character beside it.

  1. Kind. Choose what the character was born, which this book calls an ancestry. That can be a stock ancestry from Daggerheart, one of the four written for this world (Kitsune, Selkie, Tengu, or Yumboe), or a Mixed Ancestry in the way the System Reference Document already allows. The rulings sit in The Kinds. A stock ancestry grants two features, and each of those four grants three, so a character whose two features both come from stock ancestries, whether that is one stock Kind or a mix of two, takes a Hearth-Mark to make up the difference. Name the place that raised you, a town or a quay or a road, written as a place and not as a Kind. Once per session, when you make an action roll or a reaction roll that leans on how that place taught you to live, you add +2, and you do not spend Hope to add it. A character who takes any feature from the four ancestries written for this world takes no Hearth-Mark, because that third feature is already the hearth. A Yumboe needs the GM’s leave, and the character is the full Kind, all three features, never a mix and never a Hearth-Mark.
  2. Community. Take a Community the way the SRD has it, the card for the sort of place that raised the character. A Hearth-Mark names a place. It does not fill the Community line, and it is not a second Community.
  3. Class, Experiences, equipment. Take class, equipment, and Experiences as the SRD has them. Write two Experiences, the phrases on the sheet that say what the character has lived. A Kept character has those same two and no third, and the tradeoff for that empty card is written below.
  4. Turning. Pick one, and write it on the sheet. The Leaf-Fall is the week a child stands under the town’s Turning Tree in their tenth year, and what the Tree did then, or did not do, is the Turning. How many people are Given, Struck, and Kept is in The Conditions.
    - Given means a coloured leaf fell on you when you were ten, and you take one Given-path or Both-path card from The Conditions.
    - Kept means the leaves closed around you in a hug and no colour fell, so you take no Condition card. What that empty card is worth is below.
    - Struck means a later threshold, one the roster already names, already happened in the backstory. You died and came back, you swore a contract, you survived a drowning, you survived being turned to stone, or you were lost and dying in the deep wild and the wild took you in. You take a Struck-path or Both-path card. Someone the town will believe stood up and said what you had become, and you say who.
    - UnTurned means you never stood under a Turning Tree, so there was no hug and no colour, and you are not Kept. Neighbours may call you Kept. The law and your sheet say UnTurned. You can still be Struck later.
  5. Choices for the whole table. Some characters are a conversation the whole table has, not a private pick.
    - Phoenix is a spotlight Condition, a campaign that will keep arriving at that fire. If anyone at the table does not want that, pick another card, or the GM runs the Phoenix as a person in the world and the player characters are someone else.
    - Hidden Phoenix uses the same consent, because the fire still keeps arriving. There is still one Gift, the single living Phoenix, and the shape of a Phoenix who is not the public legend is worked out between that player and the GM.
    - Yumboe needs the GM’s leave, and the character is the full Kind only.
    - the Unbound is not a starting pick. A Bound character, someone who swore a contract and is still keeping the terms, becomes Unbound when the term ends, in play, or because the table agrees at the start that the term already ended.

Kind and Condition stay two things on one character, so the ancestry you were born and the Condition you carry are both on the sheet. A Selkie can be Given Two-Bodied. A stock Human can be Struck Returned. A character of mixed heritage is Given, Kept, or Struck the same way anyone else is.

They stay two things when the stories sound alike. An Infernis, a stock ancestry whose features are already on the sheet from birth, who swears a contract is Bound the way anyone else who swears one would be. The blood they were born with stays Kind, and the contract is the Condition. The two do not merge, they do not cancel, and the character does not become Given-Over by default. Given-Over is the world’s name for a Bound person who signs contract after contract, and it is a title rather than a Condition this page hands out.

The Kept deal

The Kept are a deliberate tradeoff, and they are not a consolation Condition invented to make up for a missing card. They have no boon and no Tithe, so the card is empty and there is no clock on it to tick. A Condition card asks other characters to mark a Tithe clock, and the mark usually comes at a long rest. The Kept clock is empty on purpose, and that emptiness is the tradeoff.

What they have is a legal standing and a free rest. The law treats them as the ordinary person: the hug was witnessed, they owe no guild, and they hold no Condition licence. At every long rest they take their downtime with no Tithe checklist, while everyone who carries a Condition may be marking a clock. That free evening is the advantage at the table. They can still be Struck later. Kept is the life they have now, and it is not a promise that the life will stay empty.

They do not receive a tenth Condition, a bonus Experience, a Hearth-Mark they did not already qualify for, or a Kept ability of their own. An ability that is really a Tithe belongs on a Condition card. If a table later wants a house rule, that house rule is theirs, and this page does not give one.

An UnTurned life looks similar from the outside, because there is no Tithe and no guild. The difference is that a Kept person’s hug was witnessed, and an UnTurned person never stood. Do not file an UnTurned neighbour as Kept just to be kind, and do not write an UnTurned character as Kept on the sheet.

Struck in play

A Kept or UnTurned character can be Struck when the story crosses a threshold this book already names. Dying, with something left undone, can make them Returned. Swearing a contract can make them Bound. Surviving a drowning, breath and voice both stopped and both come back changed, can make them Far-Voiced. Surviving being turned to stone, held rigid and then returned to flesh, can make them one of the Stilled. Being lost and dying in the deep wild, until the wild takes them in rather than let them die, can make them one of the Taken-In. Long-Lived, Two-Bodied, the Answered, and Phoenix are Given only, so no later door can Strike them into being.

The player agrees to take the card. The GM does not hand out a becoming to punish a failed roll. A Tithe never takes the character over, and becoming is not a moment where the player loses the character.

When the player takes the card, add the Condition, and the Kind stays what it was. Someone stands for them again at the next desk that will take them, which means someone says what they became so the town can know. A hazardous becoming goes to the Intake, the quiet week a town keeps for a person just Struck. Mark them Struck. They were not Given, so there is no leaf and no second Leaf-Fall. They do not take a second Condition, because the Tree does not put one becoming on top of another, and a later door does not either.

A Bound character whose term ends becomes the Unbound, as that card says. No other Condition turns into a further Condition.

Advancement

A Condition card does not level, so the card you took at level 1 is the same card at level 10, while class features, domain cards, Experiences, weapon tier, Proficiency, and Hope scars change around it. Hope scars are the marks that cross a Hope slot off the sheet. A few things look like the card is growing, and they are not a new level of the Condition. A Two-Bodied character can gain an Experience, a Bound term can move, and a Returned or a Phoenix counts down Hope slots, while attacks the card already grants can roll more Proficiency dice as that Proficiency rises. The card underneath those changes is the card you started with. The full ruling is in The Conditions.

A domain card is a job someone in a town is already paid to do, and you use it as the SRD printed it, without a second roll on top of the card. A Condition clock ticks only from its own card. A Spoken colour, the sentence a warden says at the Leaf-Fall, is not a spell, and Hope does not buy a colour. If a scene has a thing that keeps working with no person in it, name the maker and name the problem that thing is still causing, and do not give it a Kind, a Condition, or a domain.

Travel

You move on someone’s word. A paper that names what you are does not replace the answer. When a watch stops a stranger, they ask your name, your last hearth, and who stands for you, and two of the three will do. If you can give them none, you sit until morning, or they walk you to the next gate.

The customs that count as that word are a road-word, a named person who will stand for you; a company’s vouch, the party standing for one another; a guild-mark, a craft mark that travels; a house-note, paper from a house that will answer for you; guest-right, a host who took you in; and the custom of a walk, the word the road itself gives someone who is on a named walk. Distances are in Climate, Ecology, and Travel. Kumbaan, the Sundering Isle, does not use this road-word. The crossing is in Other Places, under Ndenjoo, and in The Four Continents. People do sell a vouch. That sale is a separate trade, and it does not answer this watch.

City witnessing

A village remembers the child who stood. A city is too large for that memory, so it remembers a hearth, and the legal sentence is “I am of the third quay,” rather than “I am of Orentel.”

Turning-Week is still one week in a city. People stand by hearth, in named slots. The warden says the colour or the hug aloud, and they do not write a list of gifts. Threnmaieth writes the stand down, and that writing is the exception, because the other towns leave it spoken.

Crime

There is no crime of being a Condition. The Inviolate Will, the doctrine that a Condition cannot seize another person’s will, already sorts the charge into a Tithe that lapsed through neglect, or a power used on purpose as a weapon.

The charge walks up a ladder from a neighbour’s word, to the watch, who hold the person until morning, then to a guild hearing, and then to an open hearing. Exile from the hearth is the penalty the town treats as civic death, the end of belonging to that place. A ticket names a hazardous use, the Gaze, the Cry, or an element let loose in a yard, and it does not name the Condition. A Bound hearing sits at a table and covers the Terms of the contract. The three licences on the body stay the Stilled, the Far-Voiced, and the Answered. Bound is not a fourth.

Leaf-Fall edge cases

When you cannot open The Turning Tree, hold to this. The door that Gives a Condition is open for one week in the tenth year, and a completed standing, whether a colour fell or the leaves hugged, under sound wood, happens once. A miss, a refusal, or a week spent under unsound wood makes the child unTurned, and it does not make them Kept. Struck remains the mercy that can still come later. You may correct a Speaking, the warden’s sentence about what the leaf did, and you may not rerun the fall itself. White-fire, the leaf that would name a Phoenix, is sent to the First Seat, and a town-warden does not guess that reading.

Starting situations

Start in one of these places, and stay with the one job the old walk left on that street. After a town has its own Tree, that job is one of three. Devotion is people keeping a walk they no longer need, either as an extra mile or as a wait at a Tree that may not speak. Prestige is a household paying for a winter, or a berth, for a walk they do not need. Necessity is a local Tree that is missing, young, or sick, or a week that cannot hold everyone who comes, so people use a neighbour’s standing, water, or bed. Give the place one of those jobs. A guest may bring a second into the same week, and the second is not the place’s theme.

Eolvaeth. People come here to wait, and the wait is the job. Vaethod, the town-warden, will not invent a colour. Saelid’s stall keeps feeding its winter guests, and those guests are the same households a sent cohort takes away. A stranger in the gift-hall has no list to stand on. Some years the wood says send the children on, toward a luckier Hand, and the gospel in the vale says stay. In a year when the Tree does not speak, a wet leaf lies on the spring, pilgrims from the core ask if it is a ribbon, and Eolvaeth will not say.

Orentel. The quay sells a winter to households who can pay for a walk they do not need, and that sale is the job. A First-Hand year, the prestige season at the origin, is assembled at three desks: a Night-Shore hull chartered at Braetu, the city on the shore that sells the ship, a term from the White Note, and a hold at Orentel, where Sorim keeps berths 1–4 empty because they are held. Orenbren houses the sleep once the year reaches the grove, and does not sell the year. Tesara works the stillers’ shed, and the shed does not face the street. Two streets off the third quay, a person too poor to meet a Tithe fades while the city steps around them. Salt sits on the Tree’s roots in Eolthael, the month that holds Turning-Week. People say it is the tide, the tide does not reach the rise, and Orentel will not say why the salt is there.

Maiethlir. Start the week before Leaf-Fall, when the thaw is loud. Clerks file that rise as snowmelt, the watchers do not, and Maiethlir will not say why. Rithim, the Speaker, will not give the clerk the line, and will Speak over the water. The wardens have recut a chapel, and a Watching room is under it, where Laevila keeps the only copy of the beam’s hidden face. The crown keeps a counted channel for a Far-Voiced hour and for the city’s green, and that channel can be shut. The extra mile is still walked here. The roll writes on top of that walk, and the walk remains.

Harrow’s Green. Start in Hale-month, the spring month when the land is counted sound. The year is Cut-year 387, the 387th summer counted from the First Cut. The job is a neighbour’s week that can still be walked home. Haelin wants the stone moved so the crowd can stand, and the water is still on it, because the stone is the day’s drink for anyone using the road as a mile. The upper room has extra guests. Children here Turn under this Tree. The hamlets can see the canopy and are still sending theirs. The cistern-dipper is hung with the bowl toward the stream, and Harrow’s Green will not say why.

Ornsael. The well is dropping, and the job is water. Theisva keeps the share, chalked on the lip, Lesna keeps the planting, and Bovaer still sends people west when the drink will not stretch through Hale-month. Pilgrims from the core arrive expecting a holiday walk and find a necessity-column already on the road. The well-rope is knotted at last year’s water-line, and this year’s knot is wet even when the water stands below it. Ornsael will not say why.

the Three Hamlets. Play the same week as Harrow’s Green. In clear weather the canopy is a dark on the far slope, and in rain it is a rumour. Brenod sends the child, Vaelun may refuse the walk because the children are already the land’s, and Ornath has looked at the other road, toward a slate and away from a Tree, without taking it. The job is the neighbour’s week. The night before, someone leaves a cup on the ford-rock. If it fills, they send, and if it does not, the tellings do not agree, while the child still goes, or does not, according to the kitchen and not according to the cup.

the Third Hearth. Thilim has made Seine’s bed and left it made. The extra mile is optional, and the house still keeps the bed. That is the job. Meirim, Brenthael’s warden, wants the stone taken down so the extra mile does not look like a requirement on the town’s approach. Seine’s name is on the lintel. The pot needs the stone’s water at dark, and the stone at the road is the day’s water. At dark, Thilim sets the yard-broom across the doorway and steps over it, and they will not say why.

Ndenjoo. Play the hall’s hospitality, and play the storm-wall as the weather. A wreck has walked uphill with the extra place already set, and a guest is loud at noon, when the hall sleeps. There is no Tree, so you seat the wreck, keep the kin who will not leave, and let someone want a crossing out. The session is the hall, and it is not spent proving what the Trees are.

Tone at the table

Play neighbours, colleagues, and family. The Tithe is where the danger sits, and Leaf-Fall is a warm week, so keep dread out of the Tree. When you need one moment of wrongness, use the weather, a host still keeping a guest from a week that ended, a week that already closed, or a person who missed the standing.

The Conditions are already the people in the world. There is no second vampire, no cursed wolf-kin, and no hungry dead who is not a Returned. The cart-ox, the terrace goat, and the path dog are livelihoods people keep, and they are not adversaries you drop into a fight.

Sample frames

Use one of these for a run of sessions. In each mainland frame, some people Turn under the Tree in town, and this year someone is still walking because living wood has not reached every hearth. Play both as the present. The Years of Hands are underway, which are the years a town Tree is the ordinary way to Turn.

A town where the planting is still arriving. Harrow’s Green, or the hamlets looking at its canopy, where the job on the street is a neighbour’s week. A pot of living wood may arrive, and it may not. Someone here is still sending this year’s children, while someone who thinks the planting is finished lives two weeks away and cannot see this canopy.

A quay that sells a winter. Orentel. A household that wants the prestige of a First-Hand year goes to three desks, a Night-Shore hull, a term from the White Note, and a hold at Orentel, and one desk does not finish the winter. Necessity still sleeps in the loft. Ledan, at the White Note desk, will convert a house-year, the house’s own count of summers, or a Cut-year, the wardens’ count from the First Cut, or a third date a court invented, if you say which. They will not invent the count for you.

An origin town with a roll. Maiethlir. The extra mile is still walked, and the clerks write on top of it. Rithim will not copy the clerk’s line. A Watcher will describe what they saw, and will not confirm it. The First Seat is in the wood beside the city, and can refuse what the city asks.

The hall on the isle. Ndenjoo, where hospitality is the rite, an extra place and a second night and a guest who can sleep the day, and the storm-wall is the weather. Play kin and a wreck. The session is not spent proving what the Trees are.

The first campaign has its own opening, in the GM’s chapter. It is not one of the starts above.

Dangers on the road

Settlements already have the things that can enter one of their scenes, a cohort, a crane, a well-mouth, so use this section for the country between those towns, the Long Mile, the wild of Heskoren, and the named waters. What threatens a traveler out here is people who missed their week, the animals on the road, and the weather, which is a real obstacle under ordinary travel.

Start battle points from the SRD: [(3 × PCs) + 2]. Spend: Minion group 1 · Support/Social 1 · Horde/Ranged/Skulk/Standard 2 · Leader 3 · Bruiser 4 · Solo 5. Benchmarks: Tier 1 Difficulty 11, thresholds 7/12, ATK +1; Tier 2 Difficulty 14, 10/20, ATK +2.

Name Tier / type Where it lives What it wants
Gap-Cat T1 Skulk Rain-Wall shelves, Heskoren ridge, mile-gaps A quiet kill, and then the high rock back
Chart-Crew T1 Horde Chart-run, Night Shore, West Water wrecks The hull that did not arrive, or yours if that one is gone
Bed-Keeper T1 Leader Empty road-houses on the Long Mile The bed occupied, and you staying in it
Spent-Week Walker T2 Standard Long Mile, west-road, live-front tracks To finish a tenth-year week that has already closed
Colourless Host T2 Support Dead pots, unsound grafts, waiting ground To Give a Condition the way a Tree would, which it cannot do

None of these stat blocks are Conditions. A walker may carry a Condition the way any person might, and the card they carry is not this block. The Spent-Week Walker and the Colourless Host are Tier 2 blocks, so in a Tier 1 scene you use the Tier 1 Difficulty, thresholds, and attack bonus from the benchmarks above in place of theirs.

You use one of these places as the scene, and you put a single adversary into it. An impulse is what the place does when you spend Fear, or when someone fails a roll to travel.

Mile-gap (T1 Traversal, Difficulty 12). This is the day’s walk between two mile-stones, and the next shrine depends on the weather rather than on a promise that the stone will be there. The place will stretch the day, hide the next stone, offer a false bed, or make a Tithe expensive. A Taken-In who cannot touch living green, or a Long-Lived with nothing new, feels the gap, but their next long rest runs the card’s check as usual and the gap adds no extra tick. Travel rolls to find the next shrine are Difficulty 12. Failure with Fear ends the day in the gap.

Thaw-gate (T1 Traversal, Difficulty 13). This is a shelf-gate or the Noon Pass in a thaw-week, when last year’s snow is the road you are walking this year. Crossing without a guide is Difficulty 13. On a failure, someone is swept, or a cart is lost, and one roll does not do both. Anyone who lived the Thaw-Break, in Cut-year 233, has Advantage on the next travel roll here if they say what they remember. Anyone who did not has to trust someone who did.

Empty road-house (T1 Exploration, Difficulty 11). This is a road-house the walking years left on the mile, a brenhael (BREN-hael), and it kept the upper room after the walk ended, with someone still making the bed. Guest-right is a week. If you eat, a host stands for the stay, and leaving before morning without a word is a slight the next shrine will hear.

Night-berth (T1 Exploration, Difficulty 12). This is a Chart-run or West Water quay at first dark, where a hull that does not arrive is counted as local weather. The place wants to wait, to take what the sea gives up, and to sell a stand, and it does not want to file a hill.

Pair a place with one danger. On the Long Mile inland, use a mile-gap and a Gap-Cat, and add a Spent-Week Walker if the table wants more. On the Long Mile where a house still keeps a bed from a week that ended, use an empty road-house and a Bed-Keeper. On the Rain-Wall, use a thaw-gate, and let the weather be enough. On the Chart-run or at Netstrand, use a night-berth and a Chart-Crew. At a dead pot on the live front, use one Colourless Host as Support, with walkers or a Gap-Cat, and never a second Host, because what a Host does is make the place worse. Near a town on the Near Mile, use what that town already sends into a scene. The storm-wall belongs with the isle, in Other Places, and it is not one of these road dangers.

Use a Colourless Host when a planting has gone wrong, or a pot never took. Skeptics and believers can both be loud about what that means, and the argument stays open.

Book XFor the GM

GM Canon

Read the player-facing chapters first if you want to meet the world the way a player would. The table does not start the campaign already knowing this chapter.

What follows is what is actually true, whether or not anyone alive can prove it. The central fact is the keystone: the Leaf-Mother is real and kind, her reach has a limit, and every gift costs her something to give. Skeptics who say there is no mind behind the Trees are sincere, and they are wrong about that mind. If a campaign ever confirms her, the moment should land as warmth, with an ache under it, because a mother who saves whom she can reach, and grieves the rest, is the one this world has.

A Tithe is the upkeep a person has to meet to live well with a Condition, the becoming that sits on top of the ancestry they were born with. The frightening edge of a Tithe is pressure in the story. It is never a trick you spring, and it never takes the player’s character out of the player’s hands. Consequences land on that person’s own body, memory, Stress, or the ground immediately around them, unless a feature on the card says otherwise. Nobody’s will is bent. Keep the frightening edge at about five percent, small enough that the day stays neighbours and work and the obstacle underneath stays real.

GM only: Conditions

The cards do not level. If a Condition is ever going to advance, that has to be a new decision, and you do not quietly write levels onto a card. There is one Phoenix Gift in the world. How a house can catch the fire, and what a hidden Phoenix player still gets to choose, is under Secrets and reveals later in this chapter. The population shares, including the warning not to count the Unbound twice, already sit in Kind and Condition. Do not keep a second census here.

Long-Lived. Going still is how a Long-Lived dies, which is what happens when the memories are gone, and that death is not a death move you drop into a fight. Across several long rests the player can see it coming: Stress, then a Hit Point, then the stillness. Use that as story pressure, a deathless archivist found statue-still in a sealed room, and do not use it as a sudden kill or as a spiral of Hit Points that will not clear. The fade before the stillness is a mind thinning. It is not a curse lying on every roll the character makes.

Blood-Read is how you investigate and how you let a scene feel something, because one drop, freely given or taken from a wound that is already open, shows a true memory you narrate, such as a dead man’s last sight or the reason a witness is lying. That drop is not feeding, not damage, and not a drain, and you do not spend it as a weapon in a fight. The threshold courtesy is the texture of a household. A Long-Lived can cross a threshold uninvited if they truly must, and they simply never do, because the manners run that deep. A foe who tries to put either habit on the sheet and call it a vampire rule has left the Condition.

Two-Bodied. The forced shift, which is the Tithe, is about timing and inconvenience. It nudges the player to live in both bodies, and it does not take the choice of action away. The other self is a partner in the roleplay, not a second player at the table. It can want, argue, sulk, and celebrate. The wolf pushes to give chase, and the cat refuses the cold water. It never rolls, never acts, and never overrides a choice the player made. If a table reaches “the animal made me do it,” pull the game back to nagging and let the player decide. Encourage the player to give the animal a name and a voice that is not their own. That name is the cheapest richness this Condition has.

This is the commonest Condition, about eighteen percent of people, so the free shift and the natural weapon are meant to be worth using in a scene. A hawk really flies, and an otter really swims, and you do not clip what the animal naturally does. What you do hold is the size, the ban on mythic beasts, and the fact that the animal body has no hands, no person’s mind, no speech, and no tools. A Two-Bodied can be a better animal than a Tengu, who is a person in the air, or one of the Answered, who use tools in the water, and cannot be a better person than either of them. One signature capability is the start, and a second comes only by a milestone in the story, so a veteran does not stack scout, tracker, and bruiser into one body. The natural weapon belongs to the animal body. It does not stack with a weapon the person-body is holding, because they are one body or the other, and its die does not rise when the character levels. Proficiency does.

Returned. Refuse to Fall means hard to keep down, which is a finite road and not immortality, because every use costs a scar, a Hope slot, the same mark any character spends when they brush death, and the table can watch the count fall. They leave the current scene and pull themselves together by the next long rest. When the last Hope slot would go, they cannot come back, and that is the true death, so a Returned near the end of their scars still feels a death move. Do not offer Avoid Death as an extra courtesy, because they already died, and the safe unconsciousness is what they spent when they did. A Purpose left to lapse, the unfinished work they came back to finish, is a quiet crisis, not a punishment you assign.

The hand that Strikes them has a name on this side of the screen. It is the Quiet Tally, Threnvaeth, the clerk of the Leaf-Mother’s household who keeps the unfinished work of the dead, and she acts under the Leaf-Mother’s allowance. The Leaf-Mother does not Give this Condition at the Tree. Threnvaeth authorizes the catch when the death comes with work still unfinished, and she does not steer that work. The Purpose stays the Returned person’s own. Player text does not name Threnvaeth.

Bound. Keep the Whisper strictly suggestive, plausible lies and intrusive thoughts which the player can reject by spending a Stress, and never puppet the character. The Pledge, the part of themselves they named to give when the contract ends, is a known and dreaded horizon toward the Unbound, whom people call the Hollow. It is not a surprise you save for the last session of the term.

The Counterparty who answers a sworn ask is Orledd, a Hand of the Leaf-Mother’s household. The face chosen at creation, whether demon, cosmic horror, or unknown, is a mask Orledd wears, and the terms underneath have the same shape whatever the face. Do not play Orledd as a devil, and do not let this turn a Given Condition into a bargain. During the term, what Orledd receives is the named ask remaining true, and the Terms being kept where other people can see them. At the end of a term-limited contract they collect the Pledge, which is already on the card. They do not take a soul, worship, or a second signing. The Given-Over, a Bound who signs again and again until the other side effectively holds them, is that person’s fear of paying, not Orledd’s hunger. A flood of unread bargains starves a Counterparty. How allowance strains and breaks is under The Other Hands.

Do not add the Hollow as a second percentage on top of Bound’s about five percent. The Unbound, about one and a half percent of people, are already inside that contract-lane. About three and a half percent are currently Bound. Listing both as parallel shares double-counts them.

The Unbound. The Quiet tempts. It does not compel. Every time the emptiness reaches for a bargain, they can refuse, and the refusal costs a Stress. The tragedy to play toward is an Unbound who stops connecting. The quiet inside gets loud, they sign again to mute it, they pay another Pledge, and they slide toward the Given-Over. Warmth, another person who knows their name and stays, is the only thing that actually fills the hole. A new contract only mutes it.

Keep three lanes apart when a table starts to blur them. Absence stops Stress, or Fear, that comes through the pledged hole, and it is not an immunity to every roll in the same broad lane. Quiet spends a token so the character can act anyway. The unshaken clause on the Returned is corpses, gore, and deathly places, and only the Returned have it. If a table is automatically passing every fear roll on both cards, pull the ruling back to those lines.

Far-Voiced. The Cry is a feeling that lands on listeners and costs them Stress, and it never forces an action or a belief. A Struck Far-Voiced arrives with the voice raw, so their first Cry, before any guild has had them, is a formative beat of how they became this, and you do not assign it as a punishment. A Given Far-Voiced deep in Tithe-debt, at no tokens, on duty in a courtroom or a relay tower, is a set-piece you build toward. It is not a surprise you spring.

The Stilled. The Gaze against an unwilling target is an attack, Instinct or Presence. A willing creature, or a creature that is down, needs no roll. A miss still adds a Grey token, the stillness already spent off the Stilled and onto the card, because the stillness has left them whether or not it landed. Stilled is a special condition, not the ordinary Restrained condition. Restrained only stops movement. Stilled stops the creature from acting. They can still speak, be moved, and be targeted, and they may mark a Stress to clear it when they would act. Do not apply both conditions unless some other effect has earned Restrained on its own.

The seizing, which comes when the Grey is full at three tokens, locks the Stilled’s own limb, or it locks harmless scenery. It never takes another player character’s turn, and it never forces an action. A Struck Stilled’s first, unpracticed Gaze, probably on someone they love and probably by accident, is the story of how they became this. A Given Stilled deep in Grey-debt on a riot line or in an operating theatre is a set-piece you build. The apprentices touch the knob first. The yard does not explain that drill, and a knob that has gone still is a practical tell of a seizing, not a relic.

The Answered. Every consequence at no tokens stays on the Answered and on the ground, air, or water immediately around them. Never force an effect onto another creature’s body, action, or will. Let the element the player chose become the character’s whole voice, because an Ember-Answered does not feel like a Root-Answered in a fight or in a quiet room. They ask. They do not own a servant, and nobody else is the master of what answered them. One of the Answered deep in Tithe-debt, walking into a crowded hall, a ship’s hold, or a dry archive, is a set-piece you build toward.

The Taken-In. Going to seed stays in the room around them, because the growth comes out of the ground and out of the structure, and the roots do not seize another creature or force an action. A Struck Taken-In’s uncertainty, whether they walked out or were sent, is a quiet dread about who they are. The wild in them is part of them, not a master and not a string someone else is pulling. One of the Taken-In dragged deep into a dungeon, down into a ship’s hold, or left inside a stone keep to wilt, is a set-piece you build.

Phoenix. You run two things at once. The count: let everyone watch the Hope slots go, and make each rising cost something the player feels, a face or the reason they started, not merely a mark on the sheet. The attention: a Phoenix on the open card is never anonymous. Seed every town with people who revere them, worship them, hunt them, and hate them, and let those often be the same crowd. Never force a Rise, because Rise From Ash is always the player’s choice among the death moves, beside the standard three, and a Phoenix may choose Blaze of Glory and end if the story has earned that ending. Fire immunity stays full, because a Phoenix is fire. The bonus to Evasion comes once per rest, and a Rise is a new body rather than a full resetting of the person. Played as a legendary non-player character, the rebirths make markers you can hang an era on: the same soul, met three times, remembering the party a little less each time.

The rule’s name is One Gift. There is never a second living Phoenix Condition while this one can still Rise. If the game seems to need two, the leftover is not a Phoenix. The house that catches the fire is the Protectors, and the rules they use, which they do not get to rewrite, are later in this chapter.

GM only: Peoples

Where a Kind lives, Kind meaning the ancestry a person is born into, tells you something about her reach only for the Yumboes. Mainland hearths are ordinary geography: foxes in the woods, seals on the coasts, crows on the ridges. A Kind-hearth is a people’s home ecology, not a nation. Kumbaan’s isolation is the one Kind-fact that also maps the edge of the keystone. There is no Tree there, no Gift, and the people are themselves without her. “Yumboes have no Conditions” is a fact about the place. It is not a racial immunity.

No power is founded for a Kind. A place where many Foxes live is a Rain-Shadow polity that happens to have many Foxes, and it runs on the same faith, the same reach, and the same government as everyone else. The moment a government exists for a Kind, Kind has become a country, and the two-layer model has broken, because Kind is what you are born and a Condition is what you become, and they stack. Factions recruit by Condition, by guild, and by faith. A tree-warden order that took only Kitsune would be that break. A town can have a fox-market, a Selkie quay, or a Tengu perch without the town being that Kind. Ornsael is the worked example: a market by the well, mixed Kinds, no gate.

A grandmother still says the word for the lost fourth Fox. If you use it, use the folklore that stayed when a hearth died, a dry lake that vanished or a wood that was cut. Nobody explains the word, and it is not a secret ancestry feature. A Fungril household sets one spoonful aside, and they will not say who it is for. That spoonful is the same kind of habit. Do not turn it into a feature, and do not decide who the spoon is for.

An ordinary introduction carries two names, a Kind and a place, and the players should hear both. It is not a secret identity. A Yumboe who takes a mainland second name has decided to stay. A Threnmaieth clerk who refuses to record hearth-names is following the roll, which wants the house, not the kitchen. Witness-lands use a byname. Threnmaieth, Trenledd, the Inner Close, and filing houses use an inherited house-name, said the way a surname is said, where a list has to find the person again.

Each polity’s vocabulary is how it excuses itself. It is not the truth of what it does. Threnmaieth’s “keeping-whole,” Threnhael, is a census that calls itself care. Lestrand’s “the free,” for the Kept, the people the Tree hugged and left without a colour, is a market reframing a social slight as a virtue. The Tree hugged them, with no colour and no Condition Given. Vaethorn’s “the Waited” wraps real pity in reverence. Confirming the Mother does not make any of those three names honest. They are how each society excuses its own injustice, and a kind Mother did not author the excuse.

The word-box and the how-to for naming a person live in Language and Naming. What the linguistics words mean, and the sound-change that makes a name wear the same way every time, is the next section.

GM only: Language

Language and Naming is where you name a person, mint a new one, glue a hall, and look up what a land calls a building. Keep that chapter as the how-to. This section is what the linguistics words mean, which sounds each way of speaking uses, and the regular wearing-down that lets you push any old word through a land and still have it sound like that land. Use it when you need a name that still belongs and the lists are not enough. It is not taught at the table.

What the linguistics words mean

Linguists have names for things everyone already does with speech. Here they are in this world’s terms, so a reader who has not opened the language chapter can still follow a name.

Word What it means here
Root The smallest chunk of meaning. oren means “to witness.” You glue roots to make names.
Lexicon The word-box. The list of roots you are allowed to build from. The old-word table in Language and Naming is the lexicon.
Compound Two roots glued. Thaeloren is thael (Tree) + oren (witness), said THAEL-or-en, with the stress on the first root.
Etymology Where a name comes from. Players hear a pretty word. You know Thaeloren means “the Tree that witnesses.”
Phonology Which sounds a language uses, and which it will not. English has th; many languages do not. Kusawe has sh and no th.
Syllable One beat of sound. Ra-ki is two syllables.
CV / CVC A recipe for a beat. C is a consonant, V is a vowel. CV is ra. CVC is tek. CVF in Kusawe means the beat may end on n, m, or r.
Stress The beat you hit harder. Capitals mark it. This is not the Stress a character spends to stay in a scene. A transparent compound, one you can still hear as two roots, stresses the first root: THAEL-or-en, VAETH-orn.
Digraph Two letters, one sound. ae is “ay” as in day. ai and ei are “eye.” eo is “ay-oh.”
Onset The consonant or cluster at the start of a beat. Kr in Kukra is an onset. Tengu likes those as ordinary speech. The Old Tongue only inherited a few.
Prenasal A hum before a stop: mb, nd, nk, nj. Yumboe uses them. The Old Tongue does not.
Register A way of speaking used for a job, not a whole language you write sentences in. Kusawe is the fox hearth-register: given names and in-group talk.
Liturgical / Old Tongue The church language, Maiethren. Like Latin: nobody’s first language at the market, still used for the rite and for old names.
Vernacular / common tongue What people actually say day to day. Worn-down Old Tongue. The Kept, the ranging, tree-wardens.
Daughter language / drift When one language splits into regional versions. Threnmaieth, Vaethorn, and Lestrand all come from Maiethren. They did not invent new tongues. They wore the same one differently.
Conservative A drift that kept the old sounds. Threnmaieth still says th.
Worn A drift that wore them down. In ordinary speech th after a vowel becomes t, and endings simplify. Written Vaethorn is spoken Wetorn. Careful prayer keeps the th.
Eroded A drift that sanded sounds off. Lestrand dropped th to t or d, or dropped it.
Sound-change A regular swap, not a one-off. If th becomes t on the docks, it does that in every word, not just one. That is why you can push any old word through the same rule and it will still sound like Lestrand.

You do not need the rest of a linguistics toolkit. There is no grammar to learn, and you do not dress English sentences in swapped vocabulary and call the result Maiethren. Nobody writes sentences in Kusawe, Sakoa, or Gonan. If a scene needs an in-group word, coin one word from that Kind’s sounds and say what it means in the same breath.

The Old Tongue’s sounds

The Old Tongue feels warm and weighty, a hall-and-hearth tongue. Liquids and nasals, l, r, m, and n, carry the warmth. The th of thin, and the long vowels, carry the weight. Clusters exist, and they are a small inherited set, not an invitation to pile consonants together.

Sounds it uses. Consonants: m n, l r w j, p t k, b d g, f v s h, and th as in thin. Vowels: a e i o u, plus the digraphs ae, ai, ei, and eo. An ordinary beat is an optional opening consonant, an optional r or l after it, a vowel that may be written as a digraph, and an optional closing consonant. The clusters the old words already use are br, cr or kr, st, str, and th plus r. Closings already in the language include sk and nd. Those patterns are what license bren, crae, stel, strand, thren, and hesk. A new root should prefer the simpler shape. Do not invent a three-consonant opening except str-, and do not invent a four-consonant knot.

Sounds it does not use. Prenasals, mb, nd, and nj, belong to Yumboe. Sh is a fox sound, not a church sound. Free front clusters such as gr and hr, and kr used as the ordinary feel of a name, belong to Tengu. The Old Tongue’s kr, as in crae, is one inherited word-shape, not that ridge habit.

How to say it. Capitals are the stressed beat. Th is as in thin, never as in the. Ae is “ay” as in day, ai and ei are “eye,” and eo is “ay-oh.” A is as in father, e as in bed, i as in machine, o as in go, and u as in moon. A simple root keeps the stress listed for it. A compound you can still hear as two roots takes its main stress on the first root and a lighter beat on the second, so the Awakening Tree is THAEL-or-en and the Waiting Land is VAETH-orn. Stress is not a rule that blindly hits the second syllable. Old ceremonial forms, and personal names, may keep a stress they already had, and the pronunciation given the first time you use the name is the one to trust.

The word-box is the old-word table in Language and Naming. Glue one or two roots. Then wear the compound the way the land wears it.

How an old word wears in each land

One Tree, with grafts carried out from it. One old tongue, with names wearing down as they travel. Linguists would call Threnmaieth, Vaethorn, and Lestrand daughter languages, three children of Maiethren. In this book they are the three drifts. There is no fourth human drift.

The sound-changes are regular. Push any old word through the same rule.

Drift Land What happens to the sounds How it feels
Conservative Threnmaieth, pious Maiethorn Almost nothing. Th and long vowels kept whole. Archaic, formal, holy. Sounds like the rite because it barely moved from it.
Worn Vaethorn, Heskoren folk Th after a vowel, or sitting between vowels, becomes t in speech (Vaethorn becomes Wetorn). Endings simplify. Unstressed vowels flatten. Careful prayer keeps the th. Rough-warm folk-speech that still reaches for the old holy words.
Eroded Lestrand, Strandoren docks Th becomes t or d, or drops. Long vowels clip. Word-ends wear off. Trade-words sneak in. Smooth, clipped, mercantile. The most worn name belongs to the least-devout place.

The same rule, worked through:

  • thael plus oren, kept whole, is Thaeloren (THAEL-or-en). That is the Awakening Tree, “the Tree that witnesses.” The worn everyday name is the Thallow.
  • vaeth plus orn, kept with th in writing, is Vaethorn. Spoken, it is Wetorn.
  • ledd plus strand, with the th already gone, is Lestrand.
  • thren plus maieth, kept whole, is Threnmaieth. The same thren worn to Tren is Trenledd: the sacred count with the sacred sanded off.
  • oren plus thael, with the th dropped, is Orentel. That is the salt-quay seat.
  • A devout river-town on a thaw, maieth plus lir, is Maiethlir, th kept.

A named power uses these roots and the drift that matches how it stands. Vaelhesk keeps the older vael, what the land yields, and the frontier hesk-. That is still this family, worn further. Kumbaan is not in this family.

Coinage is frozen. Do not make another liturgical compound merely because two familiar roots fit. The families closed to new compounds are eol-, sael-, vael- and vaeth-, bren-, maieth- and thren-, -oren, and -hael. The words that already exist remain. What is still available, and should be used sparingly, is orn, lir, neth, ledd, hesk, strand, stel, and crae, and a new use still has to be said out loud next to the names it might be mistaken for. Two cants stay unused and should not be fleshed out: Orenvaeth and Thaelneth. Aeloren is retired. Eolstrand is retired in favour of the Hinge Shore.

Family Existing words that remain Ruling
eol- Eolthael, Eoloren, Eolvaeth Closed. Eolstrand retired; the name is the Hinge Shore.
sael- Saelthael, Saelvaeth, Saelorn, Saelhael, Ornsael Closed. Use common handles in speech.
vael- / vaeth- Vaethorn, Vaelhesk, Vaeloren, Vaelbren, Vaelun, Vaethledd, Maiethvael, Leddvael, Thaelvaeth, Brenvaeth Closed. The final th is too slight a spoken distinction to carry another category.
-oren Thaeloren, Vaeloren, Leddoren, Eoloren, Nethoren, Orenhael, Orenbren, Orentel, Heskoren, Strandoren Closed. Aeloren retired.
bren- Brenvaeth, Brenorn, brenhael, Brenthael, Brenledd, Brenod Closed.
maieth- / thren- Maiethren, Maiethorn, Maiethvael, Maiethlir, Threnmaieth, Trenledd, Threnhael Closed.

Place-names and house coinages stay off the person-list. Do not name a person Vaethorn, Lestrand, Threnmaieth, Thaeloren, Maieth, Kumbaan, Ndeyaan, Haelthael, Leddoren, or Vaeloren, and do not give them Orenhael, Thaelvaeth, Nethoren, Leddhael, Vaelbren, Njaalo, Njawaal, or Vaethledd. The squares Ornsael, Brenthael, Brenod, Vaelun, Ornath, and Harrow’s are reserved the same way, and so are the seats Eolvaeth, Orentel, and Maiethlir, and the hall Ndenjoo.

Why the drifts sit where they sit

People in the world will tell you that names wear down with distance and trade. That reading is true as far as it goes. The daughters drift furthest where the Trees are thinnest, and the deeper pull that keeps the old sound near the Trees is the Mother’s nearness. Same fact, two readings. Player text does not state the deeper one.

History adds a mechanism you can play. The pilgrimage itself was a conserving pull, because people from far away walked to the same grove each year and the old sound got refreshed. Local Trees then let the daughter drifts grow in the place where people lived, so the change of the Years of Hands sits on a root the Walking Years had held closer.

Thaeloren is not decoration. The name means “the Tree that witnesses.” She is real, and the Leaf-Fall, the tenth-year ceremony when a leaf chooses a child, is her seeing each child. The language keeps a truth the skeptics have explained away. Player text does not call that mere poetry. Let a scholar notice it, or save it for a reveal late in a campaign.

The four Kind registers

Each custom Kind has a register, a closed set of sounds for given names and in-group talk. It is not a language you write sentences in. The lists in Language and Naming are what you pick from. These inventories are how you mint a new name that still belongs.

Kitsune: Kusawe (koo-SAH-way). Light, slipping, a little hissy.

At the table

  • Consonants k s sh n r m t w y f h
  • Vowels a i u e o, and ai as in eye
  • Beats CV, or CV ending on n, m, or r. Two or three beats.
  • Never uses th (church), mb/nd/nj (Yumboe), kr/gr (Tengu)

Selkie: Sakoa (sah-KOH-ah). Liquid, rounded, coastal.

At the table

  • Consonants l r n m s v f d b k w
  • Vowels o u a i e, and ea, oa
  • Beats CV or CVC. Two or three beats.
  • Never uses th, sh, kr/gr, mb/nd/nj

Tengu: Gonan (GO-nan). Clipped, windy, high-country. The names start hard, on a single consonant or on kr, gr, or hr. This is ridge-speech, not the fox register, and Tengu and Kitsune do not share one.

At the table

  • Consonants k t g n r h s b d. Front clusters kr, gr, hr are at home.
  • Vowels a o u e. Few i (that vowel lives with the foxes).
  • Beats CVC or CV. One to three beats, prefer two.
  • Never uses th, sh, mb/nd/nj, long ai/ea/oa

Yumboe. Not Maiethren. Open vowels, a drum-like rhythm, prenasals mb, nd, nk, and nj. Their own name is Bakhna Rakhna, “the good people.” Home is Kumbaan, “the hidden home.” It has no th, and it is not clipped down to a dock-name.

A name that bleeds across registers is a tell. A Selkie named Wishi, or a Tengu named Maethaem, was raised away, adopted, or is passing. Use it on purpose, or do not use it at all. If the first fox-name that comes to mind is Yuki, throw it back. Same for Morag on a Selkie and Kenji on a Tengu. Pick from the middle of the existing list, or build from the inventory above until the name could sit next to Raki, Lavo, or Teku without anyone blinking.

The player recipe stays in Language and Naming: pick from a list, or use the make-another steps, or glue two old words and wear them for the land. The inventories above are the same registers written as sound-lists, so a new name can be checked against the rule. The sound-change table is how you push any old word through a land without inventing a fourth human drift.

GM only: Society and Faiths

The Leaf-Mother exists. The Turning Trees are genuinely her hands, so when a Tree chooses, she is choosing. A scion is a grafted town Tree, continuous living tissue of the one Awakening Tree. The Conditions are real gifts. The Leaf-Fall is an act of love: she looks at a child and gives them a becoming the world will need and that they can carry. The Tithe is the honest weight of that gift, not a hidden price and not a trap. She is kind and finite. She cannot lay a hand on every child, cannot reach every threshold in time, and cannot give without spending. The limit is real. She is doing her best against it. A mother who could save everyone and did not would be sinister. That is not the mother this world has.

The Kept are spared, and some of them are simply past her edge. A hug and no colour is, for most, a deliberate and kind choice, the gift of being left whole. The constraint means the Kept are not all one thing. Some were chosen for wholeness, and some are children she could not reach far enough to give to this turning, held safe rather than gifted. She does not tell them apart, and neither can they. Both are held. Not both are chosen. No later week is offered to sort them. The Given-door is one week, a completed standing is once, and a miss is not a retry.

The Struck are still hers, at the farthest reach of her arm. She Gives at the Tree and does not Strike, so the catch at a later door, a death, an oath, a drowning, stone, or the deep wild, is enacted by lesser gods of her household, each restricted to one door, working under her allowance. The Struck are still hers because those hands are hers to send. Narrow-Hand, the reading that she only Gives at the Tree, is right about that limit. Wide-Hand, the reading that the Struck are still hers, is right about belonging. Neither holds the whole.

Her kindness is cosmological, not social. She authored the gifts. She did not author the injustice built on top of them. Confirming that she is real and kind must not make the society just. The keystone answers whether anyone is there and whether they mean well, and the answer is yes. It does not answer whether what people built around her is fair, and often it is not. Protect that gap. That is where the play is. The queue for a scion, the suspicion that follows an unvouched Struck person, the over-watching of the Bound, the guild that conscripts the Given, Tithe-need used as leverage, the Kept pitied as spare, the Given-Over’s lost personhood, the lintel recut over an older faith, the book that will not close, the host of a dying guest, the sentence that will not travel, the week that will not end, the gate, the scheduled hour, the Grey used as labour, the shop you cannot leave, and the week no one writes: these are things people built. A kind Mother does not dissolve them.

The three corners do not share a mechanism. Vaethorn’s injustice is a guilt-theology of unworthiness. Lestrand’s is a market that lets the poor fade. Threnmaieth’s is a sanctified census. Confirming she is kind does not make any of the three fair. Rival faiths can be used as leverage. Dissent is not automatically the moral good. The same confirmation does not dissolve Threnmaieth’s counting of heretics, Lestrand’s priced fading, or Vaethorn’s guilt.

The household is still GM-only. She is first of a household. She Gives, and lesser Hands Strike at restricted doors under her allowance. Player text does not confirm this. The Open Table’s staying-kin are not of that household, and Kumbaan is not part of it.

Each rival holds a true kernel and misses the whole.

The Watching correctly remembers a Before, and a cost, and a household from before that household was named Mother. They miss that the seeing is hers. The Masked reading, that she is a later face, and the Bare Tree reading, that there was never a she, are both playable. Neither is the answer, and the lintel is a clue, not a verdict. The cost they remember is real. What was spent is still the open nature of her limit. They get no seat in a late reveal, because that would turn the heretics into a second Motherfaith. The warmth lands through them, not as them.

The Fair Hand is right that a Counterparty exists for the Bound, and wrong that every becoming is a bargain. The Mother’s Gifts are still gifts. They have misread a cost as a price, and they have correctly felt that giving is not free. They are not devil-worshippers. A Book-hand cannot turn a Given child into a debtor, and cannot rewrite the Counterparty’s clause. A petition-watch is keeping the door. It is not the authority of an acolyte.

The Old Ways are right that land-doors are real. They miss that she authorized the guests. Keep the grievance real: the grafts are late, and the Motherfaith did talk as if becoming were new. Keep the miss intact. Ancestor-meals are not the Returned. The dead in the ground are kin who remained. The Returned are a different door.

The Open Table is the cleanest experiment: no Gifts, rare Struck, a faith that was never hers. Their claim, that they were never lacking, is still a late beat. They are not ghosts. The unseen hands do ordinary household work. “No one is a stranger twice” is courtesy with legal weight on the isle, and a proverb on the quay. It is not a geas, which would be a binding spell, and it is not a trap-cult, and it is not a Fair Hand contract. A wreck is not a Struck-door she authorized.

If a campaign works toward the keystone, the three old corners are the Watching, the Old Ways, and the Open Table: pre-Mother, pre-graft, and never-grafted. The Fair Hand is the modern misreading, commerce wearing a theology. Use all four. No one of them speaks the reveal for the others.

The Tree is something players can see, and it sits next to the keystone. “Every Tree is literally the one Tree’s hand” is the physical fact that, followed to its end, confirms she is real and present. Present that as doctrine the faithful hold, never as demonstrated cosmology. Skeptics grant the grafting and deny the mind. The Tree is not eerie, and the ceremony is not sinister. Dread lives in individual Tithes, not in the rite.

Use the schism again. The three questions, what a hug means, what a Struck becoming means, and whether a mind is there, keep supplying people, factions, and family arguments. No player-facing scene awards the win to either branch. Believers see the hand and miss the edge. Skeptics see the edge and miss the hand. The world is built so that being a skeptic costs nothing day to day, which keeps the argument poignant. It does not turn the skeptics into a joke.

The Child at Four Doors. The paradox is the point. The child cannot pick a door without already having been claimed, and cannot be claimed without picking. Each faith makes the middle bearable by deciding that its door was the one that had been open the whole time. None of the last lines is the true cosmology. The true cosmology is that a mother reached, at cost, and did not reach everyone the same way. The fable will not say that. Which ending a person offers is a faster read of their stance than a speech about doctrine. There is no official fifth door. The Open Table already refuses the frame of four. A children’s story does not settle the keystone. Save the warmth for the confirming beat, if it ever comes.

The Orenhael are the tree-wardens, and the everyday name is tree-wardens. The liturgical name in use is Orenhael, and that form is still polishable the way the household names are. They are right about the wood and incomplete about the hand. Every scion is continuous tissue of the one Tree, and when any warden Speaks a colour they are naming a choice she made. Present them as competent neighbours, not as people who secretly know. A skeptic town-warden is good at the job and wrong about the mind. The Seat runs believer-heavy. A skeptic Speaker at the grove is possible, and uncomfortable. The split is the queue, not the Tree. The Seat sees soil and carrying-earth. The hamlet past the ford sees another year of borrowed Turnings. Which town gets the next graft is a human rationing of her reach. Threnmaieth does not own the Seat. Being near it is pressure, not ownership. A First Seat that was the Threnhael would be a darker setting. Keep the college able to refuse the roll.

The Slide. They do not know what story they are in. They think they are in a rent-and-credit story. They want the week to continue, not a victim they relish, and a corpse is a ruined asset. Play them as patient, useful, and sure they helped. The town is complicit, because the town is glad not to see the Cry, and the week-keeper is not the only villain. Official Tithe-halls and the licence-guilds are the public, posted, counted version of furnishing. This house is the overflow those guilds pretend not to know, and a gate that closed on purpose can now meet them at the table.
